fields.title: Morning Comes
fields.subtitle: The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, Book Six
fields.description: The last book of the series. Wren, Tobin, Mira and Aren sail into the Sunless Sea, where no boat has gone for three hundred years, to Nightfall Spire: the Umbral Queen's tower, where the greyed stand in silent halls, where Tobin's father waits in a cell, and where Ardric, the king who sold the sun, sits on a throne and cannot die. What the Queen took must be given back, and what Ardric holds can only be let go. Then the long night comes down over Gloamhaven, and the road runs north to the Bright Mountain, and morning.
fields.about_html:
Morning Comes is the sixth and last book of The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, an adventure series by James DeGreef and Ochorus for readers aged nine to twelve. It follows on from The Midsummer Flame, and is best read after the first five books.

This is the book of the ending. Every promise the series makes is kept: lost parents found, an old friend not lost but waiting, a song finished, the sun golden again. It is about letting go of what we grasp, about carrying the light until morning, and about the morning itself, when everything is made new. Like the books before it, it never preaches; it lets the story speak for itself, for children to discover and for parents to talk about.

The book has fifteen chapters, about the length of a classic children's fantasy, each one a good evening's reading.

qa.question: Is Morning Comes the last book?
qa.answer: Yes. It is the sixth and final book of The Lamplighters of Gloamhaven, and it brings every thread of the series home.

qa.question: Do I need to read the first five books first?
qa.answer: Yes. Morning Comes carries straight on from The Midsummer Flame, and its biggest moments answer questions the series has asked since its first chapter.

qa.question: What age is Morning Comes for?
qa.answer: Readers aged nine to twelve. It has real danger and one gentle death, told without anything gory, and it ends in great joy.

qa.question: Who is Ardric?
qa.answer: The king who, three hundred years ago, bargained the sun's fire out of the sky on the Bright Mountain. He has kept it in his crown ever since and cannot die. The book tells how he lets it go.

qa.question: Does Wren find her parents?
qa.answer: Yes. Tam and Linnet Ashby, taken from Emberwick's wall when Wren was four, are found in the Queen's tower, and at last Wren hears the rest of her mother's song.

qa.question: Is it a Christian book?
qa.answer: Yes. Like the classic Christian fantasies, it tells its truths as story rather than sermon: a long night, a return no one can earn, and a morning in which all things are made new. It never names God or preaches.

qa.question: How long is the book?
qa.answer: Fifteen chapters and about fifty-six thousand words, much the length of a classic children's fantasy.

fields.title: The Black Water
fields.body_html:
The fishing village of Skerrow lay at the bottom of the cliffs where the Harrowgate Highlands fell into the sea, and it was the last place in Gloamhaven.

That is what the people of Skerrow said, anyway, and they said it with a sort of gloomy pride. The last place. Beyond it there was nothing: only the headland, a long black arm of rock reaching out into the water; and beyond the headland, the Sunless Sea. You could see where it began. The ordinary sea in the bay at Skerrow was grey, the way all the sea in Gloamhaven was grey — grey-green in the shallows, grey-blue further out, with grey waves and white foam and grey gulls crying over it. But past the end of the headland, as if somebody had drawn a line across the water with a ruler, it went black. Flat black, and still, like ink in a dish. And nothing came back from it: no gull, no wave, no light.

The fisherfolk of Skerrow fished with their backs to it. They had done so for three hundred years.

“Daft,” said Skipper Mairi Dunlop. “Daft as a brush. The lot of us.”

She was standing on the harbour wall in the grey dawn with her great red hands on her hips, looking out at the black line beyond the headland as if it owed her money. She was about sixty, and broad as a barrel, and her face was the colour and texture of an old leather boot that has been left out in the weather for a long time and enjoyed it. She wore three jerseys, one on top of another, and a pair of enormous sea-boots that had belonged to her grandmother, which she swore by.

“Three hundred years,” she said, “we’ve sat in this harbour and looked the other way. Never once put out a line past the Skerry. Never once asked what’s out there. Just turned our backs on it, like a lot of hens that think if they can’t see the fox it can’t see them.” She spat into the water. “Well, I’m sixty-one and I’ve had the Flame in me since the siege, and I’m done with it. Somebody has to be daft first.”

“Daft first,” said Wren.

“Then everybody,” said Mairi Dunlop, and grinned, so that her whole leather face cracked into creases. “That’s how it goes, hen. Somebody’s got to be daft first. And then everybody else sees it’s not so bad, and they’re daft too.” She clapped Wren on the shoulder so hard that Wren nearly went off the wall. “Come and see my boat.”

Her boat was called the Brave Gannet, and it was the oldest boat on the coast.

It was not very big. It was a broad, deep, heavy fishing-boat with one mast and a brown sail — a real brown, Mira said, staring at it, the colour of a fox’s back; the Flame had been in Skerrow a fortnight — and a little cuddy at the front where you could get out of the rain if you did not mind sharing it with the nets. It had been painted once, a long time ago, and the paint had mostly come off. It smelt overpoweringly of fish. It had been built by Mairi’s great-grandfather, she said, out of oak from a wood that wasn’t there any more, and it had been patched so often that there was probably not one plank left of the first boat; but it was still the Gannet, and it still floated.

“Most days,” said Mairi.

Tobin looked at the boat for a long time, and then at the black line beyond the headland, and then at the boat again, and opened his mouth.

“Don’t,” said Mira.

“I was only going to ask—“

“I know what you were going to ask. Don’t.”

Tobin shut his mouth.

There were to be nine of them on the Gannet.

Mairi Dunlop, the skipper. Her two grandsons, Callum and Rab, great silent red-headed lads of sixteen and seventeen who could haul a net single-handed and were terrified of their grandmother. Wren, with the lamp. Tobin, with Ash’s pole and his mother’s compass and a bag of tools and three notebooks, one of them entirely full of sums about the speed of boats. Mira, with the Chronicle. Aren. And Cinder.

And Sister Hale.

Nobody had wanted Sister Hale to come. That is to say, everybody had wanted her to come very much, and nobody had thought she should. She was old, and lame, and her arm was only just out of its sling. The Sunless Sea was four days away, Aren said, if there was wind; and nobody knew if there was ever wind. And at the end of it was the Queen’s own tower.

“So you should stay in Harrowgate,” Wren had said. “And look after everybody. Like you did on the Hill. You’re good at it.”

“I am good at it,” Sister Hale had agreed. “Very good. Best there is.” She had been sitting on the bench outside the Black Bull, with her crutch across her knees, and she had looked up at Wren with her one bright eye. “And I’ve waited seventy years, duck. Seventy years in barns and cellars and ditches, singing his songs with my back to the wall and the Guild going by on the road. I waited on the Hill. I waited for Midsummer. I’ve waited my whole life for him to come back, and I’ll go on waiting till he does.” She had patted Wren’s knee. “But I’m not waiting here. Not while you lot go off to the end of the world without me. I’m coming.”

“But—“

“I’m coming, duck.”

So she was coming.

Half of Harrowgate came down the cliff path to Skerrow to see them off, and most of Skerrow, and all of the Remnant who had come with Sister Hale’s carts, and Bracken, who was going back to Emberwick that same day to take the Beacon back from Mott — “before he gives the whole Ring away, lass, and the wall with it” — and the Heskeths, and the children of Stallbridge. They stood all along the harbour wall in the grey morning, and on the rocks, and in the doorways of the tarred fish-huts, holding up their lamps and candles and bare glowing hands. Even in the daylight, even under the pale sun, the whole harbour of Skerrow shone gold with them.

Nettle was not there.

Wren looked for her everywhere. Nettle had been told — very firmly, by everybody, again — that she was not coming on the boat. Not this time. Not to the Spire. She was going back to Emberwick with Mrs Fenn’s eldest and Bracken, in the bakery cart, and that was final. And Nettle had said nothing at all, which was not like Nettle; and that morning, when everybody else came down the cliff path, she was nowhere to be seen.

“She’s sulking,” said Mrs Fenn’s eldest. “She’ll be in the cart. Sulking. She’ll get over it.”

But Wren did not like it.

They said their goodbyes. It took a long time.

Bracken shook Wren’s hand, the way he had on the morning after the Ring was lit, a year ago; and then, rather awkwardly, hugged her, helmet and all. “You come back,” he said. “You hear me, lass? You come back. And bring that Warden of mine.” He looked over her head at Tobin. “Bring him, I said.”

“I will,” said Tobin.

Will Hesketh did not say anything. He put his big warm hands on Wren’s shoulders for a moment, and that was all, and it was enough.

Sister Hale was helped down into the Gannet by four people, and sat down in the stern on a coil of rope, and arranged her crutch, and announced that she felt very well and was looking forward to it enormously; and then the boat moved, a little, on its mooring, and she went the colour of an old cabbage and said nothing else for some time.

And Aren stood on the harbour wall at the very end, by himself, looking out at the black line.

He had been quiet all morning. Quieter than usual. Wren had seen people on the wall look at him — the Skerrow men, especially, the ones who had been Knights, and come home after the siege, and had their names given back. They did not look at him with fear, any more. They looked at him the way you look at somebody who is about to go back into a burning house.

“It’s all right,” said Wren. She had come up beside him without meaning to. “You don’t have to come. Nobody’d think—“

“I do have to,” said Aren.

He did not look at her. He was looking out past the Skerry at the flat black water, where the light did not come back.

“I took them there,” he said. “Your mother and father. Harrowgate’s father. Thousands of them. I took them all. Every one.” He was rubbing his palm; then he noticed, and stopped, and opened his hand and looked at the gold line shining across it. “I’m the only one who knows the way in. I’m the only one who knows the stairs.” He closed his hand again. “I have to go back, Wren. I have to be the one who goes back for them.”

Wren did not say anything. After a moment, she nodded.

They cast off at the turn of the tide.

Callum and Rab rowed them out across the bay, with long sweeps, the Gannet wallowing and creaking, until they were clear of the harbour; and then Mairi Dunlop put up the brown sail, and the grey morning wind off the land filled it, and the Gannet leaned over and began to move.

Everybody on the harbour wall cheered.

Wren stood in the bow with Cinder on her shoulder and watched them get smaller — the lights on the wall, and the waving arms, and the tarred huts, and the cliffs going up behind to the edge of the Highlands, where the heather was. She had never been on a boat before, except the Ferryman’s, a year ago, in the mist on the Gloam River. It was different from walking. The ground moved. Everything moved. It was like riding a very large, very slow, very wet animal that had its own ideas about where it was going.

And then, from somewhere at the back of the boat, a voice said, quite clearly, “Thtop thquashing me.”

Everybody turned round.

In the stern of the Gannet, beside Sister Hale, was a pile of lobster pots: big domed wicker baskets, stacked up and lashed together, that Mairi had not had time to unload. And the top one was moving.

It wobbled. It rocked. It said “Ow.” And then its lid came off, and out of it, like a jack-in-the-box, sticky with fish-scales and bits of weed and smelling indescribably of old lobster, came Nettle.

There was a long silence on the Brave Gannet.

“NETTLE,” said Wren.

“I’m coming,” said Nettle. She climbed out of the lobster pot with enormous dignity, and stood up in the stern, and folded her arms. There was a small crab hanging on to one of her plaits. “I’m coming, Wren. You can’t thtop me. I’m coming to get your mam and dad.”

“You are not—“

“I am. Becauthe you alwayth go. You alwayth go away and leave me and I wait and wait and you never even thend a letter and I’m not doing it any more.” Her chin was out and her face was red and her eyes were full. “I’ve got the Flame. Same ath you. Same ath anybody. He gave it me. Tho I can come.”

“Nettle—“

“I lit an oven.”

Wren looked at her. At her small furious floury face, with the crab on its plait, and the tears running down it; and her two new front teeth; and the little gold glow coming faintly off her clenched hands. And Wren thought — she could not help it — of herself. Of herself at eight, in Mott’s yard, being told for the hundredth time that she was too small, and too poor, and too nobody, for anything at all; and setting her chin exactly like that.

“Turn the boat round,” she said to Mairi Dunlop.

Nettle burst into tears.

They put her ashore at the end of the harbour wall.

It was the hardest thing Wren had done since the Moffats’ weaving-room. Mairi turned the Gannet — grumbling, but quite gently — and Callum and Rab rowed her back in, against the tide, to the steps at the very end of the wall where the crowd was still standing, staring. And Wren lifted Nettle up out of the boat, lobster-smell and crab and all, and handed her up to Bracken, who took her under one arm like a parcel.

Nettle did not fight. She did not kick, or scream, or shout, which Wren had been ready for. She only cried, quietly, the way she used to cry when she was cold in the garret, with her face turned away.

Wren climbed up two steps of the harbour wall, so that her face was level with Nettle’s.

“Nettle,” she said. “Listen. Listen to me.” She took the small sticky face in both hands and turned it round. “I’m not going away and leaving you. Not this time. Not like before. I’m going to get them. My mam and dad. And Tobin’s da. And all of them. And then I’m going to bring them home. To Soot Lane. To the bakery.” She swallowed. “And I need somebody there. When I get back. Somebody to keep the Flame in the lane. Somebody to light every door, so it’s lit when I come. So I know where home is.” She held on. “Will you do it? For me? Will you keep it lit?”

Nettle looked at her for a long time, with her lip shaking.

“Promith?” she said. “Promith you’ll come back?”

“I promise.”

“You alwayth thay that.”

“And I always do,” said Wren.

Nettle considered this. She was still crying. But she reached up, slowly, and took the crab off her own plait, and gave it to Wren, very solemnly, as if it were something precious.

“Keep it,” she said. “For luck.”

Wren put the crab in her pocket. It nipped her, all the way out of the harbour.

And so they went out past the Skerry.

The headland went by on the left, long and black and wet, with the grey sea breaking white against the foot of it; and the end of it came up, a jagged rock with a single stunted tree on top, bent sideways by the wind. And beyond it, the line.

Wren stood in the bow and watched it come.

It came closer slowly, the way the shore of a river comes closer when you are rowing across. Grey water — grey water — the little grey waves slapping at the Gannet’s bow, the gulls crying overhead, the wind cold and salt in her face. And then, right in front of them, as if somebody had drawn it with a ruler: black.

The Gannet’s bow went over the line.

And the gulls stopped.

That was the first thing. Wren had not even noticed the gulls until they stopped; they had been crying over the boat all morning, wheeling and calling, the way they always did at sea. And the moment the bow crossed into the black water, every gull turned in the air at once, and went back. Back to the Skerry, back to the grey water, back to the land. Not one of them followed. And in the silence after them Wren could hear, very clearly, the creak of the Gannet’s mast, and the slap of the brown sail, and Sister Hale being sick over the side.

The second thing was the water.

It was not like water. It was flat, and black, and thick-looking, like oil, or ink. It did not have waves — not real ones — only a long, slow, heavy heave, as if something very big were breathing underneath it. It did not make a sound against the hull. And when Wren leaned over the bow and looked down into it, nothing came back. No reflection. Not of the Gannet, or the brown sail, or the grey sky, or her own face. She took the lamp out of her coat and held it out over the side, so that its gold light fell on the black water, the way it would fall on a puddle in Soot Lane, and there should have been a little gold lamp shining back up at her from the sea—

There was nothing.

The light went into the black water and did not come back. As if the sea were drinking it.

The third thing was the cold. It came up through the planks of the boat, from below, into the soles of their feet. It was not like the cold of the Hollows, which came at you; it was a slower cold, heavier, patient, the cold of a cellar that has been shut for a long time.

Wren put the lamp away inside her coat again, against her ribs, where it was warm.

“Well,” said Mairi Dunlop, at the tiller, into the silence. Her leather face was set, and her great red hands were very steady. “That’s the gulls gone, then.”

And she set the Gannet’s course east, by Tobin’s compass, out into the Sunless Sea.

They sailed all day.

The wind off the land held, a little, cold and thin, and filled the brown sail, and the Gannet went on east over the black water with no sound at all except her own creaking. The land went down behind them, slowly — the Skerry, and the cliffs, and the dark line of the Highlands — until it was only a grey smudge, and then not even that. The sky was grey. The sea was black. There was nothing else.

Tobin sat in the waist of the boat with the compass open on his knee and watched the needle. It pointed east, and stayed east, and was warm.

Mira sat beside Sister Hale, holding her hand and the Chronicle at the same time.

Aren stood in the bow, alone, looking forward into the grey, and did not move for hours.

And Sister Hale — once she had finished being sick, which took most of the morning — sat up in the stern on her coil of rope, very pale, and wiped her mouth on her shawl, and began, in a thin cracked voice that got slowly stronger, to sing.

It was the Psalm. Though I walk through the gloaming. She sang it out over the black water, the way she had sung it in barns, and the black water did not give one note of it back. It went out from the boat and did not echo. It was like singing into a pillow. And she sang it anyway, all the way through, every verse, including the one with the goat in it.

And one by one, they all joined in.

The dark came down at the end of the day, the way it always did in Gloamhaven, quickly, like a lid.

But it was different out here. On the land, even on the blackest night, there was always something: a Ring-lamp on a wall far off, or a glimmer of moon behind cloud, or the faint grey of the sky over the edge of the world. Out on the Sunless Sea, when the dark came down, it came down all the way. The Gannet was a little island of gold in it — the lamp in Wren’s coat, and Mira’s candle, and the glow of everybody’s hands — and outside that little circle of gold, in every direction, there was nothing. Not black water. Not sky. Nothing at all.

Wren lay in the bottom of the boat on a heap of nets, with Cinder against her and Nettle’s crab asleep in her pocket, and looked up.

Tobin was lying beside her, looking up too. After a while she heard him draw in his breath.

“Wren,” he said, very quietly.

“What?”

“There aren’t any stars.”

She looked.

He was right. Even on the cloudiest nights in Gloamhaven, even through the grey, there was always a star somewhere — one, at least, very faint, low down, the kind you only see if you don’t look straight at it. Wren had found them from the roofs of Soot Lane since she was six; it was the only thing up there worth looking at.

There were none. Not one. The sky over the Sunless Sea was as black and flat and empty as the water under it, from one side to the other; and the little boat with its little gold light lay between the two of them, in the middle of nothing, going east.

Tobin felt for the compass in the dark, and opened it, and put his finger on the glass.

“Still warm,” he said.

“Good,” said Wren.

And after a long time, with the lamp against her ribs and the fox against her stomach, she slept.

fields.title: The Drowned Fleet
fields.body_html:
On the second day out, the wind died.

It did not die all at once. It got thinner, through the morning, the way a candle gets thinner when the wax runs low; and the brown sail of the Gannet, which had been filled and round, went slack and began to flap, and then to hang; and by noon — if it was noon; it was very hard to tell, out there, with the sky the same flat grey from one edge to the other and no sun showing in it at all — there was no wind whatever. The sail hung down from its yard like washing on a still day. The Gannet sat on the black water, and did not move.

“Well,” said Mairi Dunlop. “That’s the wind gone, then.”

She said it in exactly the same voice as she had said that’s the gulls gone, and Wren began to understand that this was how Skerrow folk said everything, from it’s raining to the house is on fire.

“What do we do?” said Tobin.

“Row,” said Mairi.

So they rowed.

Callum and Rab took the long sweeps, one on each side, and pulled; and when they were tired Aren took one, and Tobin the other, and then Wren and Mira together on one sweep, which did not work at all, because Mira pulled in time and Wren did not; and then Callum and Rab again. Sister Hale sat in the stern and sang to give them the stroke. Cinder sat in the bow and looked forward. And the Gannet crept on east across the Sunless Sea at about the speed of an old man walking, with the compass warm on Tobin’s knee, and the black water closing up behind the blades of the oars without a ripple, as if they had never been there.

It was the longest day Wren had ever known.

It was on the third day that the singing-stone began to hum.

Wren felt it first: a buzz against her hip, through her coat pocket, like a bee in a jar. She took it out. It was the smooth grey stone the Delvers had given her in the Deeps — it hears the cold, they had said — and it lay in her palm and trembled, and hummed, a low thin note that went up and down.

“Hollows,” said Aren. He had turned round from the bow. “Close.”

They all looked out over the side.

There was nothing. Only the black water, flat and still, going away into the grey in every direction.

And then Mira said, “Under. They’re under.”

She was leaning over the side with her face very close to the water, and her head on one side, listening. “I can hear them. Under the boat. They’re—“ She drew back sharply. “They’re coming up.”

Wren looked down.

At first she could see nothing. The black water gave nothing back. But then, deep down — very deep, she thought, though it was impossible to tell how deep — there was something grey. Something moving. It was like smoke, but under water: a slow grey shape, coiling, like smoke under glass, rising through the black as smoke rises through still air. And then another, beside it. And another. And they were all coming up, slowly, towards the bottom of the Gannet, the way bubbles come up in a pond.

“Lamps,” said Aren, very quietly. “Everybody. Now.”

They held them out over the side.

All of them — Wren’s lamp, and Mira’s, and the lamp Aren carried from the sack, and Callum’s and Rab’s lanterns, and Tobin’s hands round Ash’s pole, and Sister Hale’s two bony palms held out over the stern, glowing; even Mairi Dunlop, with one hand on the tiller and the other stretched out flat over the water like somebody warming it at a fire. A ring of gold round the little boat, over the black.

The sea-Hollows came up towards it, out of the deep, coiling.

And stopped.

They hung there, a little way under the surface, grey and faceless and slow, in a ring round the Gannet, like fish round a lantern. They did not come up into the light. But they did not go away, either. They stayed — just below, just out of reach — and watched. If Hollows can watch. They had no eyes. But Wren felt them watching, the way you feel somebody watching you across a dark room.

They stayed there all day.

And all night.

And the stone in Wren’s pocket hummed and hummed, and did not stop.

It was on the fourth day, very early, in the grey, that they found the ships.

Cinder found them. She was in the bow, where she always was, and she stood up suddenly with her ears pricked and her spark gone small and growled — not the growl she kept for Hollows; a different one, lower, sadder, almost a whine.

They looked where she was looking.

There was a ship, ahead of them, in the grey.

It was a big ship, much bigger than the Gannet — three masts, high sides, a great square stern with windows in it. But it was grey. All of it. Grey hull, grey masts, grey rags of sails hanging down from grey yards, grey ropes. It sat on the black water quite still, a little tilted, as if it had been sitting there a very long time and had got tired. And on its deck there were people.

They were standing. At the rail, and by the mast, and at the wheel. Sailors. Grey from head to foot, the way the scarecrows had been in the Heskeths’ fields. They did not move. They did not look round. They stood on the grey deck of their grey ship, with their grey hands at their sides, and stared out at nothing.

“Oh,” said Mira.

And then, as the Gannet crept on, they saw that it was not only one.

There was another beyond it. And another. And beyond those, more: a whole fleet of them, scattered across the black water as far as you could see into the grey — big ships and small, merchantmen and fishing-boats and things with oars, some with three masts and some with none, some sitting upright and some on their sides, some so old that their shapes were quite strange, the way ships were built hundreds of years ago. All grey. All still. All with their grey crews standing on their decks, staring.

“The Drowned Fleet,” said Aren.

His voice was very low.

“Every ship that ever sailed onto the Sunless Sea,” he said. “In three hundred years. Fishermen blown off course. Traders looking for a way round. Fools. Brave men.” He looked at them, one after another, as the Gannet went by. “She keeps them too. They don’t sink. They don’t drift ashore. They don’t go anywhere. They only sit here, in the grey, for ever, waiting.”

“For what?” said Wren.

Aren did not answer.

They went past the first ship close enough to touch.

Its side went up over them, grey and high and smooth, like the side of a house; and at the rail, looking down — no, not looking; facing — stood a boy.

He was about Wren’s age. Perhaps a little older. Thin. Barefoot. A ship’s boy, in a grey jersey with the sleeves rolled up and grey canvas trousers, standing at the rail with his grey hands on it, staring out over the black water at nothing; and Wren thought, looking up at him, that he must have been standing there for a very long time, because his jersey was not a kind of jersey anybody wore any more.

“Stop,” she said. “Mairi. Stop.”

Mairi Dunlop looked at her. Then she said “Easy,” to Callum and Rab, and they held water with the sweeps, and the Gannet came up slowly under the grey ship’s side, and bumped against it, very gently.

Wren climbed up.

There were the remains of a rope ladder hanging down the grey hull — grey, of course, and stiff as wire — and she went up it the way she would have gone up a chimney, quick and light, with her back against nothing and her fingers finding every hold. She came over the rail onto the deck. It was quite silent. It was like being on a ship made of ash. The grey sailors stood all round her and did not move.

She went to the boy.

He did not turn his head. He stood at the rail with his grey hands on it, facing out to sea. Close to, she could see that he had freckles under the grey, and a scar on his chin, and that his hair, grey, had once been curly.

Wren took the lamp out of her coat.

She held it out — not at him; to him — the way she had held it out to Posy. “Here,” she said. “It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything.”

And the little gold flame leaned out of its cracked chimney towards the grey boy’s hands on the rail.

For a long moment nothing happened at all.

Then — slowly — the grey began to go out of his fingers. It went the way frost goes off a window when the sun comes round: from the fingertips, up the hands, and the backs of the hands were brown, and the fingernails were bitten. It went up his arms. It went into his face. And the freckles came up brown, and the scar on his chin went pink, and his hair, from the roots, went red — a dark, curly, astonishing red — and his eyes, which had been staring out at nothing for longer than Wren could imagine, blinked.

He turned his head and looked at her.

“Who are you?” he said. His voice was rusty and cracked, like a hinge that has not been opened for a hundred years. “Where’s — where’s the captain? Where’s the land? We were only — we were only going round the Skerry, there was a blow, and then the water went—“ He looked round at the grey deck, the grey sailors, the grey sea, and his face filled up with terror. “What is this? What’s — how long have I—“

“It’s all right,” said Wren. She did not know if it was. “It’s all right. What’s your name?”

“Jory,” said the boy. “Jory Penhallow. Off the Kittiwake, out of Skerrow—“ He stopped. “Skerrow. Is Skerrow—“

“Skerrow’s still there,” said Wren. “We’ve just come from it. There’s a woman there called Mairi Dunlop who’s very loud.”

“Dunlop?” said Jory. “There’s an old Dunlop. Jamie Dunlop. He’s got a boat called the Gannet. He’s — he’s got a little girl, Mairi. She’s about three—“

From the Gannet, down below, there was a sound like somebody being hit very hard in the stomach.

Mairi Dunlop came up the rope ladder.

She came up it the way a woman of sixty-one in three jerseys and her grandmother’s sea-boots comes up a rope ladder on the side of a grey ship in the middle of the Sunless Sea: slowly, and puffing, and saying things under her breath that Wren had never heard before, even in Soot Lane. And she came over the rail and stood on the grey deck and looked at the boy for a long, long time.

“Jory Penhallow,” she said at last.

The boy looked at her, frightened.

“My da,” said Mairi, “used to tell me about a lad called Jory Penhallow. When I was small. A ship’s boy on the Kittiwake. Fourteen. Red hair. Always laughing. Went out round the Skerry the year I was three, in a blow, and the Kittiwake never came back.” Her leather face was working. “Da used to say he should have gone with them that day. And didn’t. And never forgave himself.” She swallowed. “He’s been dead thirty years, lad. My da. Thirty years. I’m sixty-one.”

Jory Penhallow looked at her. At her grey hair and her broad leather face and her red hands.

“Mairi?” he said. “Wee Mairi? Jamie’s Mairi?”

“Aye,” said Mairi Dunlop, and her voice broke right in half.

They could not take Jory with them. That was the dreadful thing.

They tried. They talked about it for an hour, in the Gannet, under the grey ship’s side. But the Gannet was small, and nine was already too many, and Jory was weak — he could hardly stand, after so long, and kept sitting down on the deck without meaning to. And they were going to the Spire. You could not take a boy who had just woken up from fifty-eight years of grey to the Queen’s own tower.

And there were the others. All the others. The grey sailors on the Kittiwake’s deck, and the next ship, and the next, and the whole Drowned Fleet going away into the grey, thousands of them, waiting.

“We can’t do them all,” said Tobin. His voice was wretched. “We can’t. There’s — there must be a hundred ships. There’s nine of us. If we stop for every one we’ll never get to the Spire. And then the Spire—“

“I know,” said Wren.

“There’s your mam and dad. And my father. And all the halls—“

“I know, Tobin.”

It was Jory who settled it, in the end. He was sitting on the deck of the Kittiwake with his back against the rail, very pale, very thin, with the Flame glowing faintly in his brown hands where Wren had left it.

“I can do them,” he said.

Everybody looked at him.

“I can do them,” said Jory again, a bit stronger. He held up his hands. “It’s in me, isn’t it? That’s what you said. It’s in me, and I can give it. Like you did.” He looked round at the grey sailors on the deck. “That’s Mr Trevail. He’s the mate. And that’s Ned, the cook. And the captain’s in the cabin, I think. I can do them. I’ve got all the time in the world, haven’t I?” His mouth twisted. “I’ve had all the time in the world for fifty-eight years.”

“You’re not strong enough,” said Mira.

“I’ll get strong,” said Jory. “Mr Trevail will help. When he’s woke. And then we’ll do the next ship. And the next.” He looked at Mairi. “And then we’ll come home. To Skerrow. All of us. And you can tell me about Da.”

Mairi Dunlop knelt down on the grey deck and put her arms round him, and held on.

“We’ll come back,” said Wren. “Afterwards. When we’ve done the Spire. We’ll come back for all of you, if you’re not home. I promise.”

“I know,” said Jory Penhallow. He smiled at her: a cracked, rusty, red-headed smile, the first in fifty-eight years. “You’ve got that look.”

So they left him there: one small brown ship’s boy with red hair, standing on the grey deck of the Kittiwake with the gold Flame in his hands, going towards the grey mate by the mast.

They looked back for a long time as the Gannet rowed on. They could see him for a long way. And just before the grey swallowed the Kittiwake up, Wren saw a second light come on beside his. Then a third, on the next ship.

On the fifth day, the dark came.

It was not night. Night was over, or should have been; it was the middle of the day by Tobin’s reckoning. But the grey sky began to come down, slowly, all round them, like a lid being lowered over a pot; and the grey went to dark grey, and the dark grey to black. And it was not empty, this dark. It was heavy. It pressed. It came down on the Gannet from above and from every side like deep water, like a weight, cold and thick and patient, and it pressed on the little ring of gold round the boat — on the lamps and lanterns and glowing hands — and the ring got smaller.

The singing-stone in Wren’s pocket did not hum any more. It screamed. A high thin shriek that went right through her.

“It’s her,” said Aren. He had both hands out over the bow. His palm was blazing gold, and his face in the light of it was set and white. “She knows we’re here. She’s known since the line. She’s — leaning on us.”

The dark leaned harder.

Wren felt the lamp go low. Not in her heart this time — she had nothing in her heart against anybody; she was holding it out with everything she had — but the way a candle goes low when a heavy door is pushed shut on it, when the air in the room is used up. It was being smothered. They all were. Mira’s lamp was a coal. Callum’s lantern went out, and he relit it with his hand, and it went out again. Sister Hale had stopped singing; she was holding her hands out over the stern with her eyes shut, and her old lips moving, and no sound coming out at all.

And the Gannet had stopped. The oars would not move in the water. It was as if the sea had turned to tar.

“Wren,” said Tobin. He was holding out Ash’s pole, gripping it with both scarred hands, and it was glowing faintly gold, and the dark was pressing down on it like a giant’s thumb. “Wren, I don’t — I don’t think we can—“

And then the wind came.

It came from behind them. From the west. From the land.

It came over the black water from the way they had come, out of the dark, across the Drowned Fleet, and it was warm.

It smelt of bread. It smelt of summer: of hay, and hot stone, and apples, and the inside of a bakery in the early morning, and something else underneath that Wren had no name for and knew all the same. It was the smell of the lamp. It was the smell of Midsummer morning on Cinder Hill.

It came up behind the Gannet and filled the slack brown sail all at once, with a crack like a clap of hands, so that the whole boat leaned over and Sister Hale nearly went off her coil of rope; and the mast creaked; and the Gannet leapt forward over the black water as if somebody had pushed her.

And the dark gave way in front of it.

It did not lift. It did not go. But it gave, the way thick mud gives when you push hard enough — and the little ring of gold round the boat blazed up, bright, all of it, every lamp and lantern and hand; and the singing-stone stopped screaming and went back to a low hum; and the Gannet went on east before the warm wind through the dark, fast, faster than she had ever sailed, with her brown sail full and round and her wake — her wake, for the first time on the Sunless Sea — shining behind her in the black water like a line of gold.

Wren stood in the bow with the lamp held up and the wind on her back and her eyes full, and did not say anything at all. Nobody did.

But Tobin, beside her, looked at the compass. And then back over his shoulder, at the way the wind had come. And then at Wren.

She knew what he was thinking. She was thinking it too.

She did not say it. Neither did he. Some things you don’t.

The wind held all that day and all that night.

And on the morning of the sixth day — though there was no morning, out there; only a different kind of dark — Cinder, in the bow, stood up and barked.

She never barked. She was a fox. But she barked now, sharp and loud, twice, and the hair stood up all along her back; and Mira, beside her, said “Rocks—“

There was a sound ahead. A low, hollow, sucking boom, coming and going, like a great beast breathing in a cave. And a smell: wet stone, and weed, and cold.

And then, rearing up out of the dark right in front of the Gannet’s bow, so close that the lamp-light ran gold over it — black rock. Wet, jagged, enormous, with the black water heaving white against its foot.

“HARD OVER—“ roared Mairi Dunlop.

The Gannet struck.

fields.title: Nightfall Spire
fields.body_html:
Nobody drowned. I will tell you that first, because I know you will want to know, and because for a while that morning, on the black rocks, none of them was sure of it.

The Gannet struck the rock bow-first, with a crunch like a giant biting an apple, and the whole boat stood up on end and threw everybody forward in a heap. Wren went over the bow. She remembered the black rock coming at her, wet and shining in the lamp-light, and then cold — a cold so huge it was like being hit — and then nothing, and then black water in her mouth and her nose and her eyes, and no up and no down, and the lamp.

She still had the lamp.

That was the thing she remembered most, afterwards. She had gone over the side into the Sunless Sea with the lamp in her hand, and she had not let go of it; and under the black water, where no light ever came back from anything, it was still burning. She could see it. A little gold flame in its cracked chimney, in her fist, in the dark, under the sea. Burning on, steady, as if it did not know it was supposed to go out.

And it was warm.

She kicked towards it — which was silly, because it was in her own hand, but it was the only thing she could see — and her head came up out of the water into the air, gasping. And a great red hand came down out of the dark and took her by the collar and hauled her up onto the rock like a landed fish.

“Got her,” roared Mairi Dunlop. “That’s all of them. That’s all nine. Count them. COUNT THEM, Callum—“

“Eight,” said Callum.

“NINE,” said Mairi. “Who’s missing? Who’ve I not got?”

Something sneezed. A shower of small, damp, offended gold sparks went up in the dark from the top of the rock above them; and there was Cinder, sitting on a ledge, soaked to the skin, glaring down at all of them with her spark sputtering at the end of her tail, as if the whole thing had been arranged on purpose to annoy her.

“Nine,” said Mairi Dunlop, and sat down on the rock very suddenly.

The Gannet was not sunk. But she was badly hurt.

She lay wedged between two black rocks with her bow stove in, and the black water slopping in and out of her, and her mast leaning over at a drunken angle with the brown sail trailing in the sea. Mairi Dunlop looked at her for a long time, by the light of Callum’s relit lantern, and did not say anything. Then she climbed down onto the rocks beside her, and put her red hand flat on the old patched oak of the hull, very gently, the way you put your hand on a horse that has fallen.

“She’ll mend,” she said at last. “Give me two days. Callum, Rab. There’s a cove, round there. I can hear it. We’ll get her off on the tide and round into the cove and I’ll mend her.” She looked up at the rest of them. “You’ll be wanting a boat. After. For coming home.”

“Yes,” said Wren. “We will.”

“Then you’ll have one,” said Mairi Dunlop. “Go on. Do what you came for. We’ll be here.”

So they went up off the rocks onto the island of Nightfall Spire, the six of them: Wren and Tobin and Mira, and Aren, and Sister Hale on her brass-mended crutch, and Cinder. And it was night.

It had been night on the Sunless Sea, after the fifth day; but that had been a dark that pressed on you from outside, like deep water. This was different. This was a night that was there, the way a wall is there, or a hill. It had always been here. It was part of the place. It was not the absence of day; it was as if day had never been invented.

There was a beach, of black shingle that crunched and slid. There were cliffs above it, black. There was a path up the cliffs, a stair cut into the rock with steps worn hollow, black. And at the top of the stair, a city.

It was grey.

It was the greyest thing Wren had ever seen, and she had seen Vaelport, where everything was white, and the Scarecrow Farms, and the Burned Country. Grey streets, paved with grey stone. Grey houses, tall and narrow, with grey slate roofs and grey doors and grey windows with no glass in them, going up and down grey hills. Grey steps. Grey bridges over grey dry gutters. It was a big city — as big as Emberwick, Tobin said, peering about in the lamp-light; perhaps bigger — and it was empty.

Not ruined. Empty. The doors were shut. The streets were swept. There were grey chairs in the grey rooms, if you looked in at the windows, and grey tables, and grey beds made up neatly with grey blankets. As if a great many people had lived here once, and tidied up one evening, and gone out, and never come back.

There was no fire anywhere. Not one. No smoke from any chimney. No lamp in any window. In Emberwick, even in the worst of the grey years, there had always been a glimmer somewhere — a candle-end, a Guild lamp, a coal in a grate. Here there was nothing. Their own little lights went through the streets like five sparks blown through a cold room, and the grey drank them, and gave nothing back.

“Who lived here?” whispered Mira.

“Nobody,” said Aren. “Not for a long time. It was a city once, before the curse. A harbour town. Thousands of people.” He looked up the grey street. “She took them all. The first of the Sleepers. Three hundred years ago. And then she kept the city the way it was, swept and tidy, because she likes things kept.” He paused. “She walks here sometimes. Alone. I’ve seen her. Going in and out of the houses. Touching things.”

Wren’s skin crept.

Cinder did not like it at all.

She went in front, as she always did; but she went with her belly low and her ears flat and her spark tucked down small under her tail, so that it hardly showed. She did not growl. That was the worst of it. She went through the grey streets in complete silence, the way a fox goes through a wood when it knows the hounds are near, and every few steps she stopped, and looked back at Wren, as if to make sure she was still there.

Mira clicked.

She had been clicking since the beach. Softly, under her breath, the way she had in the Deeps; Wren had stopped noticing it, the way you stop noticing a clock. But now, in the middle of a wide grey square with grey houses all round it, Mira stopped, and clicked again, louder, and frowned.

“That’s wrong,” she said.

“What is?”

“The echo.” She clicked again. “It came back from over there.” She pointed left. “But the nearest wall’s over there.” She pointed right. She clicked again, and turned her head, and her frown got deeper. “And that one came back twice. From two places. And one of them isn’t — there’s no wall there at all. There’s nothing.” She turned slowly round in the middle of the square, clicking, and her face in the lamp-light went pale. “It’s all wrong. All of it. Every echo’s coming back from the wrong place.”

“It’s built that way,” said Aren quietly.

They looked at him.

“The whole city,” he said. “And the Spire most of all. She built it to make echoes lie. So that nobody who comes here can find their way by listening.” He looked at Mira. “I’m sorry. I should have told you. I forgot that you’d—“

“No,” said Mira.

She stood in the middle of the grey square with her chin up, and clicked once more, very carefully, and listened; and then she shut her eyes, and clicked again, and listened, and her lips moved, as if she were counting.

“It’s built to make echoes lie,” she said slowly. “Not to make them stop. They still come back. Only from the wrong places.” She opened her eyes. “So if I know they’re lying, I can — work out how they’re lying. Like Tobin with his sums. It’s always the same amount wrong. Always to the left, and a little high.” She clicked again, and nodded. “The wall’s there. I’m sure of it.”

She pointed. Tobin held up Ash’s pole, with its faint gold glow, in that direction; and the light fell on a grey wall exactly where she had pointed.

“Oh, duck,” said Sister Hale softly.

“Anyway,” said Mira, going rather pink, “I don’t need to hear it to be frightened of it. I can do that perfectly well with my eyes.”

And then they came out of the end of a grey street, and saw the Spire.

It stood in the middle of the city, on the highest hill, and it went up.

That is the only way to say it. It went up. It was a tower of black glass — smooth, shining, faintly gleaming in the light of their lamps, like the inside of a mussel shell — as wide at its foot as Beacon Square in Emberwick; and it went up from there, and up, and up, narrowing very slowly, into the dark overhead. And it did not stop. Wren tipped her head back until her neck hurt and followed it up with her eyes, and it went on going up past where the lamp-light could reach, into the black; and there was no top. Not that she could see. It simply went up into the night until it and the night were the same.

There were no windows in it that she could see. No doors. Nothing on its smooth black sides at all. And there was no sound from it. It stood on its hill in the middle of the grey city, enormous and black and silent, and it seemed to Wren — though she could not have said why — that it was listening.

Beside her, Aren had gone very still.

He was looking up at it with a face she had not seen on him before — not since he was Varrick, on the Hill, staring at the Lampwright’s hands. It was the face of a man looking at a place where something terrible happened to him, a long time ago, which he had thought he would never see again.

“Thirty years,” he said, very low. “I lived in there thirty years. I had a room. On the four hundredth floor. With a window that looked at nothing.”

Wren did not know what to say. So she did what Cinder would have done. She went and stood beside him, close, so that her shoulder touched his arm; and she did not say anything at all.

After a moment, Aren breathed out.

“This way,” he said. “There’s a door the servants use. On the north side. Nobody watches it. Nobody comes.”

The door was very small, and very low, and very cold, and it was not locked. It had no lock. “Who would come?” said Aren.

Inside, there was a stair.

It went up. It went up in a tight spiral, round and round inside the wall of the Spire, narrow and steep, with steps of black glass that were smooth and slippery and worn hollow in the middle by thirty years of Aren’s feet and three hundred years of other feet before his. There was no light on it. There was no sound on it but their own breathing, and the tap of Sister Hale’s crutch, and the soft pad of Cinder’s paws, and Mira’s clicks going up ahead of them into the dark and coming back from all the wrong places.

And it was cold.

It was colder than the Sunless Sea, colder than the rocks, colder than anything. It came out of the black glass walls like the cold comes out of the walls of an ice-house, and went into their hands and feet and faces, and into their bones; and their breath went up white in front of them in the lamp-light, and their fingers on the black glass wall went numb. Even the lamp felt it. Wren could feel the lamp, against her ribs, under her coat, working; burning steadily, warm, but working at it, the way your heart works when you are climbing.

They had to hide it. Aren had said so, at the door. The Spire drank light, the way the Sunless Sea did; and if they went up its stairs with their lamps held up, the Queen would feel it, the way you feel a draught. So Wren carried the lamp inside her coat, against her ribs, fastened in. Mira carried hers in the Chronicle’s flour-sack, with the book. Tobin had wrapped Ash’s pole in his coat. Sister Hale kept her hands inside her shawl. And Aren went first with his scarred palm shut tight in a fist, so that only a thin gold line showed between his fingers, enough to put his feet by.

It was very dark.

They climbed for a long time.

They climbed for what Tobin, who was counting, said was eleven hundred and four steps, and then stopped counting, because it was too depressing. They climbed past doors — black glass doors, shut, leading off the stair into the Spire, every forty steps or so, on and on. They rested on a landing, and Sister Hale sat down on the top step with her crutch across her knees and her old face grey in the faint light from Aren’s fist, and said she was perfectly all right, thank you, and did not get up for some time.

And somewhere above the eleven-hundredth step, Aren stopped on a landing, and held up his fist for them to be quiet, and pointed.

There was a window in the wall of the stair. The first they had seen: a narrow slit in the black glass, looking out not onto the night but in, into the Spire — onto a long, high, dim gallery, lit by something cold and pale and grey that was not a light at all. And in the gallery, sitting on a grey bench by the wall, all alone, was a man.

He was round. He was wrapped in a grey blanket, up to his chin, and his face over the top of it was grey too, and pinched, and miserable, and wet round the eyes. He had a plate on his knees, with something grey on it, and he was eating it very slowly with his fingers, and making a face at every bite, as if it tasted of nothing at all — which, Aren told them afterwards, it did. Everything in the Spire tasted of nothing. There was no gold chain on his neck. His wig was gone; it had stayed in the ditch at Harrowgate with his chain. His plum velvet coat, under the blanket, was torn and filthy, with heather still caught in the hem.

“Prowle,” breathed Wren.

The Lord Steward of Emberwick — Keeper of the Beacon, Protector of the Ring — sat on his grey bench in the Queen’s tower and ate his grey food and shivered. And as they watched, he put the plate down on the bench beside him, very carefully, and put his face in his fat hands, and began, quite silently, to cry.

Wren had hated him for a year. She found, standing on the black glass stair in the dark looking through the slit at him, that she could not remember why.

“He ran to her,” said Aren, very low. “After Harrowgate. He thought she’d be pleased he came. She wasn’t.” He looked away from the window. “She doesn’t want anybody who’s failed. She only keeps them.”

“Can we—“ said Wren. “Should we—“

“Not now,” said Aren. “Later. If there’s a later.” He turned back to the stair. “Come on. It’s not much further.”

It was not much further.

Forty more steps, and another landing. And on this landing there was not one door but two: great tall doors, double, of black glass, going up and up into the dark further than the lamp-light reached. They were shut. They had no handles. And they were cold — so cold that the air in front of them was white with frost, and Wren’s breath froze on her lip, and the black glass steps of the landing were rimed with it like a winter field.

And from behind them there came no sound at all.

Not a breath. Not a footstep. Not a creak. A silence so thick and so complete that it was like the silence at the bottom of the strongroom under the Warden’s Hall, sixty-one steps down, with the iron door shut. A silence like a held breath, held for three hundred years.

Mira clicked, very softly.

And then she stood quite still, with her eyes wide, and her hand went out and found Wren’s arm and held it.

“It’s big,” she whispered. “It’s so big, Wren. It goes on and on. I can’t hear the end of it.” She clicked again. “And it’s full. It’s full of — of shapes. Standing. Hundreds. No — more. Thousands. They’re all standing quite still.” Her voice shook. “And none of them are breathing very much.”

Aren looked at the doors.

“The Hall of Sleepers,” he said. “The first one. There are nine.” He swallowed. “She put the oldest at the top. The newest — the ones from the last ten years, the last twenty — are here. In this one. At the bottom.” He looked at Wren. “If they’re anywhere, Wren, they’re in here.”

He put his scarred hand, the one with the gold line, flat on the black glass between the two great doors.

And they swung open, slowly, silently, inwards, into the dark.

fields.title: The Hall of Sleepers
fields.body_html:
I have thought for a long time about how to tell you about the Hall of Sleepers, and I am still not sure I can. But I will try, because it matters, and because Wren would want me to.

It was very big. Mira was right. It was bigger than the Great Forge under Vaelport, bigger than the echo-halls of Deepholm, bigger than Beacon Square and the Guild Hall and the Warden’s Hall all put together. It went away from the doors into the dark further than any light could reach, and up into the dark further than any light could reach, so that you could not see the ceiling or the far wall or the sides. And it was lit — if you could call it lit — by a cold pale glimmer that came from nowhere, the way the grey light came from nowhere in Vaelport, so that everything in it was the colour of ash.

And it was full of people.

They were standing. That was the first thing, and the worst. They were not lying down, as people do when they are sleeping. They were not sitting. They were standing, every one, on their own two feet, upright, quite still, in rows — long, long rows, going away from the doors into the dark, and on either side, and behind each other, row on row on row, like corn in a field, like trees in a wood, like nothing Wren had ever seen. Men and women. Old people and young. Some in good clothes and some in rags. Some with their arms at their sides and some with their hands still lifted, a little, as if they had been reaching for something when the grey came. Children — there were children. Not many. But some.

All grey.

All grey from head to foot, hair and skin and clothes and eyes, the way the scarecrows had been in the Heskeths’ fields, the way the sailors had been on the deck of the Kittiwake. All with their faces turned towards nothing. All silent.

They were not dead. Wren could see that, after a while. If you looked very hard at one of them — at the grey woman nearest the door, say, with her grey hair coming down out of its grey pins — you could see, after a long time, that her chest moved. Very slightly. Very slowly. Once. And then, after a long time, again. As if she were breathing in a dream, and the dream had gone on for so long that she had forgotten what breathing was for.

Thousands of them.

Wren stood in the doorway of the Hall of Sleepers with the lamp fastened inside her coat against her ribs, and her mouth open, and could not move.

“How many?” whispered Tobin, at last.

Aren did not answer at once.

“This hall,” he said. “About twelve thousand. I think. Nobody counted them.” He looked away into the grey. “There are nine halls.”

Nobody said anything.

Sister Hale had sat down on the floor, just inside the door, with her crutch across her knees. She had not fallen. She had simply sat. Her old face had gone quite still, and her one bright eye was going along the nearest row of grey faces, one after the other, slowly, the way you read a list of names on a stone; and Wren saw her lips moving, and knew that she was praying, though she had never once heard Sister Hale pray out loud.

Cinder did not go in. For the first time in her whole life, Cinder would not go in front. She pressed herself against Wren’s shins with her tail between her legs and her ears flat to her skull, and shivered.

And Mira clicked, once, very softly, and listened to it go out into the hall and not come back.

“I can’t hear the end,” she said. “Wren. I can’t hear the end of it.”

Wren went in.

She did not decide to. She had stopped deciding things, somewhere on the black glass stair. Her feet simply took her, the way they had taken her down the slope of Cinder Hill after the Lampwright, and out of Harrowgate onto the moor; and she found herself walking along the first row of Sleepers, slowly, looking at their faces.

She did not know what her mother looked like.

That was the thing she had not let herself think about, all the way across the Sunless Sea, and now it came and stood in front of her and would not move. She had been four. She had no picture of her mother; nobody in Soot Lane had pictures of anybody. She had no memory of her face. She had a ribbon, and a scrap of a song. And Aren, on the stones by the weir: She was small. Black hair. A sharp chin. You have her face.

So she looked for her own face.

She walked along the first row, and looked at every face. Grey, grey, grey. An old man with a long nose. A young woman with a round face and her hand held up to her mouth. A big man with a beard. A girl not much older than Wren, with her eyes half shut. Grey, all of them, all the same grey; it was very hard to tell what anybody had looked like, under it. She walked along the second row. The third.

She had done perhaps a hundred faces when she understood that she could not do it.

There were twelve thousand. She could walk along these rows for a week and not see half of them. She could walk past her own mother and not know. In the grey, with the faces all gone to ash, a small woman with a sharp chin looked like every other small woman with a sharp chin; and there might be fifty of those in this hall alone. A hundred.

She stopped in the middle of the fourth row, with grey faces all round her, and the cold coming out of the floor into her boots, and found that she could not breathe.

“Wren,” said Tobin’s voice, behind her. Very gently. “Wren. We’ll find them. We’ll — I’ll work out a system. Rows and columns. If we each take a section—“

“There’s twelve thousand, Tobin.”

“I know. But—“

“And I don’t know what she looks like.”

Tobin did not say anything else. He did not have anything to say. He only stood beside her, in the middle of the Sleepers, and put his scarred hand on her shoulder, and left it there.

And it was then — standing there, not able to breathe, with Tobin’s hand on her shoulder and twelve thousand grey faces going away from her into the dark — that Wren began to hum.

She did not mean to. It was what she had always done, all her life, when she was frightened, or cold, or alone, or all three. In the garret in Soot Lane with the grate cold. In the dark of the Deeps. On the Black Stair. On the long road east to Cinder Hill, talking to the lamp. It was what you did. You hummed the only thing you had.

Morning comes, morning comes, and the dark shall not keep us…

She hummed it very softly. Hardly more than a breath. The Hall of Sleepers did not give it back; the Spire was built to make echoes lie, and the hall drank the tune the way the Sunless Sea had drunk the lamp’s light. It went out from her into the grey and vanished.

She got to the end of the bit she knew. And the dark shall not keep us.

She stopped.

And Mira, three rows away, said, “Wren.”

Very sharply. In a voice Wren had never heard her use.

“Wren. Do it again.”

“What?”

“Do it again. The song. Hum it again. Now. Don’t stop. Don’t stop and don’t talk.” Mira had her head tipped on one side and her eyes shut and her whole body gone still, like a hound at a gate. “Do it again, Wren—“

Wren hummed it again.

Morning comes, morning comes, and the dark shall not keep us—

“There,” whispered Mira. “There. There. Did you hear it? No, you can’t have. Do it again. Again. Keep going—“

Wren kept going. Round and round. Morning comes, morning comes. Her voice was shaking. She did not know what Mira had heard. She did not dare hope.

And Mira began to walk.

She walked slowly, with her eyes shut, between the rows of Sleepers, deeper into the hall, away from the door — left, then right, then left again, stopping every few steps to listen, with her head tipped and her lips moving, counting. Working out how the echoes were lying, and by how much, and where the truth was. Wren followed her, humming. Tobin followed Wren. Aren came behind with his gold-lined fist. Sister Hale got up off the floor and came too, on her crutch. Cinder pressed against Wren’s legs the whole way.

Row after row. Grey faces. Deeper into the hall, further from the doors, until the doors were gone in the grey behind them.

And then Mira stopped, and opened her eyes, and pointed.

“There,” she said. “Her. By the window.”

There was a window in the wall of the Hall of Sleepers: a tall narrow slit in the black glass, looking out onto nothing, onto the night. And by it stood a woman.

She was small. She was grey, like all the others, from her hair to her boots. She was standing a little apart from the row, close to the window, with her face turned towards it, as if she had been looking out of it when the grey came and had never stopped. Her grey hair was black-straight, and cut short, raggedly, as if she had cut it herself with a knife. Her chin was sharp.

And her lips were moving.

Very slightly. So slightly you would not have seen it if you had not been looking. They moved, and stopped, and moved again — not in time with anything; not making any sound. Like a person talking in their sleep. Like a person trying to remember a word that is on the tip of their tongue.

Wren stood in front of her and stopped humming.

The grey lips stopped too.

Wren hummed again. Morning comes. And the lips moved again. Morning comes. The same shape. The same tune. Without a sound. Right in time with her.

Beside the woman, a little behind her, so close that his grey shoulder was almost touching hers, stood a big grey man. Very tall and very broad, with big grey hands hanging at his sides, the fingers thick and blunt and scarred across the knuckles, the way a man’s fingers get who has spent his life mending things with small tools; and under the grey of his broad face, if you looked hard, the faint pale marks of a great many freckles.

Wren took the lamp out of her coat.

She did not think about the Queen, or the Spire drinking light, or who would feel it. She did not think about anything at all. She unbuttoned her coat with fingers that would not work properly, and took out the little battered brass lamp with its cracked glass chimney, and it burned up at once in her hands, gold, the way it always did; and in the grey of the Hall of Sleepers, among twelve thousand grey faces, it was the only colour in the world.

She did not hold it out. Not the way she had held it out to Posy, or the boy on the Kittiwake, or Aren in the weaving-room.

She gave it.

She took the grey woman’s hands — they were cold, so cold, cold as stones in a river — and lifted them, and put the lamp into them, and folded the grey fingers round it, one by one. Truly. Not lending it. The way she had given it to Tobin at the top of the Black Stair, a long time ago, and thought she might never have it back. She let go of it. She let it be the grey woman’s. She stepped back with her hands empty and her heart going like a hammer, and the only thing she had in the world in somebody else’s hands.

“It’s yours,” said Wren. Her voice did not work. “It’s — it’s given. It’s for you.”

And the lamp blazed.

It went up in the grey woman’s hands the way it had gone up in Old Ash’s hands at the anvil in the Forge, the way it had gone up on the top of the Beacon: white-gold, roaring, so bright that Tobin threw up his arm over his eyes and Sister Hale cried out. And the light went into her.

It went into her hands first. Wren saw it. The grey went out of the fingers round the lamp like frost going off a window when the sun comes round, all at once, and the fingers were brown, and small, and strong: small brown hands, holding a lamp, so like Wren’s own that she could not look at them. It went up her arms. Into her shoulders. Into her neck.

And into her face.

The grey went out of her face the way the dark goes out of the sky in the morning: from the edges in. And her skin was brown, and her lips were red, and her cropped hair was black — true black, glossy, like a crow’s wing — and her sharp chin was Wren’s sharp chin, exactly; and her eyes, which had been looking out of a window at nothing for eight years, blinked.

And looked down.

At the lamp in her hands. And then, slowly, as if she were waking from a very long way under, up — and at the girl in front of her.

At the cropped black hair. The sharp chin. The faded red ribbon on her left wrist.

The woman’s eyes went very wide.

“Wren?” she said.

I am not going to tell you very much about the next part. Some things are not for telling. Some things belong to the people they happened to, and I think this is one of them.

But I will tell you this.

Wren did not run to her. She did not throw her arms round her, the way Nettle had in the bakery, or Posy in the Heskeths’ yard. She stood in front of her mother in the Hall of Sleepers, with her hands empty at her sides and Cinder pressed against her shins, and could not move at all. She stood there and looked at her mother’s face, which was her own face, older, with the lamp-light on it; and her own face did not do anything, because it did not know how.

And her mother did not run to her either.

Because her mother — Linnet Ashby, singer, of Pike Street by the canal in the Low Quarter of Emberwick — was looking at the girl in front of her, and the girl was twelve. And the last time she had seen Wren, Wren had been four years old, and asleep in her shawl by a Ring-lamp on the North Wall, with her thumb in her mouth; and she had picked her up, and carried her down the steps, and put her in a coal-hole, and said hum, my love, and don’t come out till morning. And then she had gone back up the steps. And then the grey had come.

And now it was morning. And the child was twelve. And there was a whole life gone between, that she had not been there for.

Linnet Ashby looked at her daughter, and her face crumpled up like a piece of paper, and she said, “Oh — oh, look at you. Look at you. You’ve grown—“

And that was all either of them could say.

Behind her, the big man moved.

The light from the lamp had gone into him too, while nobody was looking. It had gone into him sideways, from her, the way warmth goes from one person to the next when they are standing close together on a cold night. The grey had gone out of his big blunt hands, and they were brown and freckled and enormous. It had gone out of his face, and his face was broad and pink and covered all over in freckles, so many that they ran together; and his hair was the colour of sand.

He blinked. He looked round. At the window, and the hall, and the grey rows going away into the dark. At the woman beside him. At the lamp in her hands. At the girl.

His big face went quite still.

“Linnet,” he said. His voice was slow and deep and rusty, like a cart that has not been driven for a long time. “Linnet. Is that—“

“It’s Wren, Tam,” said Linnet Ashby. “It’s Wren.”

And Tam Ashby, lamp-mender, the biggest and gentlest man on Pike Street, put his two great hands over his face, and began to cry, out loud, the way a child cries, without any shame at all.

Wren did not know what to call them.

That was the thing that went round and round in her head, then and afterwards. She stood in the Hall of Sleepers and looked at her mother and father, and they looked at her, and she did not know what to call them. Mam, they said in Soot Lane. Da. She had heard other children say it all her life. She had never said it herself. Not once. Not since she was four. She did not know how it went in her mouth.

So she did not call them anything. She stood there.

And her mother, after a long time, said, very shakily, “Wren. Love. There was a song. I used to — I used to sing you a song. Do you remember?” She was holding the lamp against her chest, in both hands, the way you hold a baby. “I’ve been — I think I’ve been trying to remember it. For a long time. In the dark. I could only—“

And she began to sing it.

Morning comes, morning comes, sang Linnet Ashby, in a voice that was cracked and thin from eight years of silence, and was still the most beautiful thing Wren had ever heard, and the dark shall not keep us—

And stopped.

Exactly there. Exactly where Wren had always stopped, all her life, in the garret and the Deeps and the long road east. And the dark shall not keep us. And then nothing.

Linnet’s face went blank, and frightened.

“I can’t,” she said. “I can’t — there’s more. I know there’s more. I made it — I used to sing it all. Every night. All of it. But it’s — it’s gone. It’s not there.” She put her hand to her head. “It’s still — there’s still grey in me, I think. A bit. Where it was.” She looked at Wren, and her eyes were full of tears. “I’m sorry. Oh, love, I’m sorry. I can’t remember the rest.”

“It’s all right,” said Wren.

And it was the strangest thing. She found that it was.

“It’s all right,” she said again. “I don’t know it either. We’ll — we’ll find it. There’s more. I know there’s more.”

It was Cinder who heard the step.

She went rigid against Wren’s legs. Her ears went up. And from somewhere far off in the Hall of Sleepers — back towards the doors, or perhaps not; in that place you could not tell where anything came from — there came a sound.

Metal on glass. Slow. Heavy. Coming nearer.

A Knight’s step.

“Lamps,” hissed Aren. “Hide them. Now—“

There was no time to think. Linnet pushed the blazing lamp back into Wren’s hands — she did not even have to be told; she was a Lamplighter’s wife and a singer on the wall, and she knew — and Wren crammed it inside her coat and fastened it, burning, against her ribs. Mira’s went into the flour-sack. Aren shut his fist. The gold went out of the hall as if a door had been shut on it.

“Stand still,” whispered Aren. “All of you. Stand. Like them.”

They stood.

They stood among the Sleepers, in the rows, in the grey: Wren between her mother and father; Tobin with Ash’s pole hidden under his coat; Mira with her eyes shut; Sister Hale leaning on her crutch with her old face set like stone; Aren at the end, very tall. Cinder lay down flat between Wren’s boots and put her nose on her paws and became, as far as a fox can, a small grey heap of nothing. They stood with their arms at their sides and their faces turned to nothing, and did not breathe.

And Linnet and Tam Ashby, brown-faced, freckled, with the colour back in them, stood on either side of their daughter in the Hall of Sleepers among twelve thousand grey people, and did not move, and looked straight ahead.

The step came nearer.

It came down the row behind them. Slowly. Metal on glass. Clink … clink … clink. Wren could hear the creak of armour, now, and smell the cold that came off a Knight, which was no smell at all.

It stopped. Right behind her.

She did not breathe. She did not move. She felt the lamp burning against her ribs under her fastened coat, warm, so warm, the only warm thing in the whole Spire; and she thought, it’ll show. It’ll show through. He’ll see the light through my coat—

And then her mother’s hand, very slowly, without her mother’s face moving at all, found her hand in the grey, and held it.

The step went on.

Clink … clink … clink. Down the row. Away. Fainter. Gone into the grey.

Nobody moved for a long time after.

Then Aren breathed out, very carefully.

“She knows,” he said, very low. “Or she will soon. They walk the halls every few hours. That was early.” He looked at Linnet and Tam. “You’ll have to stay. Here. In the rows. Like this. Can you?”

“For how long?” said Tam Ashby slowly.

“Until we come back for you.” Aren’s face was very tired. “Harrowgate’s father is up there. In a cell. And there are eight more halls above this one. We can’t take you up the stair. We can’t take you down it — not yet. She’d see. If you stand here, in the rows, and keep still when they come, you’re only two more Sleepers among twelve thousand. She’ll never find you.”

“We’ve stood here eight years,” said Linnet. She was holding on to Wren’s hand so tightly it hurt. “We can stand a little longer.” She looked down at Wren. “Can’t we, love?”

Wren could not speak. She nodded.

She did not want to let go. She did not want to let go of that hand more than she had ever not wanted anything. But there was Tobin’s father, in a cell, at the top of the stair. And there were eight more halls. And there was the Queen.

So she let go.

She went back along the row, towards the doors, with Tobin and Mira and Aren and Sister Hale and Cinder; and at the end of the row she looked back.

Her mother and father were standing among the Sleepers by the tall black window, in the grey, quite still, with their faces turned straight ahead, so that you would never have known. Two more grey shapes among twelve thousand.

Except that her mother’s lips were moving.

Very slightly. Without a sound. Morning comes, morning comes.

And as Wren watched, her father’s big freckled hand, at his side, reached out a little, very slowly, without his face moving at all — and found her mother’s hand, in the grey, and held it.

fields.title: Edric
fields.body_html:
The cells were near the top of the Spire, Aren said, and it was a long way up, and Sister Hale could not climb it.

She did not argue. That was how Wren knew how tired she was. She sat on the black glass landing outside the doors of the Hall of Sleepers with her back against the cold wall and her crutch across her knees and her old face grey with weariness, and said, “Go on, ducks. I’ll keep watch. I’m good at sitting.” And then, more quietly, to Wren: “I’ll be near them. Your mam and dad. If anybody comes.”

“I’ll stay with her,” said Mira. “Somebody should. And I can hear the stair from here, both ways, if I’m careful about the lying.” She looked at Tobin. “You go. It’s your father. Wren — go with him.”

So it was three of them who went on up, and a fox: Aren in front with his fist shut, and Tobin with Ash’s pole wrapped in his coat, and Wren, with the lamp fastened against her ribs and her mother’s hand still warm in hers, though it was not there any more.

It was a long way.

They climbed past the doors of the second Hall of Sleepers, and the third. Aren did not open them. He did not even slow down. But Wren felt them as she went by — the cold coming out round the edges of the great black glass doors, and the silence behind them, the held breath of twelve thousand more grey people, and twelve thousand more, standing in the dark. She made herself not think about it. She made herself think about one step at a time.

The fourth hall. The fifth.

Tobin had stopped counting steps a long time ago. He had started, instead, without meaning to, counting something else: the number of times his hands had started to shake, and then stopped. It was eleven, by the sixth hall. He was not frightened of the dark any more. He knew that. He had sung in the strongroom. But he was frightened of what was at the top of the stair, which was not the dark at all, but his father; and he found, climbing, that it was a different kind of frightened altogether, and much worse.

What would you say to him, Mira had asked, in the strongroom. If you saw him again. After everything.

He did not know. He had thought about it on the Sunless Sea, every night, lying in the bottom of the Gannet looking up at no stars. He had made up a dozen speeches in his head. Some of them were angry. Some of them were very long. Some of them began with Actually. He could not remember any of them now.

I expect you’ll know when it’s time, Mira had said. Like the question.

He hoped very much she was right.

Above the ninth hall, the stair changed.

It got narrower. The black glass walls came in close on either side, so that Tobin’s elbows brushed them, and the cold came off them like breath. And the steps were not worn hollow any more. Nobody came up here much.

And then there was a passage, going off the stair: a long, low, straight corridor of black glass, with doors along one side of it. Small doors. Iron, not glass — the first iron Wren had seen in the whole Spire — with a little grille in each, at the height of a man’s face.

Aren stopped at the mouth of the passage.

“Here,” he said. He did not look at Tobin. “The twelfth door. On the left.”

“You’ve been here before,” said Tobin.

“Yes.”

“You brought him here.”

“Yes,” said Aren. “In the winter. I walked him up this stair and down this passage and opened that door and he went in, and I shut it, and turned the key, and walked away. He didn’t say anything. Not the whole way.” He held out his hand. There was a key in it: a big black iron key, old, that he had taken off a hook on the wall at the top of the stair without anybody seeing. “I’m sorry, Harrowgate. Tobin.” He put the key in Tobin’s hand. “You should be the one to open it. Not me.”

Tobin looked at the key. Then at Aren.

“Will you come?” he said.

Aren was quiet for a moment.

“If you want me to,” he said.

“I want you to,” said Tobin. “And Wren.” He swallowed. “I don’t think I can do it on my own.”

The twelfth door on the left was exactly like all the others. Iron. Small. A grille.
