Tobin stood in front of it with the key in his hand. He could see nothing through the grille. It was dark inside. Not the grey half-light of the Spire; dark, really dark, the dark of a room where no lamp has ever been.

He put the key in the lock. It was stiff. He turned it with both hands, and it went round with a sound that went all the way down the black glass corridor and did not come back. He pushed the door. It opened inwards, slowly, on hinges that screamed.

And then he did a thing he had not planned. He unwrapped Ash’s pole from his coat, and held it up — and it lit. Not much. Only a faint gold glow, where his scarred hands held it. But enough.

The cell was very small. A stone shelf for a bed, with a grey blanket on it, folded. A grey jug. A grey cup. A window — a slit in the black glass, no wider than a hand, looking out onto nothing. Nothing else.

And on the stone shelf, sitting upright, with his back against the wall and his hands on his knees, a man.

He was thin. That was the first thing. He was terribly thin — thinner than Tobin had ever imagined a grown man could be, his face all bones and hollows under a rough white beard. His hair, which had been silver at the temples, was white. All white. His clothes were the clothes he had walked out of the Warden’s Hall in, a year ago — a dark good coat, a white shirt — and they were filthy, and hung on him as if they belonged to somebody much bigger.

But he was not grey.

That was the strange thing. That was what Tobin saw, in the faint gold light of Ash’s pole. His father was not grey. His face was pale, deathly pale, as if it had not seen any light at all for a year; but it was a man’s face, with a man’s colour under the pallor, faint and sick, but there. His eyes were not empty. They were clear. They were dark blue — the same dark blue as Tobin’s own, which Tobin had never noticed before, because he had never once in his life looked his father full in the face for long enough to see.

And they were looking at the open door. At the light. And at the boy standing in it, with his mother’s compass in his pocket and an old man’s pole in his hands and his spectacles cracked across one lens.

Lord Edric Harrowgate, Warden of Emberwick, sat on the stone shelf in his cell at the top of Nightfall Spire, and looked at his son.

He did not move.

“Father,” said Tobin.

His voice came out as a croak. He tried again.

“Father. It’s me. It’s Tobin.”

His father did not say anything.

He looked at Tobin. He looked at Wren, in the doorway behind him. He looked, last of all, at Aren — at the tall man in the grey shirt who had walked him up this stair and shut this door — and something went across his face, very quick, that might have been fear, or might have been nothing at all.

Then he looked back at Tobin, and shut his eyes.

“No,” he said.

His voice was very quiet. It was the same voice — Tobin would have known it anywhere; he had heard it say no to him every day of his life — but there was nothing in it now. It was hollow, like a bell with a crack.

“No,” said Lord Edric. “Go away. Leave me.”

“Father—“

“Leave me.” His eyes opened. “You shouldn’t have come. You should not have come. Whatever she’s promised you — whatever she’s going to — it’s a trick, Tobin. Everything here is a trick.” He drew a breath that rattled. “Go home. Go back to Emberwick. Forget about me. It would be — it’s what I deserve.”

“I don’t care what you deserve,” said Tobin.

He was surprised to hear himself say it. So, by the look on his face, was his father.

“I’ve come to take you home,” said Tobin. “That’s all. Aren’s here, and Wren, and — we’ve got a boat. We’ve got the Flame. We can—“

“I sold you,” said Lord Edric.

The cell was very quiet.

“I sold you,” said Tobin’s father. “Do you understand? I don’t think you do. You’re a child. You don’t—“ He stopped. His hands on his knees had begun, very slightly, to shake. “I sold the lamp, first. Or tried to. To that man.” He did not look at Aren. “For the Ring. For my place. For a seat at a larger table. I sold the city. I sold every soul in it, and told myself it was for their safety. And then—“

He stopped again.

“You wrote to me,” he said. “From the Waste. You left a letter on my desk, the morning you went, and you said you loved me. You said you were sorry. You said—“ His voice cracked right across. “You told me where you were going. Because you trusted me. And I took that letter, Tobin. I took your letter, that you wrote because you loved me, and I gave it to her. As a map. So her captain would know which way you’d gone.”

Tobin did not say anything.

He had known. He had known since the grey courier on the road beyond the Gloam River, and the satchel of letters, and his father’s handwriting on a letter to the Queen. He had known, and he had carried it, all the way to Vaelport and the lighthouse and the Hill. But he had never heard his father say it.

“I sold my own son,” said Lord Edric Harrowgate. “For a throne. And I didn’t even get the throne.” He laughed: a terrible little laugh, like something breaking. “She’s kept me here a year. Clear. Not grey. She could have greyed me, any time — it would have been a mercy. She didn’t. She comes and sits in that doorway sometimes, and talks to me. Very kindly. About what I did. About you. She wants me to know. Every day.” He looked at the slit of a window, at nothing. “I’ve had a year in this room to know exactly what I am. And I know it. And I won’t come, Tobin. I’m not worth coming for. Leave me here. Please.”

Tobin stood in the doorway of the cell with Ash’s pole glowing faintly in his hands.

He could not think of any of the speeches. They had all gone. He stood there and looked at his father — at the thin white face and the white beard and the shaking hands, and the dark blue eyes that were the same as his own — and he did not know what to say at all.

And then he did know.

It came the way the answer to his question had come on Midsummer morning, all at once, from nowhere: so simple that he wondered why he had ever needed to look for it.

He did not make a speech. He told his father about breakfast.

“There was a fire,” said Tobin. “On a hill.”

His father looked at him.

“On Cinder Hill,” said Tobin. “In the Burned Country. After — after everything. After I sold Ash for a letter, Father. After I said I didn’t know him, twice, to his face. After he died.” His voice shook, and he let it. “I walked into the Queen’s camp, on the Hill, and told her to take me instead of Wren, because I thought I wasn’t worth anything any more and at least I could be worth that. And she did take me. Nearly all of me. I went grey. I was nearly—“ He stopped. “And then somebody came.”

He did not say who. He did not need to. He had never been able to say it, and he found he did not need to now.

“And he put his hand on my head,” said Tobin, “and I came back. And then he made breakfast. On a fire. Toast, and apples. He burned the first piece of toast.” A sound came out of him that was half a laugh. “He burned it black, Father. And he laughed. And then he gave the second piece to Wren, and she said how much, and he said it’s given.”

His father was staring at him.

“And then,” said Tobin, “he asked me if I loved him.”

He had to stop for a moment. He held onto Ash’s pole.

“Three times. He asked me three times. Tobin, do you love me? And the first time I said yes, and he said then keep my lamps. And the second time I said yes, and he said then look after the small ones. And the third time—“ He swallowed. “The third time it hurt. Because I knew why he was asking. Three times. For the three things I’d done. And I said you know everything. You know I do. And he said, then follow me.”

The cell was perfectly silent.

“He gave me my work back,” said Tobin. “That’s what I came to tell you. That’s all. I sold Ash for a letter, Father, and he gave me my work back. He didn’t ask me if I was worth it. I wasn’t. He knew I wasn’t. He gave it me anyway.” He took a step into the cell. “So I don’t care what you’re worth. I don’t care if you sold me. I sold him. And he gave me breakfast.”

Lord Edric Harrowgate began to weep.

He did not do it the way Tam Ashby had, out loud, like a child. He did it the way a man does who has not wept once in his whole life, not when his wife died, not ever, and does not know how: silently, with his whole thin body shaking, and his face not moving at all, and the tears simply running out of his eyes and down into his white beard and dripping off it onto his filthy shirt. He sat upright on the stone shelf with his hands on his knees and wept like that, and did not wipe his face, and did not look away from his son.

Tobin went to him.

He crossed the little cell in two steps, and knelt down on the stone floor in front of the shelf, and put Ash’s pole down beside him; and then — very carefully, the way you would touch something that might break — he took his father’s thin shaking hands in his own scarred ones.

His father’s hands were so cold. Colder than the black glass.

“Hold out your hands,” said Tobin. “That’s all you do. You don’t have to be worth it. You just hold them out.”

His father’s hands were already out. They were in Tobin’s.

“It’s given,” said Tobin.

And the Flame went out of Tobin’s scarred palms into his father’s cold ones — Wren saw it go, from the doorway, a warmth you could see, like heat over a road in summer; and a faint gold glow ran up Lord Edric’s thin wrists, under his skin, into his arms, and his chest, and his face. And the deathly pallor went out of it, slowly, the way the dark goes out of a window in the morning. And his face was a man’s face again, thin and lined and white-bearded, with a little colour in the cheeks for the first time in a year.

And for a moment, just for a breath — Wren saw it, and so did Aren — a little gold flame, no bigger than a candle’s, stood on the top of his white head, and sank in.

His father looked down at their hands. Then up at his son’s face.

“Tobin,” he said.

That was all. Just his name. But Tobin’s face did something extraordinary when he heard it, and it took Wren a moment to understand why.

His father had never called him that.

Not once. Not that Tobin could remember, in thirteen years. Boy, his father had called him; and young man; and sir, very coldly, when he was angry; and once, at a Guild dinner, in front of everybody, my son, who prefers machines. But never his name. Never Tobin. As if it were a word that belonged to his mother, and had died with her, and was not to be said in the house.

He said it now. And then he said it again, as if he were learning it.

“Tobin.”

“Yes, Father.”

“I have—“ His father’s voice cracked. He tried again. “There is something I’ve wanted to — for a very long time. Since you were small. And I never—“ He stopped.

And Tobin did not finish his sentence for him.

That was the thing Wren noticed most, and remembered afterwards, and told Mira about, on the stair. He did not finish it. He did not say it’s all right or you don’t have to or I know. He did not cut in. He did not over-explain. He knelt on the stone floor with his father’s hands in his, and waited — patiently, quietly, the way the old man used to wait on the wall when a wick would not catch — for his father to find the words.

It took a long time.

“I’m proud of you,” said Lord Edric Harrowgate at last, in a voice like something breaking open. “I’m so proud of you. I have always — your mother would have — and I never said. I never let you finish. At supper. Do you remember? You’d try to tell me about your machines. Your model of the Ring. And I’d—“

“I remember,” said Tobin.

“Tell me now,” said his father. “Please. Tell me about it now. The model. I want to hear it. All of it.” His thin hands tightened on his son’s. “I’ll not interrupt. I swear to you. Not once.”

And Tobin Harrowgate, kneeling on the floor of a cell at the top of the Queen’s tower at the end of the world, with an old man’s pole beside him and his father’s hands in his, began to tell his father about the Orrery of the Ring.

He told him about the hundred and forty-four beads. He told him about the copper flame-wires, and the spire in the middle for the Beacon, and how he had worked out the resistances. He told him about the night he saw a bead moving in the Low Quarter where no Ring-lamp was, and followed it down the Hill. He told him how the beads had all gone gold, and stayed gold. And how, in the spring, little lights had begun to come on all over the brass city where he had never wired anything at all.

It took a quarter of an hour. It was very technical. Some of it was quite boring.

His father did not interrupt once.

They were getting him up off the shelf — he was so weak he could hardly stand; Aren had one arm and Tobin had the other — when Cinder growled.

She was in the doorway. She had been sitting in it the whole time, with her back to the cell, looking out into the corridor, keeping watch. And now she was on her feet with every hair on her back standing up, and her spark blazing, and her lips drawn back off her small white teeth, and the growl coming out of her was a sound Wren had heard only once before.

On the Hill. In the Queen’s camp.

And then, from the corridor, a voice.

It was soft. It was sweet. It was very reasonable, and very kind, like warm milk going cold; and it came along the black glass corridor from the stair, unhurried, the way a person speaks who has been standing outside a door for some time, listening, and is in no hurry at all to come in.

“There you are, little sweep,” it said. “I wondered when you’d come up.”

Wren went cold from her head to her feet.

“And Varrick,” said the voice, sorrowfully. “Dear Varrick. Back again. And young Master Harrowgate, come for his father. How very touching. I did so enjoy that.” A small soft sigh. “And the old woman with the crutch, and the Delver girl, on the landing below. And the fox. And the fisherwoman, mending her little boat in my cove.” The voice smiled. You could hear it smile. “And the two in the first hall, by the window. Holding hands.”

Wren could not breathe.

“Oh, my dears,” said the Umbral Queen, gently. “Did you really think I didn’t know? I have known since the moment your little boat crossed the line. I have known every step you’ve taken on my stair.” There was a soft rustle in the corridor, like silk, coming nearer. “Come out, now. All of you. There’s no hurry. I’ve had a supper laid.”

fields.title: The Queen’s Table
fields.body_html:
The supper was laid in a long hall halfway up the Spire, and there was nothing wrong with it at all.

That was the dreadful thing. Wren had expected — she did not know what she had expected. Bones, perhaps. Cobwebs. Something out of the stories Mott’s lads used to tell in the yard to frighten the little ones. But the Queen’s table was beautiful. It was a long, long table of pale grey wood, polished like glass, running the whole length of a hall whose walls and ceiling were black glass, so that the table and everything on it was reflected over and over, dimly, into the dark, as if there were a hundred tables going away for ever. It was laid with a white cloth. There were silver dishes on it, and silver cups, and tall silver candlesticks with tall white candles in them, burning with a pale flame that gave no heat and cast no shadow. And on the dishes there was food: roast fowl, and white bread, and fruit, heaped high, apples and pears and grapes, and cakes iced white, and jugs of something pale to drink.

It was all grey. The fowl was grey, and the bread, and the fruit; the grapes were grey and the apples were grey. But it was perfect. Every grape round. Every apple shining. It looked like the most wonderful feast in the world, done in ash.

They had been brought there by Knights. Not roughly. The Knights had simply come — out of the black glass walls, it seemed, out of nowhere, in their grey armour with their empty eyes — and stood round them in the corridor outside the cell; and then walked, and they had walked with them, because there was nothing else to do. Down the stair. Past the landing where Mira and Sister Hale had been waiting, and were waiting no longer, because the Knights had them too. And into the long black hall, and the table.

They were all there. Wren and Tobin, and Lord Edric between Tobin and Aren, held up by both of them, so weak he could hardly walk. Mira, very white, with the Chronicle in its flour-sack clutched against her chest. Sister Hale, on her crutch, with her one bright eye going everywhere. Cinder, in Wren’s arms, rigid, growling without stopping, a low continuous sound like a kettle that will not boil.

And at the far end of the table, on two tall grey chairs set a little apart from the rest — washed, and dressed in clean grey clothes, and sitting very upright with their hands folded in their laps like children at a party — Tam and Linnet Ashby.

They were not grey. Not quite. The colour that the lamp had given them in the Hall of Sleepers was still in their faces. But it was faint, now, the way colour is faint in a picture that has been left in the window too long. And they were not looking at anything. Their eyes were open, and a little glazed, and fixed on the far wall; and when Wren came into the hall and saw them, and stopped, and made a sound, they did not turn their heads.

“Mam,” said Wren.

It came out of her before she knew it. The first time. The very first time in eight years she had said that word to anybody; and she said it across the Queen’s table, in the Queen’s hall, to a woman who did not hear.

“They’re quite well,” said a voice from the head of the table. “Don’t fret, little sweep. They’re only resting. I thought they might be tired.” A soft laugh. “Do sit down.”

I have told you about the Queen before. I told you how she looked on Cinder Hill, in her grey tent, beside her dark mirror: very tall, and beautiful, silver-grey from head to foot like a statue of frost given life, with a voice like warm milk going cold and eyes that were the only wholly dark thing about her.

She was the same. And she was not.

She sat at the head of the table in a tall grey chair, in a long gown the colour of mist, with her silver hair coiled up on her head and her long silver hands resting on the white cloth; and she was still very beautiful. But the beauty was thinner. That was the only way Wren could think of it, afterwards. As if it had been painted on glass, and the glass had got cold, and the paint was starting, here and there, very slightly, to crack. At the corners of her mouth. At the edges of her eyes. And under it, through the cracks — just a little; you had to look — there was something else showing. Something dark.

And she was afraid.

Wren did not see it at once. She saw it when the Queen smiled at them, as they sat down: a lovely smile, warm and sorrowful and kind. And under the table, where she thought nobody could see, the Queen’s long silver fingers were twisting in the folds of her grey gown, round and round, the way Varrick’s thumb used to rub his palm.

“Eat,” said the Queen. “Please. You’ve come such a long way. Across my sea. Up my stair. You must be starving.”

Nobody moved.

“Oh, come.” The Queen picked up a grey apple from the dish in front of her and held it out across the table to Wren, in her silver fingers. “It’s quite safe. I give you my word. There’s nothing in it. Nothing at all.”

That was true. Aren told them so afterwards: there was nothing in it at all. That was the point. Everything in the Spire was like that. The apple was perfect and round and shining, and when you bit it, it tasted of nothing — not sweet, not sour, not anything; like biting a mouthful of air. You could eat the whole feast, every dish on the Queen’s table, and get up from it as hungry as you sat down, and hungrier.

Wren did not take the apple. After a moment, the Queen put it down.

“Well,” she said, gently. “Perhaps later.”

She looked down the long table at all of them, one by one, with her dark eyes. At Sister Hale, who glared back at her. At Mira, who looked at the table. At Tobin and his father, holding hands under the cloth like children. At Aren — longest at Aren. And then at Wren.

“I know why you’ve come,” said the Queen. “Of course I do. I knew before you knew it yourselves. You’ve come to take my Sleepers away.” She sighed. “And Lord Edric, whom I’ve looked after so carefully. And your mother and father, little sweep. And perhaps a great deal more than that.” Her fingers twisted, under the table. “You think the end is coming. Don’t you? You’ve all been feeling it since Midsummer. In your hands. That little warmth. You think it’s growing, and growing, and soon there’ll be so much of it that I won’t be able to stand it, and I’ll have to go away.” Her lovely face was very sad. “And you may be right.”

Nobody said anything.

“I’m not a fool,” said the Queen softly. “I know what happened at Midsummer. I felt it. The whole of Gloamhaven felt it. Every Hollow I had, every Knight, every ash-crow — they all felt it, like a cold wind. And it’s been getting worse. It’s everywhere now. In the Rings, and in the farms, and in the mines, and in the boats. Every day there’s more of you.” She looked down at her silver hands on the cloth. “I’m losing. I know I am. You don’t have to tell me.”

“Then let them go,” said Wren.

The Queen looked up at her.

“Let them go,” said Wren. “If you know. If you’re losing anyway. Let my mam and dad go. Let all of them go. Open the halls and let them go home.”

The Queen smiled.

“Yes,” she said. “Yes. That’s exactly what I was going to suggest.”

She leaned forward over the white cloth, and her voice dropped, low and warm and reasonable, the voice of somebody who has thought of a sensible arrangement that will suit everybody.

“I’ll do it,” she said. “All of it. I’ll open every hall in the Spire, all nine, and wake every Sleeper, and let them go. Every one. Your mother and father first. You can take them home tonight, in that fisherwoman’s boat, to your little lane in Emberwick, and your father can mend lamps again and your mother can sing.” She looked at Tobin. “And Lord Edric. You may have him back, young Master Harrowgate. Of course you may. He’s yours.” She looked at Mira, and Sister Hale. “And the ships. The ones on my sea. I’ll let them sail home. And the Hollows — all of them — I’ll call them in, every one, and keep them here, and they’ll never trouble your Rings again.” She spread her long silver hands. “And I’ll go away. I’ll stay here, in my Spire, in my own dark, on my own island, and never come out of it. Never again. You’ll never hear my voice. You’ll never see an ash-crow. You’ll have the whole of Gloamhaven, all of it, for your little lights.”

The hall was very quiet.

“All of that,” said the Queen, “for one breath.”

She looked at Wren.

“Put it out, little sweep. The lamp. His lamp. The first one, that he carried down the Mountain. That’s all. Not the others — I don’t care about the others; let them keep their little lights. Only that one. The first. Take it out of your coat, and hold it up to your lips, and breathe out. Once.” Her voice was so gentle. “That’s all I ask. One breath. And everyone goes home.”

I want to tell you that Wren said no at once. That she laughed, the way she had laughed at Prowle in the bakery. That she did not even think about it.

That is not what happened. I promised to tell you what was true.

Wren thought about it.

She sat at the Queen’s table with Cinder rigid in her lap and her hand inside her coat on the lamp, and she looked down the long white cloth at her mother and father, sitting upright in their grey chairs with their hands in their laps and their faces turned to the wall, not seeing her. She thought about the coal-hole, and the tune. She thought about Pike Street, by the canal, where her father’s shop had been; she must have walked past it a hundred times. She thought about her mother cutting her hair. She did not know if her mother would cut her hair. She did not know what mothers did. She had never had one.

She thought about Nettle, on the harbour wall at Skerrow, with the crab.

She thought about twelve thousand faces in one hall, and nine halls. About a ship’s boy called Jory with red hair. About Tobin’s father. About all of it, all at once. Everyone home. Everyone. For one breath.

And the lamp was only one lamp. There were hundreds now. Thousands. The Queen was right about that. The Flame was everywhere — in the Rings, and the farms, and the boats. In Nettle. In Bracken. In Snib. In everybody. It would not go out if this one went out. It did not need this one any more—

She took the lamp out of her coat.

It burned up in her hand at once, the way it always did, gold, in the Queen’s grey hall. It was the only true colour in the room. It lit the white cloth gold, and the silver dishes, and the grey feast, and all their faces round the table; and down at the end of the table it lit her mother’s face, and her father’s; and for a moment — just a moment — the colour came up in them a little stronger, and her mother’s eyes, fixed on the wall, flickered.

The Queen’s eyes were on the lamp. They had not moved from it. They were very wide and very dark, and there was something in them Wren had never seen before, not on the Hill, not anywhere. It was hunger. And it was terror. Both at once.

Wren held the lamp in her hand and looked at it.

The little battered brass lamp. Dented. A hairline crack in its glass chimney. A little hook on top. No oil, and no wick, and no need of any. Smelling faintly of bread and summer. It had waited fifty years in a sealed flue in Thornbury House for a sweep. It had come back to her out of the Soot Canal. It had lit the Beacon and the Ring and the waystones and Posy and Pim and Tavi and half of Soot Lane. It had gone down to a coal in Vaelport and a coal on the moor above Harrowgate, and come back. It had been in the Queen’s tent, on the Hill, at her lips.

Only breathe out, little sweep.

She had nearly done it then. She had had it right up to her mouth.

It was given, Wren. Not lost.

Wren looked up at the Queen.

“No,” she said.

The Queen did not move.

“No,” said Wren again. Her voice was shaking, but it was quite clear. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry, Mam. I’m sorry—“ That was down the table, to her mother, who could not hear. “But no.”

“Why?” said the Queen.

She said it very softly. She did not sound angry. She sounded, Wren thought, as if she really wanted to know.

“Why, little sweep? You’ve seen. You know there are hundreds of them now. It doesn’t need you any more. It doesn’t need that.” She looked at the lamp in Wren’s hand, and her silver fingers twisted and twisted under the table. “Your mother and father. Everyone. For one breath. One small breath. What is one little lamp against all that?”

“It’s not mine,” said Wren.

The Queen looked at her.

“It’s not mine to put out,” said Wren. “It was given me. You can’t put out a thing that was given you. Not for anything. Not even for — not even for them.” Her eyes were running and she did not wipe them. “That’s what you don’t understand. You never have. You think everything’s a bargain. You think if you offer enough, anybody’ll sell anything. Ardric sold you the sun. My — Tobin’s da sold you his letter. Varrick sold you his name.” She did not look at Aren. “And you think I’ll sell you this. If you offer me enough. If you offer me them.” Her voice cracked. “And I’d give you anything for them. Anything that was mine. But this isn’t mine to give you. It’s his. And he gave it me. And I’m keeping it. Because he said to.”

“Keep it,” she said. “He said keep it. You’ll want it. You’ve a long way to carry it yet.”

She put the lamp back inside her coat, against her ribs, and fastened it.

“So no,” said Wren.

The Queen sat very still at the head of the long table for a long moment.

Then she smiled.

It was not the lovely smile. It was a small, thin, tired smile, and it went right through the paint on the glass, and cracked it. And for a moment — just a moment — Wren saw what was underneath. It was not a face at all. It was a dark. A cold, hungry, frightened dark, like the inside of an empty well. And then the paint closed over it again, and the Queen was beautiful.

“No,” she said. “I didn’t think you would. Not really. You’ve always been very stubborn, little sweep. Like your mother.” She looked down the table at Linnet, who did not move. “She said no to me too, you know. On the wall. Eight years ago. I asked her very nicely to stop singing. She wouldn’t.”

She turned her dark eyes on Aren.

“And you, Varrick,” she said. “Dear Varrick. Have you nothing to say to me? After thirty years? You were my favourite. Did you know that? The best of all of them. I gave you everything you wanted.” She tilted her silver head. “Power that did something. Wasn’t that what you wanted? Wasn’t that what you said, in the street outside the Guild Hall, with your little oath-scar still pink?”

Aren looked at her down the length of the table.

He was very pale. His scarred right hand was flat on the white cloth, and the gold line across his palm was shining through his skin, and he did not hide it.

“No,” he said. “Aren.”

The Queen’s smile went still.

“My name,” said Aren, “is Aren. It’s not Varrick. It never was. You gave me that. I’m giving it back.”

For a long time the only sound in the hall was Cinder, growling.

Then the Queen rose from her chair.

She rose slowly, and she was very tall, taller than Wren remembered, so tall that her coiled silver hair seemed to brush the black glass ceiling; and the pale candles all down the long table leaned away from her, as if from a cold wind. She stood at the head of the table with her long silver hands at her sides, and looked down at them all.

“Very well,” she said. “Then you will not mind, Aren, if I show the little sweep what you served.”

Aren’s face went grey.

“No,” he said. “No — not him. She’s a child, she doesn’t need—“

“Oh, I think she does,” said the Queen softly. “I think she needs it very much. She has been carrying that little lamp about the world for a year and a half, giving it away, and she thinks she knows what it is. She thinks she knows what it’s worth.” She held out one long silver hand to Wren across the table. “Come with me, little sweep. Just you. Leave the fox. I won’t hurt you. I couldn’t, while you hold that — you know that. But there’s something at the top of my tower I’d like you to see. Something I’ve kept a very long time.” Her voice was very gentle. “And when you’ve seen it, I don’t think you’ll want to keep that lamp quite so much.”

“Don’t go,” said Tobin.

“Wren—“ said Mira.

“I’ll go,” said Wren.

She did not know why. She thought, afterwards, that it was because she had said no; and having said no, she could not very well sit there and be afraid of what came after. She put Cinder down on the chair beside Tobin — Cinder clung to her coat with all four paws, and had to be unhooked, and sneezed a furious shower of sparks at the Queen across the table — and she stood up.

She did not take the Queen’s hand. She walked round the end of the table by herself, past her mother and father in their grey chairs, not looking at them, because if she looked she would not be able to go; and she followed the Queen out of a small black door at the end of the hall, and up a stair.

It was a short stair, after all the others. A narrow one, very steep, going up and round inside the black glass. And at the top there was no door. The stair simply came out, the way a stair comes out onto a roof — into a round room.

It was open to the sky. There was no ceiling. The black glass walls went up round it in a great circle, and stopped, and above them was the night: the flat black starless night of the Sunless Sea, going up for ever.

But it was not dark.

In the middle of the round room, on a dais of black glass, there was a throne. A great tall throne of black glass, with a high back, carved all over with shapes that Wren did not look at for long. And on the throne there sat something very small.

And on its head there was a light.

It was so bright that Wren threw up her arm across her eyes. It was brighter than the lamp. It was brighter than the Beacon, brighter than the Midsummer forges, brighter than the glowstones in the mines under Vaelport. It was gold — real gold, the colour of the sun in the old stories, in the Chronicle, before the curse — and it burned on top of the small thing on the throne like a sun come down out of the sky and caught in a ring. And it filled the whole round room with its blazing, terrible light, so that the black glass walls shone like gold mirrors, and there were no shadows anywhere at all.

And it was cold.

That was the thing that Wren could not understand, at first, standing at the top of the stair with her arm over her eyes. The light was so bright, so gold, so like the true Flame. It should have been warm. It should have been the warmest thing in the world.

It was as cold as the Sunless Sea.

“There,” said the Queen, very softly, beside her. “There he is, little sweep. Look. That is what the sun was worth.”

Wren lowered her arm, very slowly, and looked.

fields.title: The King Who Could Not Die
fields.body_html:
He was very small.

That was the first thing. Wren had thought — she did not know what she had thought. That a king would be big. Tall, like the Warden, or broad, like Mott, or splendid, like the pictures of kings in the shop windows on Lantern Row, with robes and swords and beards. The thing on the throne was smaller than Nettle. It sat in the great black glass chair the way a doll sits in an armchair that is much too big for it, propped up, with its tiny hands on the arms.

It was white. Not grey, like the Sleepers. White — white as paper, white as the inside of a shell, white as bone that has lain a long time in the sun. Its skin was white and its hair was white, what there was of it, a few long strands like cobweb lying on its shoulders; and its robes, which must once have been gold or red or purple, were white too, faded to nothing, the way cloth fades in a window. And it was thin. So thin that you could see the shape of every bone through the white skin of its face and hands, the way you can see the veins of a leaf held up to the light. It looked as if a breath would blow it away.

It did not move.

But its eyes were open. And they were the only living thing in it. They were dark — not the empty dark of the Queen’s eyes, but dark the way eyes are dark in a face that has been crying for a very long time — and they were looking at Wren.

And on its head was the crown.

It was very plain. That surprised her too. A circle of gold, no thicker than her finger, with no jewels on it and no points; a ring of gold resting on the white strands of hair. And in the circle, filling it, burning on it and in it and through it, was the fire.

The fire of the sun.

It was so bright Wren could not look at it straight. She looked at it out of the corner of her eye, the way you look at the sun on a summer’s day; and even then it made her eyes water. It was gold, and white, and it moved like fire moves, curling and leaping; and it never stopped. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.

And it was cold. It came off the crown in waves, the cold, and filled the round room, and went into her bones.

And it was burning him.

She could see it, now. The light was so bright, and the old white face under it so thin, that the light went through it. It went through the white skin of his forehead, and his cheeks, and his closed lips, and his tiny hands on the arms of the throne. He was lit up from the inside like a lamp-shade. There was nowhere in him for the light not to be. And his dark eyes, looking at her out of the middle of it, could not shut. The lids were open. They had been open, she thought, for a very long time.

“Ardric,” said the Queen. “King of Gloamhaven, when there was a Gloamhaven. The Bright King. That’s what they called him, in the old days.” She laughed softly. “Shall I tell you about him, little sweep? I don’t suppose your Delver friend’s book tells it properly. They never do.”

Wren did not say anything. She could not.

“He had everything,” said the Queen. “Everything the sun could give. A kingdom, golden from one end to the other. A palace. A queen of his own, and children. And the sun shining on him every day, warm, the way it did then, before.” She walked slowly round the throne, trailing one long silver finger along its black glass arm. “And he was afraid. Of the one thing the sun could not give him. He was afraid of dying.”

The small white thing on the throne did not move. But its eyes followed her round.

“So he climbed the Bright Mountain,” said the Queen, “in the night. Alone. And I was waiting. I always wait at the top of frightened people’s roads.” She smiled. “And I said to him, I can give you a crown that never fails, and a life that never ends. And he said, what is the price? And I said, only the sun.” She stopped beside the throne and looked down at the crown, at the blazing gold, with her dark eyes, and her face in the light of it was very white and very hungry. “He paid it. The fire came out of the sun and into his crown. And the sun went pale over all the land, and the curse came down, on him and everyone. And he has never died.”

She bent down, close to the white face, and said, very gently, as you might say it to a child:

“Have you, my dear?”

The dark eyes in the white face looked up at her. They did not change.

“Three hundred years,” said the Queen, straightening up. “He has sat on this throne three hundred years, with the sun in his crown. He can’t take it off. His hands won’t let him. He can’t die. It won’t let him. He can’t sleep — he hasn’t slept since the night on the Mountain. He can’t shut his eyes against it. And it gives him no warmth at all. Not one spark. It’s the fire of the sun, little sweep, the very fire that used to warm the whole world — and he holds it, and it is the coldest thing there is.” She looked at Wren. “That is what it is worth. Do you see? That is what that is worth.” She looked at Wren’s coat, at the place where the lamp was. “Fire. Light. What you carry about so carefully. It’s only fire. And this is all fire comes to, in the end, when somebody holds it. A cold old man who can’t die.”

Wren stared at the small white thing on the throne.

“I’ll leave you with him,” said the Queen. “For a little while. You can talk to him, if you like. He doesn’t say much.” She went to the top of the stair, and turned. “And when you’ve had a good look, little sweep, and you’ve understood — come down, and we’ll talk again. About that breath.”

She went down the stair. The pale silk of her gown whispered on the black glass steps, and was gone.

Wren stood at the top of the stair, alone, in the cold gold blaze, and did not move for a long time.

She was frightened. She will not mind my telling you that. She was more frightened than she had been in the Queen’s tent on the Hill, or on the Beacon, or in the Forge. It was the eyes. The dark eyes in the white face, burning from inside, open, looking at her. Three hundred years of looking.

And then she thought — she did not know where it came from — of Granny Kettle’s sheep.

There had been a storm, the second night she was at the bothy, the night before she went back. Wind and rain off the high moor, so bad that the bothy’s turf roof had leaked and the hens had had to be brought down off their beam. And in the middle of the night Granny Kettle had shouted “THE YOWES” and gone out into it with her lantern; and Wren had gone too; and they had found the sheep in a hollow, huddled together against a wall, soaked and shaking. And one old yowe had got herself caught in the brambles at the edge of the hollow, and was standing there, quite still, with her eyes wide open in the lantern-light, too frightened to move and too frightened to make a sound. Just standing, and shaking, and looking at them.

She had not been dangerous. She had been frightened. That was all.

Wren looked at the small white thing on the throne, and its dark eyes looking back at her, and she thought: he’s frightened.

And then she was not frightened of him any more.

She went across the round room to the throne.

It was a long way. The cold came off the crown so strongly that it was like walking into a wind. Her eyes ran. Her fingers went numb. The lamp, against her ribs, under her fastened coat, was working hard — she could feel it — burning steadily, warm, against all that cold, the way your heart works when you are climbing a hill. She went up the black glass steps of the dais. She stopped in front of the throne.

Close to, he was even smaller. His feet, in white slippers, did not reach the floor. They dangled.

She sat down on the top step of the dais, at his feet, the way she used to sit on Mrs Fenn’s doorstep when she was small, with her knees up and her arms round them. And she looked up at him.

“Hello,” said Wren.

The dark eyes looked at her.

“I’m Wren,” she said. “Wren Ashby. From Soot Lane. In Emberwick.” She did not know if he knew where Emberwick was. She did not know if Emberwick had even been there, three hundred years ago. “I’m a sweep. I was a sweep. I’m not sure what I am now.”

Nothing.

“You don’t have to talk,” said Wren. “If you don’t want to. I just thought — she said nobody talks to you. Much.” She hugged her knees. “That must be horrible. I used to have a garret where nobody talked to me. And it was cold. Not this cold. But cold.”

The dark eyes did not change. But something moved in the white face — so little that she nearly did not see it. A sort of tremble, round the mouth. As if the lips were trying to remember how they went.

And then a sound came out of them.

It was so quiet that she had to lean right in to hear it. It was not a voice, quite. It was a whisper like the turning of very old pages, dry and thin and papery, in a book that nobody has opened for a hundred years.

“…Wren…”

“Yes,” said Wren. “That’s me.”

“…Ashby…”

“Yes.”

A long pause. The fire burned and burned in the gold ring on his head, and the light went through his white face.

“…nobody…” whispered the king. “…says their name… to me…”

So she talked to him.

She did not know what else to do. She sat on the steps of the black glass throne at the top of Nightfall Spire, at the feet of a king who had bargained away the sun, and talked to him the way she used to talk to Nettle in the garret when Nettle was cold and could not sleep. About nothing. About everything. About Soot Lane, and the bakery, and Mrs Fenn’s five children, and the time Nettle lit the oven. About chimneys — the tall twisty ones at Thornbury House, like barley-sugar. About Mott, and his hat. About Snib, and his buttons.

And then — because it was the most important thing she knew, and because she could not think of anything else that might help — she told him about the loaf.

“I was hungry,” she said. “I was always hungry. And I was outside Grubb’s, in Crookback Market, and he’d thrown me out, and I didn’t have anything. And there was this old man, with a basket of bread. And he gave me a loaf. A warm one. And I said how much, because you always do, in the market, it’s what you say. And he said no charge.” She looked up at the king. “No charge. It’s given.”

The dark eyes were on her face. They had not moved.

“And I didn’t believe him,” said Wren. “Because nothing’s free. Everything costs. That’s what I always said. If it doesn’t cost you, it’ll cost you later.” She swallowed. “And I turned round to say something cheeky. And he wasn’t there.”

She told him about the lamp, then. About finding it in the flue, burning with no oil. About it coming back to her out of the canal. About its law. It cannot be bought, stolen or earned. Only given. And about the Ring, and the Beacon. And about Old Ash. And about the Hill.

And about the man who had come walking up the Hill at dawn, with the colour coming back into the ash where he walked.

The king’s eyes changed.

She saw it. It was the first time anything in him had changed at all. When she said the Hill — when she said Cinder Hill — the dark eyes in the white face went wide. Very wide. And the tremble round his mouth came again, harder.

“…Cinder… Hill…” whispered the king. “…she told me… she told me… he was snuffed out… on the Hill… three hundred years… her dark took him… and he was gone…”

“He was,” said Wren. “She did. They put him out. On the Hill. In the dark. My friend Mira’s got a book that tells it — the Chronicle — the one who wrote the end of it was there. He saw. The Lampwright let her. He opened his arms.” She was not sure she had the words right; she had only heard Mira read it once, on the Hill, and she had been crying. “He took the whole curse into himself. Your bargain. And every grey year since. All of it. Like a wick takes oil. Nobody made him. He chose.”

The king had stopped breathing. Or nearly.

“And then on the third morning,” said Wren, “the fire woke.”

“…no…” whispered the king. “…no… she said… she said he was gone… gone for ever… she said…”

“She lies,” said Wren. “Not all the time. Only when it matters.” She wiped her eyes on her sleeve. “He came back. He’s alive. I’ve seen him. I’ve had breakfast with him.” She heard her own voice go up. “He made toast. On a fire on the top of Cinder Hill. And he burned the first bit. Black. And he laughed. And then he gave the second bit to me, and I said how much, and he said no charge, it’s given—“ She stopped, because her throat had closed. “And it was him. The man with the bread. In the market. It was him, all along.”

The king was staring at her.

His eyes in his white face were full. Wren saw it. They were so dry, she would have thought, after three hundred years of the crown’s light burning through them; but they were full, the way a cup is full, and as she watched, the fullness spilled over, and ran down — one tear from each eye, down the paper-white cheeks, slowly. And where the tears ran, the light from the crown could not quite get through. They left two thin dark lines in the blazing white of his face, like cracks in ice.

“…why…” whispered Ardric. “…why would he… after what I…”

“Because he does,” said Wren. “That’s all. That’s what he’s like. He just does.”

The king was quiet for a long time after that.

Wren did not say anything else. She sat on the step at his feet and hugged her knees and waited, the way Tobin had waited for his father in the cell. The fire burned on his head, cold and gold. The black starless sky went up overhead for ever.

And at last the papery whisper came again. Very small. Smaller than before. Not a king’s voice at all. A child’s.

“…would he have me…”

Wren looked up.

“…after what I did…” whispered the king. “…the sun… I sold the sun… everyone… the farmer in his field… the child in her cradle… I sold them all… for this…” The tiny white hands on the arms of the throne twitched, very slightly, and were still. “…would he… have me… after that…”

And Wren thought of Tobin.

Tobin, who had sold Ash for a letter, and said he did not know him, twice, to his face. Tobin, by the breakfast fire, with his scarred hands, being asked three times. Then follow me.

She thought of herself. I wish it had been you. And the toast held out across the fire. And the lamp at her own lips, in the tent.

And she thought of a tall man in a grey shirt on the wall of Harrowgate in the dusk, with his palm shining.

“He had Tobin,” she said. “And Tobin sold his best friend. He had me, and I said things you wouldn’t believe. I nearly put it out.” She looked up into the dark burning eyes. “And he had Varrick. The Queen’s own captain. Who served her thirty years, and took my mam and dad, and walked past me in the coal-hole. He had him. On the road. He called him by his name.” She held the king’s gaze. “So yes. I think he’d have you. I think he’d have anybody. I think that’s the whole point of him.”

The king’s eyes held hers for a long time.

Then they moved. Slowly, as if every tiny movement cost him a year. Down. To his own hands, on the arms of the throne.

They were clenched. Wren saw it now. They were not resting on the arms of the black glass throne; they were gripping them, so hard that the white knuckles stood up like the knuckles of a skeleton, and the tiny fingers were curled tight into the carvings — and had been, she understood, for so long that they had grown into that shape and could not uncurl. He had sat on this throne for three hundred years gripping the arms of it, holding on, because if he let go he would die.

Or because the crown would fall.

Or because he did not know how.

“…I can’t…” whispered the king. “…I can’t let go… I’ve tried… a hundred years… they won’t…”

“I know,” said Wren softly. “It’s all right. You don’t have to now.”

And then there were feet on the stair.

Heavy feet. Metal on glass. Knights.

Wren scrambled up off the step. Two Hollow Knights came up out of the stair-head into the blazing gold of the round room, grey and empty-eyed, and walked towards the dais; and behind them, on the stair, very soft, the Queen’s voice.

“Time to come down now, little sweep. You’ve had your look.” A pause. “I hope you’ve understood.”

The Knights took Wren by the arms. Not roughly. They did not need to be rough.

She did not fight. She looked back over her shoulder as they walked her across the round room towards the stair — back at the throne, and the small white thing on it, and the terrible cold blazing crown.

The king’s eyes were following her.

All the way across the room. All the way to the top of the stair. They did not leave her face for one moment; and as she went down the first step and out of the gold light into the dark, she saw his white lips move, once more, very slowly, shaping a word that she could not hear.

She thought it was her name.

fields.title: What Tobin Built
fields.body_html:
The Queen did not lock them up together. She was too clever for that.

She put them in the cells at the top of the Spire, in the long black glass corridor with the small iron doors, one to a cell: Wren in one, and Tobin in the next, and Mira, and Sister Hale, and Aren at the very end, furthest from the stair. She put Cinder in a cell of her own, which Cinder took very badly; they could hear her through the wall for an hour, yelping and scrabbling and sneezing sparks at the iron, until at last she went quiet, which was worse. And she sent Lord Edric back to his old cell, the twelfth on the left, and shut the door on him, and turned the key.

“There,” she said, in the corridor, very kindly. “You can think it over, little sweep. All of you. Take as long as you like. I have all the time in the world.” A soft laugh. “And so do your mother and father. I’ve put them back in their hall, by their window. Standing. I thought they’d be more comfortable.”

And she went away down the stair, and they heard the whisper of her silk go down and down into the dark, and stop.

Wren sat on the stone shelf in her cell with her back against the black glass wall, and did not cry.

She had the lamp. The Knights had not taken it; they could not. It burned against her ribs inside her coat, steady and warm, the only warm thing in the cell. She could have taken it out. She could have lit the cell gold. But she did not, because there was no point; and because she thought, if she took it out and looked at it, she might not be able to stop herself crying after all.

She thought about the king.

She thought about his tiny white hands gripping the arms of the throne, grown into that shape. About the two thin dark lines his tears had made in the blazing white of his face. Would he have me?

She thought about her mother, standing by the window in the first hall, with her lips moving.

She thought: we have to get out.

And then, through the wall, from the next cell, she heard Tobin say — quite loudly, and with enormous satisfaction — “Oh. Oh, that’s beautiful.”

“What is?” said Wren, through the wall.

“The lock,” said Tobin’s voice. “Wren, have you looked at the lock? On your door? Look. Look at it.”

Wren got off the shelf and looked at the lock.

It was a lock. It was a big black iron lock on the inside of the door, with a keyhole. She did not see what was beautiful about it.

“Not the keyhole,” said Tobin, impatiently, as if he could see her. “The bolt. Look at the bolt. At the top. Where it goes into the wall.”

Wren looked. At the top of the iron door, where the edge met the black glass frame, there was a bolt: a thick iron bar that slid out of the door into a hole in the wall. And on the end of it, going into the hole — she had to stand on the shelf to see — there was a little loop of chain. Thin, black, iron chain, very fine, going away into the wall through a hole no bigger than her finger.

“It’s connected,” said Tobin’s voice. He sounded as if Midsummer had come again. “All of them. Every bolt. Mine’s the same. There’s a chain on the end of each bolt, going into the wall. And I’ve been listening — Mira, are you listening? — and the chains all go the same way. Towards the end of the corridor. Towards the stair.”

“I’m listening,” said Mira’s voice, from further down. “Tobin, I don’t—“

“It’s a master lock,” said Tobin. “There’s one mechanism. Somewhere. That holds every bolt in this corridor shut at once. Probably every bolt in the Spire. She doesn’t have to lock every door with a key — the key’s only for show. There’s a chain from every bolt, running through the walls, all joined up, to — to something. A drum, probably. Or a lever. And something’s holding it tight. Keeping all the bolts shot.” His voice went up. “If you let go of that one thing, Wren — every bolt in the Spire would come undone. At once.”

“Every bolt?”

“Every door in the Spire. The cells. The stairs. The—“ He stopped. “The halls. The Hall of Sleepers. All nine. If they’re on the same chain. And I bet you they are. She’s very tidy, Aren said. She likes things kept.” His voice dropped. “And I think I know where it is. I could hear it, when they brought us up. When we passed the big shaft.”

There was a shaft, in the middle of the Spire.

Aren told them about it, through the walls, in a low voice that carried down the black glass corridor from the end cell. Wren had seen it, without understanding what it was, when they climbed the servants’ stair: every so often the stair had passed a slot in the inner wall, and through the slot there had been nothing — a great round empty well, going straight up the middle of the Spire from bottom to top, in the dark, with the cold coming up out of it like breath. And in the well, hanging, chains.

“The great lift,” said Aren. “It was built when the Spire was built. By hollowed men — thousands of them. To carry things up. Stone, and glass. And her.” A pause. “She doesn’t use the stair, mostly. She goes up and down the shaft. There’s a cage.”

“And a counterweight,” said Tobin. “There has to be. For the cage. A big one. At the bottom.” He was talking very fast now, the way he did when a machine was coming clear in his head. “And I heard it. When we passed. There was another chain, a different one, going down the side of the shaft, very tight, humming. Like a harp string. All the little chains from the bolts would have to join it somewhere. And then it would go down to — I bet it’s the same counterweight. Or one beside it. Something heavy, hanging, pulling all the bolts shut.” He took a breath. “If you cut it. Or knocked out the pin — there’ll be a pin, holding it, there’s always a pin — the weight would drop. And every bolt would come back.”

“How do you know all this?” said Mira. “You can’t see any of it.”

“I can see the bolt,” said Tobin. “And I heard the chain. And I’ve built a model of every lamp in the Ring of Emberwick, wired to one spire in the middle.” He sounded almost embarrassed. “It’s the same thing, really. Only backwards.”

“But we’re locked in,” said Wren. “We can’t get to the shaft. We can’t get to anything.”

There was a silence through the wall.

“No,” said Tobin. “No. That’s true. We can’t.” He did not sound beaten, though. He sounded like somebody working on a sum. “But the chain comes in. Into the cell. Through the hole by the bolt. It’s very thin. And it’s under tension — very tight — I can feel it, if I put my finger on it, humming.” A pause. “And I’ve got Ash’s pole.”

“So?”

“So it’s got a hook on the end,” said Tobin. “A brass one. For lamps. And brass is soft and iron’s hard and that’s no good — but the hook’s not the point. The pole’s the point. It’s long. It’s very long. And it’s warm.” His voice went quiet. “When I hold it, it’s warm. It’s got the Flame in it. You saw it on the wall at Harrowgate. You saw it on the boat. And the chain is her chain, Wren. It’s made of the same stuff as the rest of this place. It’s cold. It’s — it’s like the glowstones, a bit. Like the Hollows. And what does the Flame do to anything that’s hers?”

Wren was quiet.

“Burns it,” said Mira softly.

“It might,” said Tobin. “If I hold the pole against the chain where it comes into my cell. And — and give it. Not push it. Not use it as a weapon. You can’t do that, it only goes low. But if I hold the pole there and give it the Flame. Freely. Just — let it go into the chain. The way you’d light a wick.” He breathed out. “Then it’ll go along the chain. Like the Flame goes along the copper in the Orrery. Like it went down the flame-pipes in Emberwick, from the Beacon to the Ring. All the way along. Into the wall. Down to the shaft. Down to the—“

“The pin,” said Aren, very softly, from the end of the corridor.

“The pin,” said Tobin.

Nobody said anything for a while.

“It’s a very good idea,” said Mira at last. “Is it a possible idea?”

“I don’t know,” said Tobin honestly. “I’ve never done it. Nobody has. It might do nothing. It might — I don’t know what it might do. The chain might melt. The bolts might fuse. Every door in the Spire might stick shut for ever.”

“Well,” said Sister Hale, from her cell, in her cracked strong voice. It was the first thing she had said since the supper. “Well. They’re shut now, aren’t they, duck?”

Tobin laughed. It was a small shaky laugh, but it was a real one.

“Yes,” he said. “Yes, they are.”

“Then do it,” said Wren.

It was Sister Hale who sang. She said somebody had to, to cover the noise, in case there was noise; and anyway, she said, she wanted to.

She sang the Lamplighters’ Psalm. She sang it from her cell at the top of Nightfall Spire as loud as she had ever sung anything — louder than in the barns, louder than on Midsummer morning, louder than on the cart coming over the hill to Harrowgate — in her cracked, old, terrible, glorious voice, and the black glass corridor took it and threw it about and sent it back from all the wrong places, so that it seemed to come from everywhere at once. Though I walk through the gloaming, I will fear no dark. And Mira joined in. And Aren, from the end cell, in a low rough voice, remembering the words as he went. And Lord Edric, from the twelfth cell on the left, very faintly, very badly, a long way behind everybody — he had never been allowed the old songs, and had forbidden them in his own house; and he was learning them now, from an old woman through a wall, line by line.

And Wren, in her cell, sang too.

And under the singing, in the next cell, Tobin Harrowgate stood on his stone shelf with Ash’s pole in his scarred hands, and held the end of it against a thin black humming chain where it came out of the wall by the bolt; and shut his eyes; and gave.

Nothing happened for a long time.

Wren, in the next cell, could not see. She could only hear Tobin breathing, through the wall, slow and careful. And the singing. And then — under the singing, so faint she thought she had imagined it — a sound.

A thin, high, singing sound. Like a wet finger round the rim of a glass.

It was the chain. It was the little black chain coming out of the wall by her own bolt, at the top of her own door. She climbed onto her shelf and looked at it, and it was humming — not the tight cold hum it had made before; a different note, higher, sweeter, rising. And as she watched, the little black links of it went, very faintly, gold.

The gold ran along it. From the hole in the wall, from Tobin’s side, along the loop and up into the end of her bolt — and through, and out of the other side, and on, into the wall towards Mira’s cell, and the next, and the next. Like the Flame running through copper. Like the Ring of Emberwick going gold, one lamp after another, from the Beacon. She could hear it going, now, in the walls of the corridor — that thin sweet singing note, travelling, getting fainter as it went, along the black glass towards the stair, and the shaft.

And down.

Down the shaft. Down the great humming chain on the side of it. Down and down through the whole height of Nightfall Spire, past the nine halls, past the long hall with the table, past the landing where they had first opened the doors, all the way to the bottom, to wherever the chain ended.

Wren held her breath.

From somewhere very far below — so far that it was less a sound than a shiver in the black glass under her feet — there came a crack. Like a great bone breaking.

And then a long, long, falling roar, like a mountain sliding into the sea.

And every bolt in Nightfall Spire came back at once.

It was not quiet. I will say that.

Every iron bolt on every iron door in the long black corridor at the top of the Spire shot back out of its hole in the wall at the same moment, with a noise like a hundred hammers hitting a hundred anvils, all together. The doors swung open. Wren’s door swung open so hard that it hit the wall and bounced back and nearly shut again. And from somewhere below, all down the Spire, through the walls and the stair and the great shaft, came the same noise, over and over, getting fainter, as door after door after door after door came unbolted and swung: clang — clang — clang — clang —

Cinder came out of her cell like a cork out of a bottle and went straight past Wren’s legs, down the corridor, and bit the first Hollow Knight who came running up the stair, hard, on the ankle.

The Knight looked down at her in its empty grey way. And where she had bitten it — through the grey iron greave, through to whatever was underneath — there was a small, neat, smoking ring of gold. The Knight sat down on the top step of the stair, quite suddenly, and stayed there.

“Good fox,” said Sister Hale, coming out of her cell on her crutch. “Oh, good fox.”

They went down.

They went down the black glass stair in a rush — Wren in front with the lamp out at last, blazing in her hand, lighting the whole stair gold; Tobin with Ash’s pole, his face shining; Mira with the Chronicle; Sister Hale on her crutch with Aren’s arm under hers; Lord Edric between Tobin and Aren, stumbling, but on his feet. And Cinder, ahead of everybody, a streak of grey and gold.

The Knights came up at them, and fell back from the lamp, shrieking, and fled down the stair ahead of them like smoke going down a chimney.

They passed the doors of the ninth hall. They were standing open, both of them, wide, on their great hinges, with the frost-white air coming out. Inside, in the grey, twelve thousand Sleepers stood in their rows, and did not move.

“No time,” said Aren. “The first hall. Wren’s — it has to be the first. Then the rest. Then—“

“No,” said Mira.

She had stopped at the open doors of the ninth hall, and was looking in.

“No,” she said again. “Aren — we don’t have to do them in order. We don’t have to do them ourselves.” She turned round, and her face was alight. “Don’t you see? It’s like Soot Lane. It’s like the Scarecrow Farms. We don’t have to light every one. We only have to light the first.”

And she walked into the Hall of Sleepers, and took the hand of the nearest grey woman in the nearest row, and said, “Good evening. I’m Mira,” and gave.

It went through the ninth hall like fire through dry grass.

That is the only way I can say it. The grey woman woke, in the lamp-light, with the colour coming up in her face — and turned, in astonishment, to the grey man beside her, and without even knowing what she did, put out her warm hand to him. And he woke. And turned to the next. And the next woke, and the next, and the next, down the row and across to the next row and the next, faster than anyone could follow it, a long gold ripple going away through the grey in every direction like the rings when you drop a stone in a pond, until the whole of the ninth Hall of Sleepers, twelve thousand people, was waking at once — blinking, stirring, crying out, calling names. Names that had not been said in that hall for three hundred years.

Some of them were so old. Wren saw them as she ran past the doors: people in clothes nobody had worn for longer than anyone could remember, with faces from the old pictures, looking round them in utter bewilderment at the black glass walls and the gold light and each other. Some of them were children. And all of them — every single one, as they woke — turned to the next one and put out their hands.

“Go on,” shouted Mira, from the middle of it, over the noise. “Go on, Wren! Go to your mam! We’ll do this! Go!”

So they went on down. And it went with them.

Because the Sleepers who had woken in the ninth hall came out of it onto the stair, in their hundreds, and went down — and up — to the other halls, with the Flame in their hands. Because the doors of every hall were open, now, every bolt drawn back. Because the people who woke in the eighth hall went to the seventh, and the seventh to the sixth. Down and down the whole height of the Spire, from hall to hall, like the Flame going down the copper pipes from the Beacon, the waking went; and the black glass stair filled up with people — bewildered, weeping, laughing, holding each other up, holding each other’s hands, every one with a little gold light in their palms — going down.

Wren ran ahead of them all.

She ran down past the eighth hall and the seventh. Past the long black hall with the table, where the white candles had all gone out and the grey feast lay on the white cloth untouched. Past the slit in the stair-wall where they had seen Prowle — and he was there, still, in the long gallery, on his grey bench, with his grey blanket round him and his mouth open, staring at the gold light coming down the stair; and as Wren ran past, a woman in a dress from three hundred years ago leaned in at the gallery door and held out her warm hand to him, and he took it before he could stop himself.

Past the sixth hall, and the fifth, and the fourth.

To the first.

The doors were open. Inside, in the grey, the waking had already begun — it had come down the stair before her; it was everywhere now — and the hall was full of gold and noise and people. But Wren did not see any of them. She ran between the rows, the way Mira had walked, without needing to count, without needing to listen, straight to the tall narrow window in the black glass wall.

They were there.

They were standing by the window. They were not grey. They were not glazed, or faint, or fixed on the wall. They had woken — properly, all the way — the moment the Flame came into the hall, and they had turned round from the window, and they were looking for her.

Linnet saw her first.

She did not say anything. She held out her arms.

And this time — I am glad to tell you; I have been waiting to tell you for a long time — Wren ran into them.

I said I would not tell you very much about that part. I will keep my word. But I will tell you this: that Tam Ashby put his great freckled arms round both of them, his wife and his daughter together, and lifted them clean off the floor, and held them there; and that he was crying out loud, like a child, without any shame at all; and that the three of them stood like that by the window of the first Hall of Sleepers, in the gold, for a long time, while all round them twelve thousand people woke up.

It was Aren who found them, after a while. He came between the rows with Lord Edric on one arm and his face very grey and very tired.

“Wren,” he said. “The shore. Look.”

He pointed at the window.

They looked out. The tall narrow slit in the black glass looked out over the grey city of Nightfall, down the hill, to the cliffs and the black shingle and the Sunless Sea.

And the sea was full of lights.

They were coming in from the west, out of the dark, across the black water. Hundreds of them. Little gold lights on the bows of boats — fishing-boats, and coasting-boats, and rowing-boats, and things with sails and things with oars. Highland boats from Skerrow and all down the coast. Boats from Vaelport, with lamps on their masts — Pim’s, Wren found out afterwards, and the Pellows’, who had sailed round the whole coast of Gloamhaven in nine days because the fisherwomen had brought them Mira’s letter. And in among them, bigger, slower, three-masted, ancient, with their grey sails gone brown and red and patched, and their decks crowded with people holding up their hands — ships. Old ships. Ships from the Drowned Fleet. And at the front of them all, on the bow of a great three-masted merchantman with KITTIWAKE in faded gold letters on her stern, a small figure with red hair, waving a lantern over his head.

And in the cove below the cliffs, with her bow mended and her brown sail up, the Brave Gannet; and on her deck, roaring something that Wren could not hear but could quite well imagine, a broad woman in three jerseys.

“Daft first,” said Wren. Her voice was shaking. “Then everybody.”

It was then — in the middle of it all, with her mother’s arm round her and her father’s hand on her head and the whole Hall of Sleepers awake and moving round them towards the doors, towards the stair, towards the boats — that Wren looked up.

Up. Through the black glass ceiling. Through the eight halls above, and the corridor of cells, and the long hall with the table. Up to the top of the Spire.

To the round room open to the sky. And the throne. And the small white thing sitting on it, alone, in the cold gold blaze, with its hands gripping the arms of the throne and its dark eyes open.

Everybody was going down. Everybody was going home.

Nobody was going up.

“Mam,” said Wren.

The word came out quite easily, this time. She did not even notice.

“Mam. Da. Go with Aren. Go down to the boats. I’ll come. I promise I’ll come.” She pulled out of her mother’s arms. “There’s somebody I’ve got to see first.”

“Wren—“

But she was already gone, between the rows, towards the doors and the stair; going up, against the whole tide of the waking Spire coming down.

fields.title: Ardric’s Choice
fields.body_html:
It was a long way up, against the tide.

The whole of Nightfall Spire was coming down the stair. Wren had to fight her way up through it — through people, hundreds of them, thousands, pouring down the black glass steps from the halls with the Flame in their hands, weeping and laughing and calling out names, holding each other up. Old men and young women and children. A man in a fur hat from some century nobody remembered. A girl in a nightgown. Two old ladies with their arms round each other, singing something in a language Wren had never heard. They filled the stair from wall to wall, and they were going down, all of them, to the boats; and Wren went up through them like a salmon going up a weir, squeezing and ducking and saying sorry, sorry, excuse me, sorry, with the lamp held up over her head so it would not get knocked out of her hand.

Nobody stopped her. Nobody had time. But once, on the landing by the fourth hall, an old woman in a shawl caught her by the sleeve as she went past, and peered into her face with eyes that had just woken up from two hundred years, and said, “Going the wrong way, love.”

“I know,” said Wren. “I’ve got to.”

The old woman looked at her a moment longer. Then she let go, and patted Wren’s cheek with a warm hand.

“Then go on,” she said. “Go on, then. Go on.”

Above the ninth hall, the stair was empty.

Everybody had gone down. The doors of the cells stood open along the black glass corridor, and nobody was in them. The stair beyond went on up, narrow and steep, into the dark, and there was nobody on it but her.

And Cinder.

Wren had not known Cinder was with her. She had thought the fox had gone with Mira, or Tobin, or with Aren down to the boats. But at the top of the corridor, where the narrow stair began, Cinder was sitting on the bottom step, with her tail curled round her feet and her spark bright and steady, as if she had been waiting there for some time and was beginning to wonder where Wren had got to.

“Oh,” said Wren. “There you are.”

Cinder stood up and went in front, up the stair, the way she always did. And after a moment Wren followed her.

The round room at the top of the Spire was just as she had left it.

The black glass walls going up in a circle, and stopping. The black starless night overhead, going up for ever. The dais. The great black glass throne. And on it, propped up like a doll in an armchair that was much too big, with his tiny feet dangling and his hands clenched on the arms of the throne, the king; and on his head the crown, with the fire of the sun burning in it, so bright that the whole round room blazed with cold gold light and there were no shadows anywhere.

His eyes were open. They were looking at the stair-head. They had been looking at it, Wren thought, ever since she went down.

She came across the room to him through the cold.

She did not say anything. She went up the black glass steps of the dais, the way she had before, and sat down on the top step at his feet, with her knees up and Cinder against her side. And then she took the lamp, which was burning gold in her hand, and set it down on the step beside her. Close. Close to the throne, so that its small warm light fell on the king’s tiny white clenched hands on the arms of the throne.

That was all. She did not ask him for anything.

The king looked down at the lamp.

His eyes moved. Slowly. From her face, down to the little battered brass lamp on the step, with its cracked chimney and its small gold flame. They rested on it for a long time.

The lamp burned. It did not blaze. It did not roar up the way it did when it was given to someone. It only burned, small and steady and gold, the way it had burned on the windowsill of her garret in Soot Lane on the first night, when she lay on her straw mattress and peeked at it and found that the room was warm.

And the room was warm.

Not all of it. The crown’s cold came off the throne in waves, still, and filled the round room, and went into Wren’s bones. But in the little circle of light round the lamp, on the top step of the dais, there was warmth. It was not much. It was about as much as you would feel from a candle. But it was warm, the way the true Flame is warm, the way summer is warm on a wall, and a hand is warm on your shoulder in the dark. And it fell on the king’s white hands.

Wren saw them change.

Not much. Not the way Posy had changed, or the Sleepers, or her mother. The grey was not in him; he was not greyed; there was nothing in him for the Flame to drive out. He was only cold. He had been cold for three hundred years. And now, very slowly, in the light of the little lamp, his tiny white clenched hands on the arms of the black glass throne went — not pink; not anything so much as that — but a little less white. As if somebody had breathed on them.

The king made a sound.

It was not a word. It was a long, thin, shaking breath, going in; like a person who has been under water for a very long time, coming up.

“…warm…” he whispered.

“Yes,” said Wren.

“…it’s warm…”

“Yes. It always is.” She did not move. “It’s not much. It’s only a little lamp. But it’s warm.”

The king looked at the lamp, and at his hands in its light, and two more tears ran down his white face, and left two more thin dark lines where the crown’s light could not get through.

They sat like that for a long time. I do not know how long. Wren did not know either. Down below, far down, she could hear the Spire emptying: the noise of the stair, and the shouting, and the singing, and the boats. Up here, there was only the cold, and the blazing crown, and the little lamp on the step, and the king breathing.

And then the Queen came up the stair.

Wren knew it was her before she saw her. The lamp knew. Its flame bowed — not away; it never bowed away from anything — but down, low, the way a candle bows in a draught when a door is opened onto a cold night. And the cold in the round room got worse. Much worse. It came up the stair-head like water coming up a well, and filled the room, and the black glass walls frosted over white.

She came up out of the stair into the gold blaze, and stopped.

She was not beautiful any more.

Not quite. The shape of her was the same — very tall, silver-grey, in her long mist-coloured gown, with her silver hair coiled up on her head. But the paint on the glass had cracked. All over. It had cracked at the corners of her mouth and the edges of her eyes and right across her lovely forehead, and through every crack, now, the dark showed: a cold, hungry, empty dark, like the inside of a well. Her face was like a window with frost on it, and the frost was thin, and through it you could see the night.

And she was frightened. You did not have to look for it now. It was in her eyes, and her mouth, and her long silver hands, which were not still at all, which twisted and twisted in front of her as if they had a life of their own.

She looked at the empty stair below. She looked at the king on his throne. She looked at the little lamp on the step, and Wren beside it, and the fox.

“So,” she said.

Her voice was not warm milk going cold. It was only cold.

“So. They’re all gone, then. All my Sleepers. Down the stair. Into the boats.” She laughed, a thin cracked little laugh. “Every one. Three hundred years of them. And my Knights, running about my stairs like headless hens, biting their own tails. And that fool Prowle, weeping, with some old woman’s hand in his.” She looked at Wren. “Was it the boy? With the chain? I suppose it was. Clever little Harrowgate. His father always said he was good with his hands.”

Wren did not say anything.

“And now,” said the Queen, very softly, “you’ve come for him.”

She did not look at Wren after that. She looked at the king.

She went past Wren, up the steps of the dais — Cinder snarled at her, low and dreadful, and she did not even glance at the fox — and stood beside the throne, and bent down over the small white thing on it, close to his face, the way she had before.

“My dear,” she said. “My dear. Look at me.”

The king’s eyes moved, slowly, from the lamp to her face.

“She wants you to let go,” said the Queen. “Doesn’t she? That’s why she’s come. That’s why she sits there, with her little light. She wants you to take your hands off the arms of your throne and let go of your crown.” Her voice was gentle, and terrible, and very close. “And you know what will happen if you do. Don’t you, my dear? You know. You’ve always known.”

The king’s white lips trembled.

“You’ll die,” said the Queen. “That’s all. The fire will go out of the gold, and the gold will go cold, and you will go cold with it — the ordinary way, the way everyone does. You’ll be three hundred years old in a moment. And you’ll die. In this room. On the floor, very likely, at the feet of a little sweep from Soot Lane.” She smiled. “And then you’ll go into the dark.”
