“No,” said Wren.

The Queen did not look at her.

“Into the dark,” she said to the king. “My dark. For ever. There’s nothing else, you know, my dear. There never was. All those stories — the Lampwright, and his breakfast fires, and his it’s given — they’re stories, for children. For sweeps. He won’t want you. Why would he? After what you did? You sold his sun.” Her face came closer. “He’ll never have you. Not after that. Nobody could. You will go into the dark, alone, the way you always knew you would, the night you climbed my Mountain. And it will be cold. And it will never, ever end.”

The king’s eyes, in the blazing white of his face, were wide and full of terror.

It was the old lie. Wren knew it. It was the oldest lie the Queen had. It was the one she had told Ardric on the Mountain, three hundred years ago, when he was afraid. It was the one she had told Varrick in the street. It’s useless. Nobody will have you. Lie down. It is easier in the grey.

And the king believed it. Wren could see him believing it. She could see the terror of it go through his tiny white body, and his clenched hands clench harder on the arms of the throne.

“That’s not true,” said Wren.

She did not shout. She did not stand up. She sat where she was on the top step, with the lamp beside her and Cinder against her side, and looked up at the king, past the Queen, as if the Queen were not there.

“It’s not true,” she said. “She’s lying. She always lies, when it matters.” Her voice was shaking, and she let it. “He’d have you. I told you. He had Tobin. He had me. He had Aren — she calls him Varrick, but that’s not his name. He had him.” She swallowed. “He came up the Hill. The Hill where she put him out. And he made breakfast. He’s not in the dark. He came back out of the dark. And he’ll come back out of it for you, too, if you go into it. I know he will.” She held the king’s eyes. “Morning comes. That’s what my mam used to sing. Morning comes, and the dark shall not keep us. It’s an old song. It’s older than you. It’s true.”

The Queen turned round and looked at her.

For the first time, she looked at Wren with nothing on her face at all. No smile. No sorrow. No kindness. Only the frost, and the dark showing through it.

“Be quiet,” she said.

“No,” said Wren.

And the king spoke.

It was the papery whisper. The turning of very old pages. But it was a little louder than before — enough for Wren to hear it without leaning in; enough for the Queen to hear it, beside him.

“…you…” whispered Ardric.

He was not looking at the Queen. He was looking at Wren.

“…you hold it…” whispered the king. “…I can’t… I can’t hold it any more… you hold it…”

And he opened his hands.

I want you to understand what that cost him. I am not sure I can make you. I am not sure anyone who was not there could understand it.

His hands had been clenched on the arms of the black glass throne for three hundred years. They had grown into that shape — the tiny white fingers curled tight into the carvings, the knuckles standing up like bones, the tendons in the backs of his hands like wires. They had not moved since the night on the Mountain. He had not been able to move them. He had tried, he had told Wren, for a hundred years.

And now he opened them.

It took a long time. It took everything he had. Wren saw it, in his face: the terrible effort of it, the dark eyes squeezing almost shut, the white lips drawn back off his teeth. The fingers moved — one, and then another — so slowly, a hair’s breadth at a time, peeling up off the black glass as if they had been glued there. Wren heard them creak. She heard a sound come out of the king that was not a word, a thin high sound of pure effort, like a very old door being forced open in a very cold wind.

And the Queen did not stop him.

She could not. Wren understood that, afterwards. She stood beside the throne with her silver hands twisting and the frost cracking all over her face, and she could not reach out and close his fingers again, any more than she could have reached out and taken the lamp off the step. A grasped thing can only be let go. Nobody can make you let go. And nobody can stop you.

The king’s hands came up off the arms of the throne.

They came up slowly, shaking, white, tiny, empty, into the blaze of the crown’s light. And they went up — slowly, slowly, shaking — to his own head. To the plain circle of gold resting on the white cobweb strands of his hair, with the fire of the sun burning in it.

And he took it off.

He held it out to Wren.

Not up. Not forward, the way you thrust a thing at somebody. Out. In his two tiny trembling white hands, held out to her at the height of her face, the way you hold out a loaf to somebody who is hungry.

“…it’s given…” whispered Ardric.

Wren took it.

She did not think about it. She did not think: it’ll burn me. She did not think: it’ll freeze me. She did not think about the Queen, standing over her, or the cold, or the blaze. She only saw an old man holding something out to her that he could not hold any more, and she put out her hands and took it from him, the way you take a heavy bag from somebody who is too tired to carry it.

It did not burn her.

It was heavy. Very heavy, heavier than anything that size had any right to be — heavier than the sack of lamps had been on Varrick’s horse; heavy as a stone; heavy as a whole sun. Her arms went down under the weight of it, and she had to hold it against her chest. And it was cold, still, at first. The cold came off it into her hands and her arms.

And then — while she held it — the fire in it lay down.

That was the only way she could ever describe it afterwards. It did not go out. It did not go dim. It lay down: the way a dog that has been snarling and pacing and barking at a gate all day lies down at last, with a long sigh, when its master comes home and puts a hand on its head. The leaping, curling, terrible blaze of it went quiet in the gold ring, and settled, and burned steady and low. And the cold went out of it. Not all the way. But it stopped pouring off it into the room. It sat in Wren’s arms, against her chest, beside the place where the lamp usually was, and was heavy, and quiet, and gold.

And it was the warmest thing she had ever held.

And the king—

The king was only an old man.

It happened in a moment. Between one breath and the next. The blazing light that had filled him from the inside for three hundred years went out of him, the way light goes out of a lampshade when the lamp is taken away; and he was not white any more, not blazing, not paper. He was only an old man. A very, very old man — so old you could not have said how old; brown and wrinkled and shrunken and bald, with a few white wisps of hair, and a face like a dried apple, and hands like dry leaves. Tiny, in the great black glass throne. Light as a feather.

And his eyes closed.

For the first time in three hundred years, the king of Gloamhaven shut his eyes.

And then — very slowly — he opened them again. And looked at Wren. And she saw that they were brown. Not dark; not burning. Just brown. An old man’s tired brown eyes.

And Ardric laughed.

It was the smallest laugh Wren had ever heard. A tiny, dry, cracked, astonished laugh, like a dry leaf blown along a step. As if something had happened to him that was so surprising, so unexpected, so impossible, that there was nothing whatever to do about it but laugh.

“Oh,” said the king. And his voice was not a whisper any more. It was an old man’s voice, small and quavering and quite clear. “Oh. Oh, my. It’s gone. It’s — I’m tired.” He laughed again. “I’m so tired. I haven’t been tired for — oh, my word—“

The Queen screamed.

It was the second time in all the long history of Gloamhaven that the Umbral Queen had ever raised her voice. The first had been on Cinder Hill, at dawn, when a stranger came walking up out of the Burned Country with scars on his hands.

This was worse.

It was not a sound, really. It was a dark. It came out of her mouth and her eyes and the cracks in her face, all at once, the way smoke comes out of a burning house when the roof falls in: a great black roaring rush of cold and night, pouring out of her into the round room at the top of the Spire, and up into the starless sky, and down the stair, and out through the black glass walls. The whole of her dark. Everything she had. Every grey year, every Hollow, every cold. All at once.

The lamp on the step bowed down low under it, and burned on.

The crown in Wren’s arms burned on.

Cinder stood in front of them both, between them and the Queen, with every hair on end and her spark blazing like a torch, and did not move one inch.

And under Wren’s feet, under the dais and the throne and the round room, through the whole of the black glass tower from its starless top to its roots in the black rock of the island, Nightfall Spire gave a long, low, terrible groan — like a living thing, like a great beast that has been wounded — and began, from top to bottom, to crack.

fields.title: The Long Night
fields.body_html:
Wren did not remember, afterwards, exactly how they got down.

She remembered pieces. The crack running across the floor of the round room, black, from the foot of the throne to the stair-head, wide enough to put her hand in. The black glass walls going ping, high and sharp, all round, like ice on a pond in a thaw. Cinder’s teeth in her sleeve, pulling. And the king — the old man; he was only an old man now — sitting in the great black throne with his eyes shut and a little puzzled smile on his face, as if he were waiting for somebody to tell him what happened next.

She remembered thinking: I can’t carry him.

She had the crown. It was so heavy that she could only hold it in both arms against her chest, the way you hold a sleeping baby, and even then her knees were shaking. And she had the lamp — she had snatched it up off the step and stuffed it inside her coat, burning, beside the crown. And there was the old man, light as a feather, but he could not walk; she could see that. He had not walked for three hundred years. And the Queen’s dark was pouring out of her into the room like black water out of a burst pipe, and the Spire was cracking, and the Queen herself—

She did not look at the Queen. She did not want to remember what she saw if she did.

And then there were feet on the stair. Big ones. Heavy and fast and coming up three steps at a time. And a voice — a slow, deep, rusty voice, like a cart that has not been driven for a long time, roaring:

“WREN!”

It was her father.

He came up out of the stair-head into the round room like a bull coming through a gate: big and freckled and sandy-haired and red in the face, with his shirt torn and his great hands out in front of him; and he did not stop. He did not look at the Queen, or the throne, or the cracks. He saw Wren, with the crown in her arms, and he crossed the round room to her in four strides and picked her up — crown and lamp and fox and all — under one arm, as if she weighed nothing at all.

“Da,” said Wren, into his shirt. It came out quite easily. “Da. Da. The king—“

Tam Ashby looked at the old man on the throne.

He did not ask who he was. He did not ask anything. He was a lamp-mender from Pike Street, and he had been a Sleeper for eight years, and he had woken up an hour ago to find his daughter grown; and there was a very old man sitting in a big chair in a house that was falling down, who could not get up. That was all Tam Ashby needed to know. He put out his other arm and scooped the king of Gloamhaven up out of his throne like a bundle of washing, and tucked him against his chest.

The old man opened his eyes, and looked up at Tam’s big freckled face, and blinked.

“Oh,” said Ardric. “Hello.”

“Hold on,” said Tam Ashby. And he turned round, with his daughter under one arm and the king under the other, and ran.

The stair was falling.

Not all at once. It went in pieces. A step would crack under their feet as they ran, and drop away behind them into the dark with a sound like a breaking plate. A slab of black glass would come away from the wall above and come sliding down past them, end over end, and shatter on the landing below. The whole Spire was shaking, now — a long, slow, sickening sway, like a tree in a wind — and the cracks were running down the walls faster than Tam could run, like lightning going down a sky.

But it was not dark.

That was the strange thing, the thing Wren held onto afterwards. The Queen’s dark was pouring down the stair behind them, black and cold and roaring. But the stair itself was lit. All the way down. Because everybody who had gone down it, all the waking Sleepers, thousands of them, had gone down it with the Flame in their hands — and wherever they had touched the black glass walls, on the way, putting out a hand to steady themselves, there was a mark. A handprint. Glowing faintly gold in the black, like the marks of warm hands on a cold window.

Thousands of them. All the way down. A stair of gold handprints in the dark.

And Tam Ashby ran down it, three steps at a time, with Wren and the king and the crown and the lamp and the fox; and the dark came after him and did not catch him.

At the landing by the first hall, Linnet was waiting.

She had not gone down to the boats either. Of course she had not. She was standing at the top of the next flight with her hands out and her face white, and when she saw them coming she did not say anything at all; she only turned round and ran down the stair in front of them, lighting the way.

They came out of the servants’ door at the bottom of the Spire into the grey city, and the city was full of people.

All of them. All the Sleepers. Every hall had emptied. They were pouring down the grey streets of Nightfall in their thousands, towards the cliffs and the shore and the boats — old and young, in every kind of clothes from every century, carrying each other and holding each other up, with their hands glowing gold; and the grey streets under their feet were not grey any more where they went. And the Knights were among them. Hollow Knights, in their grey armour, staggering and lost. Some of them were being led by the hand.

And behind them all, the Spire.

Wren looked back once, from Tam’s arm, at the end of the street. She wished afterwards that she had not; and she was glad, afterwards, that she had.

It was falling.

It went slowly, the way great things fall. The whole enormous tower of black glass, going up and up into the starless dark further than any eye could follow, was leaning — leaning out over the grey city towards the sea, very slowly, as if it were bowing. Cracks ran up and down it, black on black. And out of the cracks, and out of the top of it, and out of everywhere, the dark was pouring: the Queen’s dark, all of it, the way smoke pours out of a chimney when the fire below has been choked; a great black roaring flood of cold, going up into the sky and out over the sea and away over the edge of the world.

And then the Spire broke in the middle and fell into the Sunless Sea.

The noise of it went on and on. The black water went up in a wall. The island shook so hard that everybody in the streets of Nightfall fell down, all at once, and lay there, and the shingle on the shore went rattling down into the sea.

And when they got up again, the Spire was gone.

They got everybody into the boats.

I do not know how they did it. Mairi Dunlop said afterwards that she did not know either, and she had been doing it; she said it was the most daft thing she had ever seen, and she had seen a good few, and she wouldn’t have missed it for all the herring in the Highlands. There were thousands of people on the shore of Nightfall, and the island was shaking, and the black water was heaving and churning where the Spire had gone down. And there were hundreds of boats.

Highland boats. Vaelport boats. The old ships of the Drowned Fleet, with their patched sails. The Kittiwake, with Jory Penhallow in her bows, roaring orders in a voice that had been rusty yesterday and was not rusty now. The Pellows’ little blue-doored fishing-boat from Lantern Steps, with Mr Amos Pellow at the oars and Mrs Rose Pellow in the bow holding up a lantern and Pim, sleeves rolled up eight times, standing on the gunwale shouting for Mira.

They came in to the shore, and took on people until they were full, and pushed off, and the next came in. Over and over. In the dark. And every boat had a light on its bow, and every person had a light in their hands, so that the shore of Nightfall Spire was gold from end to end, and the black water in front of it was gold with their reflections — their reflections, Wren saw, from Tam’s arm; the black water was giving them back, now; the lamp-light was not going into it and vanishing; it was coming back.

The Brave Gannet came in last.

She had been the first in, and she had made eleven trips, and she was the last to leave. Mairi Dunlop was at the tiller and Callum and Rab at the sweeps, and the boat was so low in the water with people that the black sea was slopping in over her sides; and Tam Ashby waded out to her through the shallows, up to his waist, with Wren and the king above his head; and Linnet after him. And Aren after her, with Lord Edric over his shoulder. And Tobin and Mira and Sister Hale, Sister Hale on Callum’s back, with her crutch held up over her head like a banner, singing.

And then, just as Rab pushed off from the shingle with his sweep, a voice from the shore.

“Wait!”

They looked back.

A round figure was running down the black shingle towards the water, in a filthy torn plum velvet coat with a grey blanket flapping off its shoulders. It had no hat and no chain and no wig. It was crying. It ran into the sea up to its knees, and then up to its waist, and stopped, and stood there in the black water with its fat arms held out towards the boat.

“Please,” wailed the Lord Steward of Emberwick. “Please — please don’t leave me — I’ll pay — I’ll pay anything — I’ve got gold — I’ve got a strongbox—“

“Oh, for the love of—“ said Mairi Dunlop.

She leaned over the stern of the Brave Gannet, reached down with one great red hand, took Guild Master Cuthbert Prowle by the collar of his plum velvet coat, and hauled him up out of the Sunless Sea and over the side and into the bottom of the boat, where he lay among the nets like a landed codfish, gasping.

“Pay,” said Mairi Dunlop, with enormous scorn. “Pay, he says.” She turned back to the tiller. “Row, Rab.”

And then the dark came down.

It had been coming all along. It had poured out of the Spire as it fell — all of it, all the Queen’s dark, three hundred years of it at once — and gone up into the sky, and out over the sea. And now it came down.

It came down over the Sunless Sea like a lid on a pot. And it did not stop at the sea. They could see it going — or rather, they could see the last of the grey light going, ahead of it, west, towards the land. It went over the edge of the world. It went over the Highlands, and the Harrowgate moors, and the Greywaste, and Emberwick, and Vaelport, and the Burned Country, and the Bright Mountain. All of Gloamhaven. Every field and town and road. The pale cursed sun, which had risen every morning for three hundred years like a coin seen through dirty water, did not rise.

Night.

Not the night of Gloamhaven, which was dark enough. Not even the night of the Sunless Sea, with no stars. This was a night there had never been before: the Queen’s whole dark, let out at once, everywhere, thick and black and cold and pressing, like the dark at the bottom of the strongroom with the iron door shut, but over the whole world. You could not see your hand in front of your face. You could not see anything at all.

Except the lamps.

It was Tobin who saw it first.

He was sitting in the bows of the Gannet with his father’s head on his knee, because his father had fainted in the shallows and had not woken; and he was looking back the way they had come, west, towards the land. And he made a small sound, and then said, very quietly:

“Wren. Look.”

They all looked.

There was nothing. It was black from one side of the world to the other. The sea and the sky were one dark.

And then you saw them.

Lights. Tiny ones. Specks. Pin-pricks of gold, far, far off over the black water, low down, along the line where the land must be — so small you would think you were imagining them. One. And then another, beside it. And then, when your eyes got used to it, more. Dozens. Hundreds. All along the coast of Gloamhaven, and going back inland, behind it, as far as the eye could reach and further; scattered across the black like seeds across a field. Little gold lights in the dark. In every village and farm and Ring-town. On every road.

“It’s the Orrery,” said Tobin.

His voice was shaking.

“It’s the Orrery. It’s the — Wren, it’s the whole country. Like the beads. Like the little lights in the brass, when they came on in the Low Quarter. It’s—“ He stopped, and swallowed, and tried again. “Every one of those is a person. Every single one. Somebody holding a candle, or a lamp, or just their hands, in the dark. Holding on.” His eyes were full. “The Ring-lamps are going. They’ll all be going out, all over, every Guild lamp in every Ring. The dark’s too much for oil. And the glowstones — every glowstone in Vaelport will be cracking. But not those. Those won’t go out.” He wiped his face on his sleeve. “It’s not lamps. It never was. It’s people. It’s everybody we ever gave it to, and everybody they gave it to. And they’re all — just — holding on.”

Nobody said anything for a long time.

The little lights burned on, all along the edge of the world, in the dark.

“Where to?” said Mairi Dunlop at last.

It was very dark in the Gannet. Only the lamps in people’s hands, and the glow of their palms, lit it at all. The boat was packed so full that people were sitting on each other’s knees; the old man that had been a king was asleep in Tam Ashby’s lap, with his bald brown head tucked under Tam’s chin; Prowle was still in the bottom of the boat among the nets, weeping quietly. All round them in the dark, the other boats, every one a little gold light, were waiting.

“Back to Skerrow?” said Mairi. “We’ll want land. These folk have been standing up for three hundred years, some of them. They’ll want to lie down.”

Wren looked down at the thing in her arms.

The crown. The plain circle of gold, heavy as a stone, with the fire of the sun lying quiet in it, banked and low and steady, like the coal in Granny Kettle’s pocket for the morning. In all this dark, in the Queen’s whole night let out over the world, it was burning. It was the brightest thing in the boat, brighter than the lamp. And it was warm.

“Not Skerrow,” said Wren. “Not yet.”

She held it up a little, so that they could all see it.

“It’s not ours,” she said. “It’s not mine. It was never his, either.” She looked at the old man asleep in her father’s lap. “He took it. On the Mountain. Three hundred years ago. And she had it, and he had it, and nobody could let go of it, and the sun went pale.” She swallowed. “It’s got to go back. Where it came from. To the Mountain. Where he took it.”

“The Crown’s going home,” said Mira softly.

“Yes,” said Wren. “It’s going home.”

Tobin felt in his pocket, in the dark, and took out his mother’s compass.

He clicked the lid open. Inside it, in the glow from Wren’s crown, they could see the engraved letters: Home is where the light is.

And the needle was turning.

It turned as they watched, slowly, the way it had turned on the hill above Harrowgate: as if a patient hand were moving it. Away from the east, where the Spire had been and was not any more. Round. Past south. Past west, where the little lights of Gloamhaven were burning along the edge of the dark. On round. And it settled, at last, trembling, and then quite still.

North.

North-and-a-bit-east. Where it had pointed every day for a year and a half, from the morning they walked out of the Grey Gate of Emberwick onto the Greywaste. Towards the faint pale tooth on the edge of the world, that they had never yet come near.

The Bright Mountain.

Tobin put his finger on the glass. It was warm.

“North,” he said. “Mairi — north. Along the coast. As far as you can. And then we walk.”

Mairi Dunlop looked at him, and at the compass, and at the crown in Wren’s arms. Then she looked out at all the little lights in the dark, all round them on the black water, every boat; and she put her great red hand on the tiller.

“North it is,” she said. “Daft first.”

And the whole fleet turned with her.

Wren sat in the stern of the Gannet that night, with the crown in her arms and the lamp inside her coat and Cinder in her lap, and her mother’s shoulder against her own.

She did not sleep. She did not want to. She sat and watched the little lights of Gloamhaven burning along the edge of the dark, as the boats went north, and she thought about all of them: Nettle in Soot Lane, with her candles. Bracken at the Beacon. Mott. Will Hesketh in his field, and Posy. Granny Kettle in her bothy by the tarn, shouting at the dark. Every one of them, holding on.

And in her father’s lap, across the boat, the old man who had been a king slept.

He slept the way a very small child sleeps after a very long day: all at once, deeply, with his mouth a little open. His bald brown head had slipped down off Tam’s chest in the night, and Linnet had taken off her shawl and folded it up and put it under his cheek, against the gunwale, for a pillow. And he lay there in the dark on the Sunless Sea, with his head on a singer’s shawl, and his tiny hands — open; quite open; uncurled — lying loose on his blanket.

He was smiling in his sleep.

It was, Wren thought, the first time he had slept in three hundred years.

fields.title: The Road North
fields.body_html:
They came to land on the second day of the dark, though you could not have told it was a day.

There was no dawn. That was the thing none of them could get used to. All her life, Wren had known the grey: the pale sun coming up thin and cold over the roofs of Emberwick like a coin that somebody had rubbed too long, and the long dim afternoons, and the gloaming. It had never been much of a day. But it had been a day. You knew where you were in it.

Now there was nothing. The Queen had let out all her dark at once, the night she had been gathering for three hundred years, and it lay over the whole of Gloamhaven like a lid on a pot. The pale sun did not rise. Mairi Dunlop said it was morning because her stomach said so, and her stomach, she said, had never yet been wrong about breakfast; and when her stomach said it was night again they all lay down in the bottom of the boats and tried to sleep. That was the only way to tell.

And all the way up the coast, on their left hand, the little lights of Gloamhaven burned along the edge of the black.

The fleet came in at last at a place where the cliffs fell away into a long grey beach of shingle, very far north, further north than any of the Skerrow boats had ever been. Mairi brought the Gannet in through the shallows with her great red hands steady on the tiller and her face screwed up against the dark, and the shingle hissed and crunched under the keel, and they stopped.

“That’s as far as the water goes,” she said. “Out you get. Mind your feet.”

They got out. Behind them, one by one, the other boats came grinding up onto the stones — the Kittiwake, with Jory Penhallow in the bows, already shouting at his crew to bring her round, the lubbers; and the fishing boats from Skerrow; and the long black hulls of the Drowned Fleet, every one with its little lights burning, and three hundred years of sailors climbing stiffly over the sides onto dry land and standing there swaying, the way people do who have been a long time at sea. Some of them knelt down on the shingle and put their hands on it. One old sailor lay right down on his back on the stones and laughed and laughed and could not stop.

Jory came splashing up the beach to Mairi and stood in front of her, dripping.

“I said I’d get strong,” he said.

“So you did,” said Mairi Dunlop. She looked him up and down. “You’ll do, Jory Penhallow. You’ll do.”

And then — though she was sixty, and red-handed, and had never in her life, Wren was fairly sure, hugged anybody she was not related to — she put her arms round the ship’s boy from three hundred years ago and hugged him, wet and all, until he squeaked.

They had brought out more people than there was any way to count. Tobin tried. He gave up somewhere after two thousand, because they kept moving.

The Sleepers from the Spire had been standing for so long that standing was the only thing their legs remembered how to do, and now that they could sit down, most of them did, all along the beach in the dark, in long rows, like people waiting for a fair to begin. Sister Hale went up and down between them with her brass-mended crutch, singing, and giving out the bread that Mairi had brought from Skerrow, which was not nearly enough and somehow went round. Linnet went with her. Linnet was still slow, and her hands still shook when she held anything up for long; but she knew a great many of the people on that beach. Some of them she had stood beside for eight years in the Hall of Sleepers. She went from face to face in the lamplight, saying names.

Wren sat on a big flat stone above the shingle, with the crown in her lap and Cinder pressed against her side, and watched her.

She was still not used to it. She thought she might never be. That the small, sharp-chinned, black-haired woman going up and down the beach in the dark with her shawl round her shoulders was her mother — that she had a mother, and that the mother was there, and you could go up to her and touch her sleeve. Every so often Linnet would look up from whoever she was talking to, and look round for her. Just to see. And when she found her, she would smile, a quick small shy smile, as if she were not sure yet whether she was allowed.

Wren smiled back, every time. She was getting better at it.

“Wren,” said Mira.

She was standing on the shingle below Wren’s stone, with her head on one side, the way she stood when she was listening to something a long way off. Aren was beside her.

“What?”

“Listen.”

Wren listened. There was the sea behind them, very small and flat and oily, hardly making a sound. There was the murmur of two thousand people on a beach. Sister Hale singing. Somebody’s baby. Mairi Dunlop telling Prowle that if he did not stop crying she would put him back.

“I can’t hear anything.”

“Not here,” said Mira. “There.” She pointed away from the sea — inland, into the dark. “Feet. Lots of feet. Coming this way.”

Aren had gone very still. Wren saw his hand go to his side, where in the old days there would have been a sword. There was nothing there. He took the hand away again.

“Hollows?” said Tobin. He had got up from where he was sitting with his father.

Mira clicked her tongue, twice, sharp and quick, and listened. Then she clicked again. And then — slowly — she began to smile.

“No,” she said. “Not Hollows. Hollows don’t talk.”

And over the top of the rise above the beach, out of the black, came a light.

It was only a little one. It was somebody holding up a candle in a tin lantern, high over their head, the way you do when you are walking in the dark and want to be seen. And behind it, another. And another. And another, and then dozens, a long wavering line of little gold lights coming over the rise and down towards the sea; and under them, faces.

The first face was grey and bearded and very wide, with eyes like a mole’s screwed up against even that little light; and below the beard was a great barrel of a chest; and below that, the shortest, broadest, most solid legs that Wren had ever seen.

“Gorrim,” said Tobin.

“Bright-hand,” said the Speaker of the Delvers, gravely, and bowed. “We are come up out of the Stair.”

And then he saw Mira, and his grave face crumpled up all at once into something that was not grave at all; and Mira, who had never in her life before seen the faces of her own people coming towards her out of the dark, stood quite still on the shingle and looked at them, one after another, with her mouth open.

“You’re all beards,” she said at last, in an astonished voice. “Nobody told me.” And then she was running.

They had all come.

That was what Wren could not take in, that night on the beach, and for days afterwards. Not just the Delvers, though they had come — Gorrim and Mother Hessa and half the Deep, carrying their children on their shoulders, blinking and muttering and pointing at things. Tavi came running down the shingle and stopped dead in front of Wren and then flung his arms round her, lantern and all, so that the candle went out and had to be lit again off the lamp. The Delvers had felt the dark come down, Gorrim said, all through the rock, like a great weight settling; and every glowstone in the Deep had cracked in the same hour, crack, crack, crack, all down the Stair; and then they were in the black for the first time in all their history. And they had sat in it for a while. And then Mother Hessa had got up and said, quite crossly, that she was not going to sit in the dark like a beetle under a stone while the bright-hand’s girl was out in it somewhere, and she was going to go and find her. And they had all got up and come.

“How did you know where to come?” said Wren.

Gorrim looked at her, puzzled, as if the question did not make sense.

“North,” he said. “Where else would you go?”

And it was not only the Delvers.

All that long night on the beach — if it was a night — the lights kept coming. Over the rise, down the cliff paths, along the shore. Little lights, one or two at a time, or a dozen, or a cart-load. Flame-bearers. People the Flame had rested on at Midsummer, or people who had been given it since by somebody else, or by somebody else again. Folk from the Harrowgate Highlands, in their plaids, with their dogs. Remnant from the Greywaste, who had walked out of their bothies when the dark came down and simply started north. A woman from Vaelport with two small children and a glowstone necklace, cracked right across, round her neck, which she said she was keeping to remind her. Farmers from the Low Quarter. A cart-load of miners. And none of them had been told to come. Nobody had sent for anybody. In every house and farm and village in Gloamhaven where somebody was holding a light in the dark, somebody had looked up, and thought, north — and gone.

“Like birds,” said Tobin, watching them come. “In autumn. Nobody tells them. They just go.”

“It’s the same as the compass,” said Mira. “Isn’t it? They’ve all got one. Inside.”

Just before Mairi’s stomach said it was morning, a last little group of lights came down the cliff path, very slowly, and very sulkily; and when they got to the bottom, they turned out to be Snib.

Snib, and behind him a whole troop of Gutterlings — twenty or thirty of them, small and hunched and greasy and suspicious, and every one of them holding, very awkwardly, between their two grubby hands, a flame.

Snib saw Wren and stopped. He shuffled his feet. He looked at the ground. He looked at the sea.

“Don’t want no fuss,” he said.

“I’m not making a fuss,” said Wren.

“Only Gribble got it off me,” said Snib. “And Mudge got it off Gribble. And then they all wanted it. Every one. Wouldn’t leave me alone about it. Went on and on.” He scowled at the troop behind him, who scowled back. “So I said. All right. North. Fine.” He looked at her sideways. “We’re not staying.”

“No,” said Wren gravely. “Course not.”

Snib sniffed, enormously, and went and sat down on the shingle with his back to her. Every one of his Gutterlings went and sat down in a row beside him, with their backs to her too, holding their flames.

They set off north at what Mairi’s stomach called morning: a great slow straggling crowd of people walking up off the beach and onto the moors, and then off the moors onto the flat, and then on into the Greywaste.

It was not like the Greywaste Wren remembered.

She remembered it grey: flat grey ground, and grey grass, and the grey sky coming down to meet it all round at the edge of the world, and the wind. Now it was black. There was no edge, and no sky, and no ground except the little patch you could see by your own light. You walked in a pool of gold, with the dark going on for ever in every direction. Ahead of you, other little pools of gold. Behind you, more. A long, long line of them, winding north over the Greywaste, as far as you could see either way.

And all along the road, every mile or so, there were waystones.

Wren had never noticed them before. She thought now that perhaps she had seen them, the first time, on the long walk from Emberwick a year and a half ago, and thought they were only stones. They were tall, rough grey pillars, as high as a man, standing by themselves at the side of the old road, and every one had a little square niche cut in it near the top, facing the road, with a sooty stain above it where something had once burned.

“Lamplighters,” said Aren, when she asked. It was the first time he had spoken in hours. “Before. Before the bargain. They kept a light in every one, all the way from the Rings to the Mountain. So you could always see the next one, from the last. So that you’d never be lost.” He looked at the empty niche, and then away. “I used to know a song about them. Ash taught me. I’ve forgotten it.”

“You’ll remember,” said Wren.

Aren looked at her. Then he nodded, slowly, as if she had told him something that was true.

Tam carried Ardric.

He had carried him off the Spire and down into the boat, and in the boat he had held him on his knee for three days and nights in the dark, and when they came ashore he had simply picked him up again; and now he carried him north over the Greywaste in his arms, the way he would have carried Wren when she was four. The old man weighed nothing. He was wrapped in Linnet’s shawl and two blankets and Mairi’s second-best jersey, and still he was cold, and still he was so small inside it all that you might have thought Tam was carrying a bundle of washing.

He did not talk much. He slept most of the time, the way he had in the boat: all at once, and deeply, with his mouth a little open. When he woke up he would look about him in the dark, puzzled and mild, at the long road and the little lights going north, as if he could not quite remember where he was or how he had got there; and then he would see Wren walking beside him, and his face would clear.

“Ah,” he would whisper. “It’s you.”

“It’s me,” Wren would say.

“Is it still dark?”

“Still dark. Not for long.”

“Not for long,” Ardric would say, as if he were trying the words. And then he would go back to sleep.

Once — late, on what Mairi’s stomach said was the first evening — he woke and was frightened. Wren saw it come into his face, the old terrible fear, the look he had worn on the throne for three hundred years: his eyes going wide and his tiny hands scrabbling at the blankets, at his chest, at his head, feeling for something that was not there.

“It’s gone,” he whispered. “It’s gone, I let it — I let it go, I shouldn’t have, I’ll—“

“It’s here,” said Wren. “Look. I’ve got it.”

She opened her coat a little, and showed him the crown, lying against her chest beside the lamp, with the sun’s fire banked low and quiet in it.

Ardric looked at it for a long time.

“You’re carrying it,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Doesn’t it hurt?”

Wren thought about it.

“No,” she said. “It’s heavy. But it doesn’t hurt.”

“It hurt me,” said Ardric. “Every day. For three hundred years.” He looked at her, puzzled, as if she were a riddle he would very much have liked to have the answer to, before it was too late. “Why doesn’t it hurt you?”

“I don’t know,” said Wren honestly. “Maybe because I don’t want it.”

The old man was quiet for a while.

“No,” he said at last. “No. I suppose that’s it.”

And he lay back against Tam’s chest, and his hands went still on the blanket, and opened; and the fear went out of his face. He did not ask about the crown again.

They stopped, at the end of that first long day’s march, by a waystone.

It was a big one, bigger than most, standing by itself on a little rise above the road with the dark all round it; and the people coming behind them spread out across the Greywaste round about and sat down where they were, and the little lights settled over the black ground like a field of fallen stars. Somebody was singing, far off. Somebody’s dog was barking.

Tam sat down with his back against the waystone and Ardric in his arms. Linnet sat down beside him. Wren sat on the other side, with the crown in her lap, and took the old man’s hand.

It was very small. Smaller than her own. The skin of it was so thin she could see the bones, and it was cold, as cold as it had been in the Crown Room. But it held on to hers.

“Wren,” he whispered.

“I’m here.”

“I’m tired.”

“I know,” said Wren. “You can sleep.”

“I’m always sleeping now.” He seemed to find this funny; there was a small dry sound in his chest that might have been a laugh. “Three hundred years and I never slept. Not once. Not one night. And now I can’t stop.” His eyes went past her, out into the dark, north, where the Mountain was. “Is it far?”

“Not very far now.”

“I won’t get there,” said Ardric.

He did not say it as if he were frightened. He said it the way you might say it’s raining. Wren opened her mouth to say of course you will — and then shut it again, because it would not have been true, and he would have known, and he had been lied to enough.

“No,” she said. “I don’t think you will.”

“That’s all right,” said the old man. He shut his eyes. “That’s all right. I thought I’d mind. I always minded. It was all I ever minded. And I don’t.” He was quiet for a long moment. “Wren.”

“Yes?”

“You said — in the tower. Before.” His voice was very faint now, like pages turning in another room. “You said he’d made you breakfast. On a hill. And you said—“

“He burns the first bit,” said Wren. Her throat had gone tight. “Every time. He burns the first piece of toast. And he eats it himself, so you get the good bits.”

“Yes,” whispered Ardric. “That was it. That was the thing.” His fingers moved a little in hers. His eyes were shut, and his face was quite smooth, and there was a little smile at the corner of his mouth, the same puzzled, waiting smile he had worn in the Crown Room when the crown came off. He sounded half asleep already; he sounded like a very small boy at the end of a very long day, asking one last thing before the candle went out.

“Will there be toast?”

“Yes,” said Wren. “Yes. There’ll be toast. He burns the first bit.”

Ardric smiled.

He did not say anything else. He went to sleep, there by the waystone, in Tam Ashby’s arms, with his head on Linnet’s shawl and his hand in Wren’s: deeply, all at once, the way he had slept in the boat. Wren sat and held his hand in the dark. And after a while she knew that he had not just gone to sleep; and she went on holding it anyway, for a long time, until Linnet put her arm round her.

He was not afraid. That was the thing Wren remembered, afterwards. Of all the things about that night, that was the one she kept. The king who had been frightened of dying for three hundred years, more than of anything in the world, so frightened that he had sold the sun to put it off — at the end, he had not been afraid at all.

They buried him at the foot of the waystone, in the morning, if it was morning.

It did not take long. The Delvers dug the grave; they were very quick, and very gentle, and they did not say anything while they did it, which for Delvers was a great deal. Tam laid him in it, still wrapped in his blankets, with Linnet’s shawl folded under his head. His hands were open on his chest. Sister Hale sang something, very low, an old Remnant song with no words in it that Wren had never heard, and the people standing round on the rise and in the dark beyond it hummed along, the ones who knew it, and the ones who didn’t kept quiet. Mairi Dunlop took off her hat. So did Prowle, Wren noticed, though he had been crying so long by then that perhaps he did not notice he was crying for something else.

Then they filled it in, and that was all.

Wren stood by the waystone afterwards with the lamp in her hand. The empty niche was just above her head; she had to stand on tiptoe. It was full of three hundred years of dust and dead leaves and a very old, very surprised spider, who went away. She blew it out. And then she reached up, and touched the lamp to the old sooty stone at the back of the niche where the waystone-light had once burned; and the Flame went in.

It caught on the bare stone and stayed there. A small, steady, golden flame, burning on nothing, in a niche in a stone by the side of the old road, above the place where the king was sleeping. So that you would always see the next one, from the last. So that you would never be lost.

“Goodbye,” said Wren, to the stone.

Then she turned round, and went back to the road, and they went on.

Behind them, the line of people coming north saw the light in the waystone and stopped, every one of them, just for a moment, as they went by.

And as each one went by — Wren did not see this; Tobin told her, a long time afterwards — each one reached out with their own light, whatever it was, a candle or a lamp or a flame cupped in their hands, and touched the next waystone they came to. And the next.

So that by the end of that day, if anybody had been able to stand very high up over the Greywaste and look down — the way Tobin used to look down at his Orrery, on the round table in his attic — they would have seen the old road north lit all the way. A line of little gold lights, one by one, every mile, going on through the black. Each one in sight of the last.

It was in the middle of what should have been the second night that Wren heard it.

They had stopped to rest by another waystone, and lit it, and nearly everybody was asleep. Tobin was asleep with his head on his pack and his father’s coat over his feet. Mira was asleep curled up beside Aren, who was not asleep, but sat watching the dark with his scarred hand on his knee, glowing faintly. Sister Hale was snoring. Cinder was curled up in Wren’s lap with her nose under her tail, and the crown was a heavy warm weight inside Wren’s coat, and her mother was asleep against her shoulder, breathing slow.

And very far off, in the dark — so far that at first she thought she had dreamed it — someone was humming.

Wren held her breath.

It came from the north. From the Mountain. It was very faint, like a sound you hear across water on a still evening, a long way from shore; and it was a man’s voice, low and warm and unhurried, the way you hum when you are doing something with your hands and do not know that you are doing it.

It was her mother’s tune.

Morning comes, morning comes, and the dark shall not keep us —

She knew it before she knew she knew it. She had known it all her life. She had hummed it on chimney-pots and in coal-holes and in the Black Stair and in the Hall of Sleepers, and every time, it had stopped there. At the same place. Where she did not know any more.

And it did not stop.

It went on. The faraway voice in the dark went on, past the place where it always stopped, into notes she had never heard; and they were the right notes, she knew they were the right notes, the way you know the next stair in your own house in the dark; and they went up, and up, and turned, and came home.

Then it was gone.

Wren sat very still for a long time in the dark, with her mother asleep on her shoulder and the fox in her lap, listening as hard as she had ever listened to anything. There was nothing. Only the little lights, and the sleepers, and Sister Hale snoring.

She did not wake anybody. She did not tell anybody. She thought, afterwards, that nobody else had heard it at all, and that perhaps it had not been meant for anybody else.

But she did not sleep again that night. She sat and looked north, where the voice had come from; and her face, in the lamplight, would have surprised anyone who saw it.

They came to the foot of the Bright Mountain on the third day of the dark.

You could not see it. That was the strange part. All her life, on a clear grey day, from the top of the highest chimney in Emberwick, Wren had been able to see it — a faint pale tooth on the very edge of the world, far away to the north, that the grown-ups said was only cloud. And now they had walked all the way to it, and it was right in front of them, and they could not see it at all. There was only the dark, and the road going up into it, and the ground under their feet beginning to climb.

And snow. There was snow on the road now. It squeaked under their boots.

And the waystones went up.

You could see them, if you looked. Just. One empty niche in a pale grey pillar, at the edge of the lamplight, a little way up the slope. And above it, far up in the dark, at the very edge of seeing, a faint grey shape that might have been another. And then nothing.

The whole long straggling crowd of them stopped at the foot of the slope and stood there in the snow, every one with their light, two thousand and more little pools of gold in the black, looking up.

Tobin took out his compass. The needle was pointing straight up the road. It was so warm he had to change hands.

“Well,” said Mairi Dunlop, into the silence. She looked up the mountain, and then down at Wren. “You first, lass. You’re the one with the crown.”

Wren looked up the road.

She thought about the old man under the waystone. And about the voice in the dark, humming, past the place where it always stopped. And about all the little lights behind her, all over Gloamhaven, holding on.

“Come on, then,” she said.

And she put her foot on the mountain, and began to climb.

fields.title: The Last Offer
fields.body_html:
The road up the Bright Mountain was the longest road Wren had ever walked, and she had walked a good many by then.

It went up and up in the dark. It went back and forth across the face of the mountain in long slow zigzags, the way old roads do on steep places, so that you were always climbing and never seemed to get any higher. The snow got deeper. The air got thinner and colder, and it hurt to breathe it, a clean sharp hurt right down at the bottom of your chest. Your legs ached, and then they stopped aching and went numb, and then they ached again, worse. And always, on either side of the little gold pool of light you walked in, there was the dark: so close and so black that you could have put out your hand and touched it, and so big that it went on for ever.

But there were the waystones.

Every few hundred yards, at a turn of the road, there would be another one: a tall grey pillar standing in the snow, with its empty niche near the top. And every time, Wren stopped. She stood on tiptoe, or Tobin gave her a leg up, or Aren lifted her, and she blew out three hundred years of dust and dead leaves and the odd sleepy beetle, and touched the lamp to the old sooty stone at the back. And the Flame went in, and caught, and stayed, small and steady and gold on the bare rock.

And then they went on, to the next one.

It was Mira who turned round first and saw it.

They had stopped at a waystone at the corner of a zigzag, high up, and Wren had just lit it, and Mira — who could see further in a little light than any of them — had gone to the edge of the road to look back down the way they had come. She stood there for a moment, with her head on one side. Then she said, “Oh,” in a voice Wren had never heard her use before.

They went and stood beside her.

Below them, the mountain fell away into the dark. And going down it, back and forth, back and forth, across the whole black face of the slope, was a line of light.

The waystones. Every one that they had lit. Each one a single gold point in the dark, a little further down than the last, zigzagging away beneath them down the side of the Bright Mountain, back and forth, smaller and smaller, until the line ran out onto the flat at the bottom and went on — straight now, and very faint — away across the Greywaste to the south, light after light after light, along the old road. As far as you could see. Further.

And between the waystones, on the road, were the people.

They were climbing behind. Every one of them. The whole long straggling Gathering of them that had come over the rise to the beach, and joined the road on the Greywaste, and walked north through the Long Night: they were all coming up the mountain behind Wren in the snow, every one with their own light. You could see them. Little moving gold specks on the road, between the steady gold points of the waystones. Hundreds and hundreds of them, winding up and back and up the side of the mountain in the dark, all the way down to the bottom, and out of sight.

The Remnant from the Greywaste, with Sister Hale somewhere among them, singing. The Delvers, slow and steady, with their children on their shoulders. The Highlanders in their plaids. The miners, the farmers, the boat-folk from Skerrow, the sailors of the Drowned Fleet, three hundred years late for wherever they had been going. Snib and his Gutterlings, sulking up the mountain in a tight little knot, holding their flames.

All of it. All of them. A road of light going up the Bright Mountain in the dark, the way the beads had lit one after another across the Low Quarter on Tobin’s Orrery.

“I can’t see the top of it,” said Mira. “I mean the bottom. It just keeps going.”

“It goes all the way back,” said Tobin. His voice was not quite steady. “Doesn’t it. All the way. To Emberwick. To — to the first one. In the garret.”

Wren did not say anything. She only stood and looked at it. Then she turned round and looked up — up, at the dark above them, where the road went on climbing and the next waystone was waiting, and there was no light at all.

“Come on,” she said.

It got colder as they climbed. That was to be expected, on a mountain, in the snow. But after a while Wren began to think it was not only the mountain.

It was the old cold. The Queen’s cold. She knew it as well as she knew her own name by now. It did not come down out of the air, the way weather does. It came up from inside: up from your stomach and your chest and the back of your neck, a creeping grey cold that made you want to sit down in the snow and stop. Just for a minute. Just to rest. It made the lamp in her hand feel small and far away, and the crown inside her coat feel heavier than a crown could possibly be, and the top of the mountain feel so far off that there was no point, really, none at all, in—

“Wren,” said Aren.

He had stopped on the road just ahead of her. He was looking up.

There was somebody on the road.

She was standing in the snow at the next turn, just at the edge of the lamplight, the way she had stood on the Hill of Cinders: tall and still and silver-grey, with her hands folded in front of her. She was by herself. There were no knights behind her, no Hollows, no court of shadows, no Prowle. There was nothing behind her but the dark. She did not have a crown. She did not have anything.

It was the Queen.

And she had changed.

Wren had seen her lovely. On the Hill of Cinders, under the pale sun, she had been the loveliest thing Wren had ever seen, lovelier than anything in a shop window in the First Ring: silver and soft and kind, like moonlight on frost, so that you wanted to go to her and be told everything was all right. And in the Spire she had still been lovely, mostly, even with her voice going high.

Now the loveliness was wearing thin.

That was the only way Wren could think of it. Like frost on a window when somebody has lit a fire inside the room: still there, still sparkling, still making pretty shapes, but thinner every minute, so that through the thin places you could see what was on the other side. And what was on the other side was dark. Not black, exactly. Not anything. Just dark, and cold, and very, very hungry, the way an empty room is hungry.

She was afraid.

Wren could see that too. It was in the way her folded hands held each other, too tightly. In the way her eyes kept going past Wren, up the mountain, to the top. In her voice, when she spoke: still soft, still kind, still reasonable. But underneath it, very faintly, like a crack running through a bell, something that shook.

“Hello, Wren,” said the Queen.

Wren did not say hello back.

She stood in the snow with the lamp in her hand and the crown in her coat, and Tobin on her left and Mira on her right and Aren a little in front, and Cinder against her ankles, growling very softly in her chest. And behind them, far down, the whole long road of lights, climbing.

“You’ve come a long way,” said the Queen. “All of you. I’m impressed, truly. I didn’t think you’d get this far. Nobody ever has.” She smiled. It was a lovely smile. It was very thin. “And you’re so tired, my dear. Look at you. You can hardly stand. Your feet are frozen, aren’t they? Your hands. It’s so cold up here. It’s so far to the top. And you’re carrying so much.” Her eyes went to the front of Wren’s coat, where the crown was. “Such a heavy thing. For such a little girl.”

“I’m all right,” said Wren.

“Of course you are.” The Queen’s voice was very gentle. “Of course. You’re always all right. That’s what sweeps say, isn’t it? I’m all right. When they’re frozen on a roof in the dark, with no supper and no mother, and nobody to say goodnight. I’m all right.” She tilted her head. “But you needn’t be, any more. That’s what I came to tell you. You needn’t go one step further.”

She held out her hand.

“Give it to me,” she said. “That’s all. Only that. The crown — and I’ll go away. I’ll go away for ever. You’ll never see me again. I’ll take my dark, all of it, the whole long night, and go somewhere you’ll never find me, and never trouble you or anyone you love again.” She smiled. “Isn’t that what you want? Isn’t that what you’ve wanted all along? For me to go away?”

It was true. That was the worst of it. That was always the worst of it, with the Queen. It was true, and it was what Wren wanted, more than almost anything; and she could feel how easy it would be.

“No,” said Wren.

The Queen’s face did something then. Just for a moment. The frost went very thin, and Wren saw through it, and looked away.

When she looked back, the Queen was smiling again.

“Not just the crown,” said the Queen softly. “I see. You want more. Well, why not? You’ve earned it.” She took a step closer. The cold came with her. “The lamp too, then. The lamp and the crown, both together. And in return—“

She stopped, and smiled, and let the moment go on.

“In return,” said the Queen, “I’ll give you the rest of the song.”

Wren went still.

“You don’t know it, do you?” said the Queen. “Not all of it. You never have. Your mother sang it to you every night when you were small — oh, every night, my dear, I know, I was there, I had her in my hall for eight years and she sang it in her sleep — and then I took her, and you were four, and you only ever remembered the beginning. Morning comes, morning comes, and the dark shall not keep us.” Her voice, saying the words, was very sweet; it sounded like a music box. “And then it stops. Doesn’t it? It always stops. You’ve hummed it on every rooftop in Emberwick, and every time you come to that place, and there’s nothing there. Just a hole. A hole where your mother was.”

Wren could not speak.

“I know the rest,” said the Queen. “Every word. I’ve heard it in my halls a thousand times. I could sing it to you now, right here, on this mountain. The whole thing. All the words your mother sang to you, every night, that you’ve lost. You could have them back.” She held out her other hand, so that both her hands were out. Long and white and very beautiful, and shaking, ever so slightly. “Give me the lamp and the crown, Wren, and I’ll give you your mother’s song.”

It was very quiet on the mountain.

Behind her, Wren heard Tobin take a breath and not let it out. She felt Mira’s hand find hers in the dark. She felt Cinder go stiff against her ankles. And she felt — deep inside her coat, against her chest — the lamp, burning, warm; and the crown beside it, heavy and quiet.

And she thought about the old man under the waystone, who had bargained away the sun because somebody had offered him something he wanted more than anything in the world. And she thought about Tobin, at the supper table, a long time ago, when his father had sold the lamp. And about herself, in the Glowstone Market, with the stone in her hand.

And she thought about the voice in the dark, two nights ago. Humming. Very far off. Going on, past the place where it always stopped, into the right notes — the notes she had never heard and had known at once, the way you know the next stair in your own house.

Nobody gave him that, she thought. He didn’t make a bargain for it. He just — sang it. Because he knew it.

“No,” said Wren.

The Queen’s hands stayed out.

“I don’t want it,” said Wren. Her voice was shaking, and she let it. “Not from you. I don’t want it from you.” She swallowed. “I’ll have it given.”

For a moment nothing happened at all.

Then the Queen’s face broke.

It went the way ice goes on a puddle when you stamp on it: all at once, in a hundred places. The loveliness cracked across and fell away, and what was underneath came through. It was not a face. It was not anything. It was dark: a great cold hungry dark the shape of a tall woman, with two holes in it where the eyes had been, and it opened its mouth — if it was a mouth — and the night came out.

It came at them like a wave.

Not like the Hollows. Not like the dark on the Black Stair, or the cold in the Spire. Worse than all of it. It was everything the Queen had left, all the dark of three hundred years, all the night she had poured out over Gloamhaven, coming down the mountain road at them all at once in one great black roaring rush; and it was cold, cold beyond anything, a cold that went straight in through your skin and your bones and found the place right at the middle of you where you were you, and pressed on it, and pressed.

The lamp in Wren’s hand bowed down to the size of a seed.

The light went out of the road. Out of the snow. Out of the waystones below. Wren could not see Tobin. She could not see Mira. She could not see her own hand in front of her face. There was nothing in all the world but the dark, and the cold, and the weight pressing down on her, pressing, pressing her into the snow, and a voice that was not a voice any more, saying over and over: Give it to me. Give it to me. Give it to me. GIVE IT TO ME—

And then Tobin said, “No.”

He was standing on the road in front of her. She could not see him; she could hear him. He had Ash’s pole in both hands — the old ash-wood pole with the iron cap and the hook, that Ash had leaned on all the way across the Greywaste, that Tobin had carried since the Hill of Cinders — and he had planted it in the snow of the road, in the middle of the path, the way Ash used to plant it in the cinders when he wanted to stand up straight. And he was holding on to it with his scarred hands, and the scars were burning gold, and the dark was pouring past him on both sides like a black river round a rock.

He was not shaking.

Wren heard that. That was the thing she would always remember about Tobin on the Bright Mountain. All the way from Emberwick, he had shaken: at the Grey Gate, on the Stair, in the Market, on the Hill. His voice had shaken, and his hands. And now, with the whole of the Queen’s night coming at him down a mountain road, he stood in the snow with the old man’s pole in his hands, and his voice did not shake at all.

“No,” said Tobin again. “You don’t get any more. You’ve had enough. You’ve had my father and you’ve had Ash and you’ve had the sun. You’re not having her.”

“Wren,” said Mira, very close, in her ear. “Hold my hand. Don’t let go.”

She clicked her tongue. Sharp and quick and clear, three times, into the black.

And she began to walk.

She could not see. Nobody could see. There was no light on the mountain any more, none at all, nothing for even Mira’s eyes to catch. But Mira had walked the Spire in the dark, and the Black Stair, and every crooked passage of the Deep before she ever had eyes at all, by the sound of her own tongue coming back to her off the stones. She clicked, and listened, and stepped; clicked, and listened, and stepped. Up the road. Round the turn. Past the place where the dark was thickest, past the place where the Queen had stood. Her hand in Wren’s was small and hot and quite steady.

“Snow,” she said. “Step up. Rock on the left. Good. Click. Road goes round — this way. There’s a stone here, mind your knee. Click. Keep going. You’re doing it. Keep going.”

And then the cold came between them — a great black weight of it, pressing in, trying to pull their hands apart — and somebody else was there.

Aren.

He did not say anything. He did not have anything in his hands: no sword, no pole, no lamp. He had only his own two hands, and the old oath-scar on the right one shining gold in the dark like a seam of ore in a rock. He stepped in between Wren and the place where the Queen was, on the high side of the road, and stood there. That was all. He simply stood there, between them, with his scarred hand open at his side, the way a man stands in a doorway when he means that nobody is coming through it.

“Varrick,” said the dark. It was not a voice any more. It was a cold that had a name in it. “Varrick. My Grey Captain. Come here. Come to me. You’re mine. You’ve always been mine. You know you have. Varrick—“

“No,” said Aren. “Aren.”

He did not say it loudly. He said it the way you say your own name to somebody who has got it wrong, without any fuss. And the dark pressed and pressed on him, and he did not move.

And ahead of them all, in the black, there was a spark.

It was very small. A single point of fire, low down, near the snow, a little way up the road. It bobbed as it went. It went on ahead, up and round the turn, and stopped, and waited, and went on again.

Cinder.

Wren had not even felt her go. The little fox had slipped out from against her ankles in the dark, and gone ahead up the road, the way she always went ahead: on the Greywaste, on the Black Stair, on the Hill. Her coat was out. Her eyes were out. There was nothing left of her in all that night but the one spark of fire at the very tip of her tail, burning, a single gold point in a world of black. And she went on up the mountain with it, a few yards in front, and stopped, and looked back, and waited. This way.

“Follow her,” said Mira, in Wren’s ear. “Follow the spark. I can hear the road. You follow her.”

So Wren climbed.

She climbed the last stretch of the Bright Mountain in the Queen’s last dark with her eyes shut, because there was no point in having them open. She climbed with Mira’s hand in hers, and Mira’s voice in her ear — step, rock, good, click, keep going — and Tobin somewhere behind her holding the road with Ash’s pole, and Aren beside her, between her and the cold, and Cinder’s one spark ahead. She climbed with the crown inside her coat, so heavy now that every step felt like lifting a sack of coal up a ladder; and the lamp beside it, so small it was hardly there, a seed of warmth no bigger than a fingertip against her chest. But there.

It was there. It did not go out.

And as she climbed, she hummed.

She did not decide to. It just came, the way it had always come, on chimney-pots and in coal-holes and in the Hall of Sleepers: her mother’s tune, very quietly, under her breath, through her chattering teeth. Morning comes, morning comes, and the dark shall not keep us. Over and over. To the place where it stopped. And then back to the beginning again.

She did not know the rest yet. That was all right. She knew it was there.

Morning comes. Morning comes.

The road went up, and up, and then it did not go up any more.

Wren’s foot came down on flat ground, and stayed there, and she nearly fell over, because she had been climbing so long that her legs had forgotten how to do anything else. Mira’s hand jerked in hers and steadied her. Behind them, somewhere, Tobin was gasping. The snow was not deep here; it squeaked under her boots and then gave way to something hard and bare, like rock.

And the cold was gone.

Not all of it. The mountain cold was still there, the clean sharp cold that hurt to breathe. But the other cold — the Queen’s cold, the grey creeping cold from inside — was not. It had stopped, behind her, all at once, the way the wind stops when you step round the corner of a house. As if there were a line drawn across the top of the road, and it could not come over.

Wren opened her eyes.

She was standing on the top of the Bright Mountain. She knew it at once: there was nowhere higher to go. It was a plain flat place, wide and bare, of snow and grey rock, open on every side to the black sky; and all round the edge of it, in a great ring, stood old grey stones, taller than men, leaning a little, like people who have been waiting a long time and have got tired of standing up straight.

And in the middle of the ring, on the bare rock, there was a fire.

It was not large. It was not much larger than the breakfast fire on the Hill of Cinders, where the toast had burned. It burned on nothing — no wood, no coal, no oil; on the bare stone — and it was gold, the deep warm gold of the lamp, and it threw its light out across the snow to the stones and a little way beyond; and it had been burning there, Wren knew, for longer than anyone could remember. Since before the bargain. Since before the Rings. Since before there was anything to remember with.

It had never gone out.

And somebody was sitting beside it.

fields.title: Morning Comes
fields.body_html:
He was sitting on a stone by the fire, with his elbows on his knees and his hands held out to the warmth, the way a man sits by a fire at the end of a long day’s work. He was not tall. He was not splendid. He wore a plain brown coat, travel-stained, and old boots, and there was a basket at his feet with a cloth over it. His face was brown and weathered and creased round the eyes from laughing. He was looking into the flames.

He looked, Wren thought, as if he had been sitting there a long time. As if he had known exactly how long they would be, and had not minded, and had kept the fire going.

He looked up.

And he saw her, standing at the edge of the ring of stones in the snow, with the lamp in one hand and the crown inside her coat and Mira’s hand still clutched in the other; and he smiled.

“Wren,” he said.

That was all. Just her name. The way he had said it by the breakfast fire on the Hill of Cinders, with the toast burning. The way nobody else in the whole world said it.

Wren could not speak.

She stood there in the snow, and her mouth opened, and nothing came out of it, and her eyes went hot and then wet, and she did not care. She could not have said a single word if the whole mountain had depended on it. She could only look at him. And then — because she could not look at him any longer, because it was too much, the way the sun is too much — she looked away, at the other side of the fire.

And there was somebody else there.

He was standing, not sitting. That was the first thing.

He was very tall — taller than the standing stones, nearly, or so it seemed to her then — and his beard was long and white and came down over his chest. It was not singed. It was white all the way through, both sides, clean and soft as new snow. He wore a long coat, and it was not patched, and it was not grey: it was blue, the deep blue of the sky just after the sun has gone down, the old Lamplighters’ blue. He was not stooped. He was standing up quite straight, on two legs, in the snow, with nothing in his hands at all — no poles, no stick, nothing — and his hands were in his pockets, the way they had never been in all the time she had known him, because he had always needed them for the poles.

He looked down at her from under his great white eyebrows. And his eyes were the same. Exactly the same. Fierce and kind and a little bit cross.

“Hm,” said Old Ash. “You took your time, child.”

Wren ran.

She dropped Mira’s hand. She did not drop the lamp, or the crown, though she never afterwards knew how. She ran across the top of the Bright Mountain through the snow, round the fire, and hit Old Ash in the middle of his blue coat so hard that a smaller man would have gone over backwards; and he did not go over. He stood there on his two good legs like a tree, and put his long arms round her, lamp and crown and all, and held on.

He smelt the same. Smoke and lamp-oil and old wool and something underneath it that was just him. She had forgotten. She had not known she had forgotten.

“You died,” said Wren into his coat. It came out muffled and wet and furious. “You died. On the Hill. I saw you. I held your hand. You died—“

“Hm,” said Ash, over her head. “I did, didn’t I.” He sounded, of all things, faintly surprised, and rather pleased with himself. “Turned out not to be the end of it. There’s a thing.”

“He told me,” said Wren. “He said you weren’t lost. He said you were waiting. He said — and I didn’t — I tried to, but I didn’t, not properly—“

“No,” said Ash. “Well. Nor would I have.” He patted her back with one enormous hand, rather hard, the way you pat a horse. “Nor would I have, child. You did all right.”

And then he did not say anything else, and nor did she, for a long time.

The others were coming.

Tobin came up over the edge of the mountain-top with Ash’s pole in his hands, gasping, his spectacles white with frost, and stopped dead at the edge of the ring of stones. Mira was beside him. Aren behind. And Cinder—

Cinder did not stop at all.

The little fox shot across the snow like a spark off an anvil, past Wren and Ash, round the fire, and flung herself headlong at the man sitting on the stone. He caught her. He was laughing. She was all over him — climbing up his front and down his back and round his neck, her tail going like a flag, licking his ears, his chin, his eyebrows, yipping and squeaking and grumbling and making a noise like a kettle — and her coat was coming back. Wren saw it. In the dark on the road up, Cinder had been almost nothing, a single spark in the black. Now, in his hands, the red was pouring back into her fur from the tip of her tail, the way colour runs into a cloth dropped in dye: red, and russet, and the dark gold of embers; and her eyes were bright; and her tail was alight from end to end.

“Yes,” he said, laughing, holding her up. “Yes. I know. I know. You did very well. I know.”

Cinder sneezed in his face, and settled into the crook of his arm, and looked round at all of them as if to say that she had found him, and they could all stop worrying now.

Tobin was still standing at the edge of the stones.

He had not moved. He was holding Ash’s pole in both his scarred hands, upright, in front of him, the way he had held it on the road below with the dark pouring past; and he was looking at the old man in the blue coat as if he were afraid that if he blinked, he would not be there.

Ash looked at him for a long moment, over Wren’s head.

“Lad,” he said.

Tobin came across the snow. He came slowly. He stopped in front of Ash, and stood there, and held out the pole.

He did not say anything. He did not need to. Wren could see it all in his face: the Grey Gate, and the Stair, and the Market, and the Hill. Two times he had said he did not know this man, to his face. And the pole, that he had picked up out of the cinders where it fell, and carried every step of the way since, the whole length of Gloamhaven, because it was the only thing of Ash’s he had left. He held it out with both hands, the way you give a thing back that was never yours.

Ash took it.

He looked at it for a while. He turned it over in his long fingers. He ran his thumb along the old ash-wood, worn smooth and dark where his own hand had held it for fifty years; and along the new smooth patch below that, where Tobin’s had held it for one. He looked at the brass hook, and the iron cap. He looked at Tobin’s hands.

Then he gave it back.

“Keep it, lad,” said Old Ash. “I don’t seem to need them.”

Tobin took the pole back. His face did something very complicated, and then he bent his head over it, and Ash put his great hand on the back of Tobin’s neck and left it there.

Then Ash looked past them both. At Aren.

Aren had not come into the ring of stones. He was standing just outside it, at the edge of the light, in the snow, with his hands at his sides. He was looking at the ground. He looked, Wren thought, exactly as he had looked in the Moffats’ weaving-room at Harrowgate, on the day she had forgiven him: like somebody who has come to the door of a house he used to live in, and does not know if he will be let in, and has decided not to knock.

Old Ash looked at him for a long time.

“Lad,” he said.

That was all. It was the same word he had said to Tobin. It was the word he had said, Wren supposed, more than thirty years ago, to a boy in an apprentice’s coat on Emberwick’s wall, before anything had happened at all.

Aren came into the ring. He came across the snow to where Ash was standing, and he did not say anything, and he knelt down in front of him. Right down, in the snow, on both knees, with his head bowed.

Ash did not say anything either.

He reached down and took Aren’s right hand — the scarred one, with the old oath-scar across the palm shining gold — in his own; and he pulled him up off his knees. Not gently. Firmly. The way you pull somebody up who has fallen down in the street, and has been sitting there long enough, and it is time to get up now. And when Aren was standing, Ash did not let go of the hand. He held on to it. And the two of them stood there together in the snow, the tall old man in blue and the plain quiet man in grey, hand in hand, and looked at each other, and did not need to say a thing.

There were no speeches. Wren was glad. She thought she would have cried even more if there had been, and she did not think there was any more crying left in her.

She was wrong about that, as it turned out.

And then the Gathering came up the mountain.

They came up over the edge of the summit in ones and twos, and then in dozens, and then in a great slow tide: out of the dark, up the last stretch of the road, with their lights in their hands. They came up into the ring of stones and stopped, every one of them, the way Wren had stopped; and looked at the fire, and at the man sitting beside it with a fox in his arms; and went quiet.

Sister Hale came up, on her brass-mended crutch, with her bonnet over one ear, and stopped, and put her hand over her mouth. Linnet and Tam came up behind her, Tam with Lord Edric leaning on his arm. Mairi Dunlop came up, and took off her hat. The Delvers came up, all of them, and stood blinking with their children on their shoulders; and old Gorrim, seeing the man by the fire, said something under his breath in the Delver tongue that Mira told Wren afterwards meant the Warm Man, and went down on one knee. Mira was crying. She had been crying since she came over the edge, quite quietly, without making any fuss about it, with her eyes fixed on him: because she knew his voice.
