She had heard it on a ferry, once, in the dark, before she ever had eyes.

They kept on coming. Hundreds. Thousands. Remnant and Highlanders and boat-folk and sailors three hundred years late; Jory Penhallow, and the woman with the cracked glowstone, and the farmers and the miners. Snib and his Gutterlings, at the very back, in a sulky knot, who came up over the top and saw him and stopped sulking all at once, every one of them, and stood with their mouths open. They filled the top of the Bright Mountain from one side to the other, packed in among the standing stones and beyond them, every one holding up their own small flame. And still, behind them, down the long dark side of the mountain, the road of lights went on and on.

And the man by the fire looked round at them all. At every one. As if he knew every face.

Perhaps he did.

Wren was still holding the crown.

She had almost forgotten it. It had been so heavy for so long that she had stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing a pack on your back after a day’s march. But now she felt it again, inside her coat, against her chest, beside the lamp: the plain gold circle, and in it the fire of the sun, lying banked and low and quiet, like a coal kept in for the morning. Waiting.

She let go of Ash. She went round the fire.

He was still sitting on his stone, with Cinder in his arm. He watched her come. He did not hold out his hands. He did not ask for anything. He only waited, the way he had waited for her all along: for her to come of her own accord, or not.

Wren stopped in front of him. She opened her coat. And she took out the crown, in both her hands, the way you lift a sleeping baby out of a cradle, and held it out to him.

“It’s yours,” she said. “I think. Isn’t it? It was always yours.” Her voice was shaking. “He took it. The king. A long time ago. Here. And then he couldn’t let go of it, and she couldn’t take it, and the sun went grey. But he let go in the end. He did. He let go, and he gave it to me, and he wasn’t frightened any more. He wanted me to tell you that.” She had not known that until she said it; but it was true. “And I’ve brought it back.”

He looked at the crown in her hands. Then he looked at her.

“Thank you, Wren,” he said.

And he took it.

He did not put it on.

He held it for a moment in his two hands, the plain gold circle with the sun’s fire lying in it; and Wren saw the scars on his hands. Old, deep, round, like burns. She had seen them before, on the Hill, and in the market, a long time ago, with the bread. She saw them now in the light of the crown, and the light of the crown seemed to know them. It did not lie down, the way it had for her, in the Crown Room. It rose up. It leaned towards him, out of the gold, the way the lamp had always leaned; the way a plant leans towards the window.

He reached into the circle of gold with one scarred hand, the way you would reach into a grate to lift out a coal.

And he lifted the fire out.

It came out of the crown in his hand. It lay in his open palm, burning — a small round blaze of gold and white, no bigger than an apple, so bright that Wren could not look at it straight and could not look away. And everybody on the top of the Bright Mountain, every one of the thousands of them, took a breath at once.

He stood up.

He held the fire in his hand for a moment longer, looking at it, the way you look at something you are fond of that has been lost for a long time and has come home. Then he turned to the east, where there was nothing, nothing at all, only the black of the Queen’s last night, over the edge of the mountain and the whole of Gloamhaven below it; and he lifted his hand, and opened it.

And he gave it back to the sky.

It went up.

It went up out of his hand like a spark going up a chimney — slowly at first, and then faster, and then very fast, and very small, a single point of gold rising and rising into the dark, over the edge of the world. And it was gone.

And for one long moment nothing happened.

Wren stood by the fire, with the lamp in her hand, and held her breath. Everybody held their breath. The whole mountain did.

And then, far away, at the very edge of the world, in the east, down along the line where the black sky met the black land, there was a line of grey.

Only a line. Thin as a thread. And then it was not grey, it was paler than grey. It was white. And then it was not white. It was — it was a colour Wren did not have a name for; she had never seen it before in her life. It was pink, and it was gold, and it was something in between that had no word; and it was spreading. It was running along the edge of the world from one side to the other, the way fire runs along the edge of a piece of paper. And the dark above it was going thin, and blue, and then not dark at all.

And the sun came up.

I have tried, many times, to tell people what it was like, and I have never managed it, and I do not expect I shall manage it now. But I will try once more, for you.

It was not the pale sun. It was not the thin cold coin that had come up over Gloamhaven every grey morning for three hundred years. It was the sun: gold, and huge, and blazing, and warm, rising up over the edge of the world like a great door opening; and its light came across the whole land in one long rush, from the east to the west, from the sea to the mountains, the way the tide comes in over flat sand. You could see it coming. You could see the light run across the Greywaste below them, mile after mile, faster than a horse could gallop, faster than a bird; and everywhere it touched, the colour came.

It came the way water comes out of a broken dam. All at once and everywhere. Down the side of the Bright Mountain, the snow went white — not grey; white, so white it hurt — and the sky above went blue, a blue so deep you could have fallen up into it. The Greywaste was not grey. It had never been grey. It was gold and brown and a dusty soft green, and there were little flowers in it, purple, that had been there all along. The far hills were blue and the near hills were green, and the rivers were silver, and away to the south-east, very small and very far, the sea was not black any more but blue and green and sparkling all over like a field of glass. And all of it was moving: the light running over it, and the shadows of a few small clouds running over the light, and the whole land waking up under it, like a sleeper turning over in a warm bed.

And the warmth.

That was what Wren remembered best. Not the colours, even. The warmth. It came on her face like a hand. It came through her coat and her jersey and her skin and right down into her bones, where the grey cold had lived all her life without her ever knowing it was there; and it found the cold, and the cold went. Just went. The way frost goes off a window when the sun gets round to it. She had not known, until that moment, that she had been cold every day of her life. She had not known there was any other way to be.

All round her on the top of the mountain, people were making noises. Not words. Just noises. Somebody was laughing. Somebody was saying oh, oh, oh, over and over. The Delvers had their hands over their eyes and were peering out between their fingers and shouting. Mairi Dunlop was standing with her arms stretched out wide and her face turned up to the sun and her eyes shut, like a woman standing in rain after a drought.

And Wren lifted up the lamp.

She did not know why. She just did. She held it up in both hands, the little brass lamp from the chimney of Thornbury House, the Lampwright’s own lamp, the first light; and it was burning gold, as it had always burned. And for the first time in her life, for the first time since she had found it in the soot behind the bricks, it was not the brightest thing anywhere.

The sun was brighter. Everything was brighter. The whole world was lit, and the lamp in her hands was only one small light among all of it, as small as a candle in a sunny window, hardly to be seen at all.

And she was glad.

She had not known she would be. She had carried it so long; she had hidden it inside her coat in the dark, and held it up against the Hollows, and given it away, over and over, to every grey face that would take it, and kept it burning through every night there was. And now she held it up in the morning and you could hardly see it for the sun, and she was so glad that she laughed out loud.

That’s what it was for, she thought. All along. It was for keeping until this.

The Queen was there, once more.

Wren saw her. She did not think anybody else did. Away at the edge of the summit, past the last of the standing stones, where the rock fell away into the morning, there was a shadow on the snow. Only a shadow: tall and thin, the shape of a woman, lying long across the white where there was nothing to cast it. It was very faint. The sun was shining straight through it.

And as Wren watched, the sun went on rising. Higher, and higher, up into that deep blue sky; and the shadow got shorter. It drew in on itself, the way shadows do when the sun climbs, smaller and paler and thinner, a shadow at noon, a little dark smudge on the snow at the foot of nothing.

And then there was no noon left for her to be a shadow in.

Because the light was everywhere. It was on every side of everything at once; and a shadow needs somewhere the light isn’t. And there was nowhere, any more, that the light was not.

Wren looked at the place where the smudge had been. There was only snow there, white and shining.

She did not look again.

Somebody was coming down the far side of the mountain-top.

Not up from the road, where the Gathering had come. From the other side. From the north, where the summit sloped away gently into a long white shoulder of snow, and there was no road at all. A little group of people, walking up out of the sunlight, the way Ash must have come; and they were all of them dressed in plain clothes, and none of them carried anything; and Wren did not know any of them.

They came into the ring of stones, and the Gathering made room for them.

One of them was a young man. He was not tall, and not handsome, particularly. He had ordinary brown hair, and an ordinary brown face, and brown eyes, and he wore a plain green coat, the green of new leaves, like a farmer’s son on his way to market. He was looking about him at the sun, and the snow, and the colours, and the people, the way you look at things when you have just woken up from a long sleep and the world is new; and his face was the happiest face Wren had ever seen.

He saw her.

And he stopped. And he came across the snow to her, quite slowly, and stood in front of her. And then he bowed. Right down, low, the way people bow in stories to a queen.

Wren stared at him. She did not know him. She had never seen him before in her life.

And then she did.

It was the eyes. Just brown. An old man’s tired brown eyes, in a tower at the top of the world, opening for the first time in three hundred years. Only they were not tired now, and they were not old.

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out.

The young man straightened up. He smiled at her — a small, shy, astonished smile, like a dry leaf turning over in the sun and finding that it is green.

Nobody said his name.

Behind him, by the fire, the man in the plain brown coat had picked up the crown again: the empty circle of gold, with no fire in it now, nothing but gold, plain and warm and shining in the sun. He turned it over once in his scarred hands. Then he held it out — not to Wren, but past her, to the young man.

And the young man took it, and held it, and looked at it for a long time. And did not put it on.

He hung it carefully over the hook of Ash’s pole, where Tobin was holding it upright in the snow beside him — the way you hang a lamp-ring on a lamplighter’s pole, to carry it to the next lamp — and stood back. And it hung there in the morning, a plain gold ring, catching the sun.

“There,” said the young man. It was the first word he had said. His voice was quite ordinary. “That’s where it goes.”

And then, because she could not think of anything else to do, and because the sun was on her face, and because it was morning — really, truly morning, for the first time in three hundred years — Wren began to cry all over again.

She had been wrong, you see. There was plenty left.

fields.title: The Colours
fields.body_html:
Nobody on the top of the Bright Mountain did anything sensible for a long time that morning, and nobody minded.

They walked about. That was mostly what they did. They walked about in the sun, on the snow, among the old standing stones, looking at things. They looked at their hands. They looked at each other’s faces. They looked at the sky, which was blue — and kept being blue, every time they looked back up at it, as if it might have changed its mind — and at the land spread out below the mountain in every direction, all the way to the edge of the world, shining. People kept stopping in the middle of what they were saying, and pointing, and saying, “Look — look at that,” and the person they were saying it to would look, and say, “Oh,” and then point at something else.

And they named the colours.

It started with the Highlanders. A big old shepherd from the moors above Harrowgate, with a crook and two dogs and a plaid round his shoulders, stood at the eastern edge of the summit looking down at the hills below, and suddenly he took his cap off and said in a great booming voice, “That’s the heather!” — and everybody turned round. And there it was, away down below on the lower slopes, mile after mile of it: the moor that had been grey all their lives, the grey bracken and the grey heather, purple. Purple and rust and soft bright green, rolling away into the distance like the sea.

“Purple,” said the old shepherd. His face was wet. “My granny told me. She said her granny said. Purple. I never believed her. I thought it was a word for old wives.” He turned round to the man next to him and took him by the lapels. “It’s purple,” he said, and shook him.

And after that everybody was doing it.

The Delvers named everything.

They had never seen colours at all, any of them. They had lived their whole lives under the ground in the Deep, by the pale light of glowstones, and before that their parents had, and their parents’ parents, back three hundred years; and Mira had told them, once, a long time ago, that the world up here was full of colours, and they had nodded politely and not known what she meant. Now they knew. And they went round the top of the Bright Mountain in a little crowd, pointing at things and arguing about them in loud deep voices, and asking Mira what everything was called.

“Blue,” said Mira. “That’s the sky. And that’s blue too, the sea, but a different one. And that’s — that’s green. No, that’s green as well. There’s lots of green. Don’t ask me why.”

“And this?” said Gorrim, holding up his own hand.

“Brown,” said Mira.

“And this?” Mother Hessa, holding up a corner of her shawl.

“That’s red. Sort of. Dark red.”

“And this?” said Tavi, holding up Cinder, who had come to see what the fuss was about and did not care for being held up.

“Orange,” said Mira. “Well. Red and orange. And gold on the end. And black on her feet, look. And—“ She stopped, and looked at the fox, and began to laugh. “She’s all of them,” she said. “Isn’t she? She’s every one.”

“And that?” said a small Delver child on Gorrim’s shoulders, pointing straight up at the sun.

Mira looked up at it. She had to shade her eyes.

“That’s gold,” she said. Her voice had gone soft. “That’s gold. Real gold. I thought I’d seen it before. In the lamp, and in the Ring, and in the Flame. And I had, sort of. But that was only—“ She swallowed. “That was only the start of it. That’s gold.”

Posy Hesketh, who was five, and had come all the way from Stallbridge in the back of a cart with a candle in a jam-jar, held tight to her father’s hand and looked about her at everything with a very serious face. And when Will Hesketh bent down and asked her which colour she liked best, she thought about it for a long time.

“The green one,” said Posy at last, firmly.

“Which green one, pet? There’s ever so many.”

Posy pointed. Down the mountain, far away, at nothing in particular. At all of it.

“That green one,” she said.

And then there was breakfast.

Wren never knew afterwards where it came from. Nobody did. There was the basket at the Lampwright’s feet, with a cloth over it, and it was not a big basket. It was the sort of basket you might take to market to bring home a loaf and a few eggs. And there were, by then, on the top of the Bright Mountain, more people than Tobin could count, and Tobin had tried again, and had given up again, somewhere after four thousand.

But the Lampwright sat down on his stone by the fire, and took the cloth off the basket, and began to make toast.

He made it on a long forked stick, the way he had made it on the Hill of Cinders, holding the bread out to the flames and turning it slowly; and he made it as if he had all the time in the world, and nobody waiting. He was humming. And when the first piece was done, he held it up and looked at it, and it was burnt. Quite black, on one side, and smoking.

“Ah,” said the Lampwright. “Well.”

He looked across the fire at Wren, and his eyes were full of laughter. And he ate it himself.

Wren laughed so hard that she had to sit down in the snow.

And then he made the next piece, and that one was perfect, golden-brown all over and crisp at the edges, and he gave it to her. And then he made another, and gave it to Tobin. And another, for Mira. And then he handed the stick to Old Ash, and took out of the basket another loaf, and another stick, and gave those to Aren; and then another to Sister Hale; and then another to Mairi Dunlop; and the bread kept coming out of the basket, and the sticks kept being handed along, and there were apples in there too, it turned out, and a great deal of butter; and in a little while there were fires all over the top of the Bright Mountain — little fires, lit from the big one, burning on the bare rock in the snow — and people sitting round every one of them, toasting bread and roasting apples and passing them along, and burning their fingers, and laughing.

And the basket never seemed to get any emptier. Wren looked into it once, when nobody was watching. There were three loaves in it. There were always three loaves in it.

She did not look again. She did not need to.

Old Ash made the tea.

Nobody asked him to. Wren thought afterwards that perhaps nobody would have dared. He produced a battered tin kettle from somewhere inside his long blue coat — it was the same kettle; she knew it at once, by the dent in the spout — and filled it with snow, and set it on the edge of the big fire; and while it boiled he went about the summit borrowing mugs and cups and jam-jars and Delver drinking-horns from whoever had them, and came back with an armful. And then he made tea.

It was dreadful.

It was exactly as dreadful as it had always been. It was dark brown and bitter and stewed and smoky, and there were bits in it, and it tasted the way the inside of a chimney smells. Wren took one mouthful and nearly choked, and Tobin’s face went through several different expressions one after another and settled, heroically, on none at all, and Mira said “Oh,” in a small voice and put hers down very carefully on a rock where it would not be in anybody’s way.

Ash poured a cup for the Lampwright last of all, and handed it to him across the fire, without a word.

The Lampwright took it. He looked into it. He blew on it.

And then he drank the whole thing straight down, every drop, without stopping, and put the cup down on his knee, and sighed, the way you sigh after a long cold walk when somebody hands you something hot.

“That,” he said, “is very good tea, Ash.”

Old Ash looked at him for a long moment, from under his great white eyebrows.

“Hm,” he said.

And he looked so pleased — so enormously, ridiculously, shyly pleased, like a boy who has been told his drawing is the best in the class — and he tried so hard not to look pleased, and failed so completely, that Wren laughed until she cried. She lay back in the snow with her mug of dreadful tea held up out of the way and laughed and laughed, until her stomach hurt and the tears ran down into her ears; and every time she thought she had stopped she looked at Ash’s face and started again.

“Hm,” said Ash, crossly, which only made it worse.

It was after breakfast that Linnet sang.

She had been quiet all morning. She had sat by the fire with Tam, on a folded blanket, close beside Wren, with the sun on her face and her eyes half shut; and something had been happening to her, slowly, all through the morning, that Wren had watched without saying anything about it. Since the Hall of Sleepers, her mother had been slow, and shaky, and pale. She had got tired quickly. Her hands had trembled when she held anything up for long, and her voice had been thin. She was like a lamp, Wren had thought, that has been lit, but has not warmed through yet.

Now, in the sun, she was warming through.

You could see it. The colour was coming back into her face, the way it had come back into Cinder’s fur, from the inside out: her lips, and her cheeks, and her brown hands. Her eyes were bright. Her shoulders had come down from round her ears. And when she laughed at Ash’s tea, she laughed out loud — properly, all the way down — and Wren turned round and stared at her. Because it was her own laugh. Exactly. The same laugh that came out of Wren herself when she was not expecting it: sudden and loud and a little bit rude, like a door banging. She had not known that you could get a laugh from somebody. She had thought it was just hers.

Linnet saw her staring, and stopped laughing, and went pink. And then laughed again.

And then, a little while later, when people had finished eating and were sitting about in the sun on the top of the Bright Mountain with their hands round their mugs, she began to sing.

She did not stand up, or make any fuss about it. She only sat there by the fire, with her shoulder against Wren’s, and began, very softly, the way you sing to a child at bedtime when you think they are almost asleep.

Morning comes, morning comes,
and the dark shall not keep us —

Wren went very still.

All around them, people stopped talking. Not all at once. It went out from the fire in a ring, the way a ripple goes out when you drop a stone in a pond: the people nearest went quiet first, and then the people beyond them turned round to see why, and went quiet too; and then the next, and the next, until the whole top of the mountain was listening.

And Linnet came to the place where it always stopped.

Wren held her breath. She did not mean to. She had come to that place so many times herself, on so many rooftops, in so many dark places, that her whole body knew it was coming; and every time, before, there had been nothing on the other side of it. A hole. A drop. The end of a stair with no more steps.

Linnet took a breath, and went on.

And on the other side of the fire, the Lampwright looked up from his cup and began to sing with her.

His voice was low and warm and unhurried. It was the voice from the dark, on the road north, humming, so far away that she had thought she dreamed it. It went under Linnet’s voice like the ground under a path; and the two of them sang together, the small sharp-chinned woman and the plain man in the brown coat, as if they had sung it together a great many times before.

And then Old Ash was singing too, in a deep cracked rumble like a cart going over cobbles. And Aren, very quietly, who had remembered it after all. And Sister Hale, in her old strong voice that had held up the Remnant for seventy years. And then the people round the next fire. And the next. All the Remnant, who had known the beginning of it all their lives, and had always stopped where Wren stopped, and now went on — and all the people who had never heard it at all, and picked it up as they went, the way you do with a good tune. Until the whole of the top of the Bright Mountain was singing it, thousands of voices, in the sun:

Morning comes, morning comes,
and the dark shall not keep us;
for the one who went under
has woken, has woken,
and down from the mountain
he comes with the fire,
and the grey shall go golden,
and the cold shall go home.
Hush now, my wren, my own, hush now —
morning comes.

Then it was quiet.

Wren sat by the fire with her knees pulled up to her chin, and did not say anything for a long time.

My wren.

Everybody else had sung my dear. She had heard them. Sister Hale and Ash and all the Remnant, and the thousands of people who had picked it up as they went along: Hush now, my dear, my own. That was how the old wall-song went. That was how the Lamplighters had always sung it, on the walls, to their children, for longer than anyone could remember.

Only her mother had sung my wren.

And the Lampwright. Wren had heard him. Under Linnet’s voice, low and warm, on the other side of the fire, he had sung my wren, too.

She turned round and looked at her mother.

“You changed it,” she said.

Linnet looked at her. Her eyes were wet.

“When you were born,” she said. “The first night. I was holding you, and singing it, the way my mother sang it to me; and I came to that bit, and I looked down at you. And you were so small, and so brown, and so cross about everything. Like a little bird in a hedge, shouting.” She laughed, unsteadily. “So I sang my wren. Instead. And your da said, that’s her name, then. And it was.”

Wren could not say anything.

She understood it then. Sitting there by the fire on the top of the Bright Mountain, in the first morning, with the sun on her face. She understood what it was she had been carrying, all her life. On chimney-pots and in coal-holes, in the Black Stair and the Glowstone Market and the Hall of Sleepers: two lines of a tune, that stopped. She had always thought it was a scrap. A piece of something lost. The last little bit of her mother left over, that she had held on to because there was nothing else.

It had not been a scrap. It had never been a scrap.

It was a promise. Morning comes. That was all it had ever said, all those years, every time she hummed it in the dark. Not morning might come, or morning used to come, or morning would be nice. Morning comes. And it had been true the whole time. Every single time she had sung it, it had been true; she just had not got to the end of it yet.

And now she had. And it had her name in it.

Tam Ashby mended her boots that afternoon.

He did not ask. He just noticed. He was sitting by the fire with his long legs stretched out in front of him and the sun on his freckles, looking at nothing; and his eyes fell on Wren’s feet. And Wren’s boots were the same boots she had been wearing since Soot Lane — a year and a half, and the whole width of Gloamhaven, and the Black Stair and the Burned Country and the Sunless Sea — and they were not so much boots, by then, as two sets of holes held together by string.

“Give us those,” said Tam.

Wren looked at him.

“Go on,” said her father. “Give them here. I can’t look at them. They’re hurting my eyes.”

So she took them off and gave them to him, and sat in the sun with her bare feet in a blanket; and Tam Ashby took a needle and some waxed thread and a strip of leather out of the pocket of a borrowed coat — Wren never knew where he got them; she supposed lamp-menders just had things like that about them, the way sweeps had soot — and he bent his big sandy head over her boots and began to mend them.

He took a long time. He did it very carefully, with his big gentle lamp-mender’s hands, stitch by stitch, humming under his breath. Every so often he held one up to the light and frowned at it and said “Hm,” exactly the way Ash said it; and once he said, “Who taught you to tie a knot like this, then?” in a voice of deep disgust, and Wren said, “Nobody,” and he said, “I can tell.”

And Wren sat beside him and watched him do it.

She did not say anything. Nor did he. But somewhere in that long quiet afternoon, with the sun on them both and the needle going in and out, something that had been stiff and shy and strange between them since the Hall of Sleepers went soft, and came right, the way a knot comes right when somebody who knows how to tie them takes it in hand.

When he gave her the boots back, they were better than new. She put them on, and stood up, and walked about in them, and they did not let in the snow.

“Da,” she said, and it came out not shy at all.

“There,” said Tam Ashby, and looked enormously pleased, and blew his nose.

Linnet cut her hair.

That was later still, towards evening, when the sun was going down in the west for the first time — going down golden, in a great slow blaze of red and orange and colours that had no names, so that everybody on the mountain stopped again to look, and some of them cried, because they had not known a sunset could be anything but grey either.

Linnet looked at Wren’s hair in that light, and made a face.

“Who’s been at this?” she said.

Wren put her hand up to it. It was short and black and stuck out all over the place, the way it always had. “Me,” she said. “With a knife. When it gets in my eyes. Up on the roofs.”

“With a knife,” said her mother.

“Well — yes.”

Linnet looked at her a moment longer. Then she held out her hand to Aren, who was sitting nearby, and Aren, without a word, took the little knife out of his belt and handed it to her, handle first.

“Sit down, then,” said Linnet. “In front of me. No, this way, where I can see. Still.” She put her hand on the top of Wren’s head and turned it, firmly, the way you turn a pot on a wheel. “We’ll do it with a knife, then,” she said. “The way you always did, I expect.”

And Wren laughed.

She laughed out loud — sudden and loud and a little bit rude, like a door banging — and behind her, her mother laughed too, exactly the same, so that for a moment you could not have told which was which. And then Linnet said “Still,” again, very sternly, and began to cut.

She did it properly. Wren could tell. Short, the way Wren liked it, but even, all the way round, so that it did not stick out any more except at the very front, where it always would; and her mother’s fingers were quick and light and certain on the back of her neck. When it was done, Linnet ran her hand once over the top of Wren’s head, the way you smooth a bird’s feathers.

“There,” she said softly. “There’s my wren.”

That night — the first night, the first real night after the first real day, with the stars coming out over the Bright Mountain one after another, more of them than anybody had ever seen, so many that the sky looked dusty with them — they sat round the big fire, the old company and one more, the way they had sat round the fire on the Greywaste a year and a half ago.

Wren, with her new boots and her new hair, between her mother and her father. Tobin, with Ash’s pole across his knees and the gold ring hanging from its hook, and his father asleep in a blanket beside him. Mira, with the Chronicle in her lap, not reading it, only holding it. Aren, quiet. Cinder, asleep in a heap in the warm ash at the edge of the fire, with her tail curled over her nose, glowing.

And Old Ash, on a stone, with a mug of his own dreadful tea, on two good legs.

And on the other side of the fire, the Lampwright, with his hands held out to the warmth.

All over the top of the mountain, and down its sides, and away across the land below as far as the eye could see, the lights were burning. Hundreds of them. Thousands. Little fires and lamps and candles, every one with somebody beside it. They did not need them any more, Wren supposed. Not really. The morning had come, and it would come again tomorrow, and the day after, and every day; the sun would rise golden, and the grey would not come back. But people had lit them anyway, that first night. Out of habit, maybe. Or out of something else. Because it was good to sit by a light with the people you loved, even when the dark was not frightening any more. Even when it was only the night.

Tobin was looking at the Lampwright.

Wren saw him do it. He was looking at him across the fire with his head a little on one side, the way he looked at the Orrery when something on it was not working the way he had expected. And she saw his mouth open, just a little, as if a question were coming up out of him that he had asked a long time ago, in the Leaning Tower, with Cinder’s chin on Ash’s boot. The Lampwright. The man in the story. Could he come back?

Old Ash had said “Hm,” that night, and looked at the lamp for a long time.

Tobin’s mouth stayed open for a moment. Then he shut it again, and pushed his spectacles up his nose, and smiled to himself; and did not ask.

He did not need to.

fields.title: Home Is Where the Light Is
fields.body_html:
They came down off the Bright Mountain in the morning, all of them together, in the sun.

It was not at all like going up. Going up had been the longest road Wren had ever walked, in the dark and the snow and the cold, with the crown like a sack of coal against her chest. Coming down was like running downhill in a dream. The snow was white and soft and squeaked under her mended boots, and the sky was so blue that you kept stopping to look at it, and the waystones stood by the road all the way down with their little flames still burning in them — you could hardly see the flames now, in the sun; only a faint shimmer in each niche, like heat over a summer road — and the whole wide shining land was spread out below them, waiting.

And the Lampwright came down with them.

That was the thing. That was the thing that was different from every other time. On the Hill of Cinders, after the breakfast fire, he had gone: there one moment, and then only the warm wind and the empty stone. And in Emberwick, at the Beacon, a warm hand on her shoulder and then nobody. And in the market, with the bread. Every time, he had come, and then he had gone, and they had had to go on without him and carry the light until he came again.

He did not go this time.

He walked down the Bright Mountain at the front of them all, in his plain brown coat, with his basket on his arm and Cinder trotting at his heels; and at the bottom he did not stop. He walked on, out onto the Greywaste, that was not grey any more, and the colour ran out ahead of him across the land wherever he went, the way it always had — only now there was hardly any grey left for it to run into, and it was more like watching the sun come out on a field that is already green.

And the Gathering went home.

It took a long time, and it went in every direction at once, the way a crowd goes home after a fair: in little knots and long straggling lines, by every road, south and east and west across the shining land, waving and calling and turning round to wave again. People who had walked north through the Long Night with a flame cupped in their two hands walked home again with their hands in their pockets, in the sun, whistling.

The Delvers went back to the Black Stair — but only to fetch their things, Gorrim said, gravely. They were not going to live under the ground any more. Not now. Not when there was all this. He waved his great hand at the sky as if it were something he had made himself. They were going to build, he said, up on the hills above the Stair, in the open; with windows. Large ones. Mother Hessa said she would believe it when she saw it, and that she was going to need a hat. Tavi said he was going to be the first Delver ever to climb a tree, and very nearly was, before they had even left the Mountain, and had to be got down.

Mira went with them, for a while. She would come back, she said. She had a great many things to tell Wren and Tobin about, and a great many things to look at first, and she could not look at all of them at once, though she was going to try.

Sister Hale went home to the Remnant’s camp on the Greywaste on the back of a farm-cart, with her brass-mended crutch across her knees and her bonnet over one ear and her face turned up to the sun, singing. She had waited seventy years, she said, and she was not going to waste a minute more of it indoors, duck, thank you very much.

Mairi Dunlop and Jory Penhallow went back to Skerrow, and the Brave Gannet, and the sea — the real sea, the green one, with gulls on it. Jory was going to crew for her, he said, until he could get a boat of his own. Mairi said he would crew for her until she said so and not a day sooner, and that he would make a passable sailor in about forty years, and boxed his ear, and put her arm round his shoulders.

The Drowned Fleet sailed home with them. Three hundred years late; but home.

And Snib and his Gutterlings, who were not staying, stayed.

Nobody quite knew how it happened. They were going to go straight back down their drains, Snib said, the moment they were off the Mountain; they did not hold with all this sun, which was bad for the eyes, and the complexion, and gave you freckles. And then they got off the Mountain, and stood in the sun on the edge of the Greywaste for a bit, scowling at it. And then one of them took off his boots. And then another one sat down in the grass. And by the evening every Gutterling in the whole troop was lying flat on his back in a meadow full of yellow flowers, with his arms flung out and his eyes shut and the sun on his face, and Snib in the middle of them, snoring.

“Don’t want no fuss,” he said, when Wren went to say goodbye, without opening his eyes.

“Course not,” said Wren.

Old Ash went with the Lampwright.

Wren had thought he might. She had seen the two of them walking together down the Mountain, side by side, the tall old man in blue and the plain man in brown, not saying much; and every so often the Lampwright would say something, quietly, and Ash would say “Hm,” and they would both laugh. And she had known.

He did not go far, though. Not at first. He walked with them all the way south across the Greywaste, a week of golden days, to the Grey Gate of Emberwick — which was not grey any more, it turned out, but a warm red sandstone that nobody had seen the colour of for three hundred years — and he stood there in the gateway on his two good legs, looking at the wall.

“Hm,” he said. “Somebody’ll want to see to those lamps.”

“I will,” said Aren.

Ash looked at him.

“I’ll see to them,” said Aren again, quietly. “All of them. The whole Ring. If you’ll let me.”

“Hm,” said Old Ash. He looked at Aren for a long time. Then he put his hand into the pocket of his long blue coat and took out a key — a big old iron key, rusty and worn — and held it out. “The Leaning Tower,” he said. “Mind the stair. Third step from the top’s rotten. Always has been.” He paused. “And the tea’s in the tin with the dent in it.”

Aren took the key. His hand was shaking.

“Master Lamplighter of Emberwick,” said Old Ash. “Hm. They’ll have to put up with you, lad. Somebody has to.”

Emberwick came out to meet them.

The whole city. It came pouring out of the Grey Gate and down the road towards them, all of it at once, the way the colour had poured down the Mountain: the Low Quarter and the Hill and everybody in between, shouting and laughing and running, so that you could not tell for a while who was meeting whom.

Bracken was there, in his helmet, which somebody had polished till it shone gold in the sun, and which he was very proud of. He had kept the Beacon burning through the whole of the Long Night, he said, three days without sleeping, and not one lamp in the Ring had gone out, not one; and then he said it again, in case anybody had missed it, and then he sat down very suddenly on a mounting-block and went to sleep.

Gristle Mott was there, wheezing, red in the face, with an armful of things he had been saving for Wren — a scarf, three pies, a pair of boots two sizes too big, a brush with a new handle — and he pushed all of them at her at once, and then stood back looking embarrassed, and then pushed the pies at her again in case she had not noticed them.

Mrs Fenn was there, and the whole of the bakery, and all the Fenn children in a row.

And Nettle was there.

Nettle came down the road like a cannonball, with her crab in her fist — it was a very old crab by now, and had seen a good deal of the world — and her hair flying and her mouth open, shrieking; and she hit Wren just about where Wren had hit Old Ash on the Mountain, and with about as much force. And then she let go, and held the crab up in front of Wren’s face, and said, “Did it work? Did he bring luck? Did you win?”

“Yes,” said Wren. “Yes. He did. He was brilliant.”

Nettle looked at the crab with enormous satisfaction, and put it back in her pocket.

Prowle was there too, at the end.

He had come south with the Gathering in the back of a Highland farm-cart, wrapped in a blanket, and had said hardly a word the whole way; and somewhere on the road he had got off the cart and walked into Emberwick ahead of them all, by himself, without telling anyone. And when Wren came through the Grey Gate, the first thing she saw was a small stout man in a crumpled coat with no gold chain on it, standing on an upturned crate in the middle of Gate Street with a barrel of oil beside him and a ladle in his hand, filling people’s lamps.

For nothing.

“It’s very bad business,” Prowle was saying to everybody who came by, in a high aggrieved voice, as he filled their lamps. “Very bad business. Ruinous. The Guild will never recover. Hold it still, madam, you’re spilling it. Utterly ruinous. Next!” He ladled oil into a lamp held up by a small boy, and scowled at him. “No, no charge. No charge. I said. Don’t argue with me, child, I’m a very important man. Next!”

He saw Wren. He went red. He looked away. Then he looked back.

“They don’t even need it,” he said to her, in a sort of wail. “Not really. Not with the sun. Not any more. Nobody needs lamp-oil in the daytime.” He ladled some more into somebody’s lamp. “But they keep coming,” said Prowle helplessly. “And I keep giving it them. And I can’t seem to stop.”

Wren looked at him for a moment. And then — though she could hardly believe it of herself — she grinned at him.

“Next!” said Prowle, crossly, and blew his nose.

Tobin went home with his father.

They walked up the Hill together, the two of them, through the gates of the First Ring, which were standing open, and up the long road between the tall houses to the Warden’s Hall. Lord Edric was very thin still, and very white, and leaned on Tobin’s arm; and Tobin had Ash’s pole in his other hand, with the gold ring hanging from its hook. They walked slowly. They were talking. Wren, coming up behind with her parents, could not hear about what. But she could see that it was Tobin talking, and his father listening, all the way up the hill; and Tobin’s free hand was waving about in the air as he explained something, the way it always did; and his father did not interrupt him once.

The great black doors of the Warden’s Hall were shut, when they got there. They had always been shut. They were the biggest doors in Emberwick, iron-bound and heavy, with the Harrowgate crest on them, and Wren had never once in her life seen them open.

Lord Edric stood and looked at them for a long time.

Then he sent for a carpenter, and had them taken off their hinges.

He did not have them mended, or replaced, or painted. He had them carried round the back of the Hall and stacked against a wall, and he left the doorway standing open, empty, with the sun going straight in down the long hall to the far end; and he never had doors put on it again, as long as he was Warden. Anybody who wanted to could walk in. And a great many people did — to complain about the drains, mostly, or to ask about the price of bread, or just to look at the Orrery, which Tobin had brought down from the attic and set up in the front hall on a table of its own, where it ticked, and where every bead in all of Emberwick glowed gold, and some that were not in Emberwick at all.

Mira came back at midsummer, as she had said she would, with the Chronicle under her arm.

They sat on the wall together, the three of them, on top of the Grey Gate, in the sun, with their legs hanging over: Wren and Tobin and Mira, the way they had sat on so many walls. Cinder lay on the warm stone between them, with her chin on her paws, watching a butterfly. Below them, the green land went away to the edge of the world. And away to the north, if you looked, there was a mountain on the horizon: not a faint pale tooth, any more, that the grown-ups said was only cloud, but a mountain, white and blue and shining, as clear as if you could reach out and touch it.

Mira opened the Chronicle on her knee.

It was very old. It had come all the way from behind the iron door in the Workshop on the Hill of Cinders. It was full, almost to the end, of writing: first in a clear, strong, unhurried hand, and then in another, small and cramped and shaking at first and steadier later — the whole long story of Gloamhaven, from before the bargain; all of it written down. Only at the very back were there pages that were blank. Clean white pages, a great many of them, waiting.

Mira took a pen out of her pocket. She held it over the first blank page for a long time.

“What are you going to write?” said Tobin.

“I don’t know,” said Mira. “Everything. All of it.” She looked at the page. “I don’t know where to start.”

“At the beginning,” said Wren. “Where else?”

Mira looked at her. Then she smiled, and bent her head over the Chronicle, and began to write; and Wren, leaning over her shoulder, read the first line as it came, slow and careful and new, in the sun:

In the last days of the long grey, a sweep found a lamp in a chimney…

Tobin had his mother’s compass in his hand.

He had taken it out without thinking, the way he did. He clicked the lid open. And there, inside, round the edge of the face, were the old engraved letters that had been there all his life, that he had read a thousand times: Home is where the light is.

And the needle was turning.

It was not pointing anywhere. Not north, to the Mountain. Not east, to the sea. Not anywhere at all. It was turning, slowly, gently, all the way round the face of the compass, and on round again; not wildly, the way a compass spins when something is wrong with it, but easily, calmly, as if it had all the time in the world. As if every way it pointed were the right way. As if there were nowhere, any more, that it could point and be wrong.

Tobin looked at it for a long time.

“Oh,” he said softly. “Oh. I see.”

“What?” said Mira.

He showed them. The needle went on turning, round and round, in the sun.

“It’s not broken,” said Tobin. His voice was not quite steady. “It’s — Wren, it’s not broken. It always pointed to where the light was. To the lamp. To the Hill. To the Spire, when he was there in the dark. To the Mountain. Always to where the light was, because that was home. That’s what it says. That’s what she put on it.” He touched the glass. “And now it’s — everywhere. The light’s everywhere. So it’s—“

“So home’s everywhere,” said Mira.

“Yes,” said Tobin. He shut the compass, and held it in his scarred hand, and looked out over the shining country, all the way to the white Mountain. “Yes. That’s it. That’s what she meant.” He pushed his spectacles up his nose. “I think she knew,” he said. “I think she always knew.”

And that is very nearly the end.

I said, a long time ago, at the beginning, that it was noon in Emberwick and you would never have known it. Well: it is noon in Emberwick now, as I finish, and you would know it. You would know it from a mile away. The sun is high and gold and warm over the chimneys of the city, and the canals are blue and green and silver, and every roof in the Low Quarter is a different colour — red and brown and slate-blue and mossy green — and the sky is the colour of the sky.

And high on the roof of Thornbury House, where it all began, a girl is sitting astride a chimney-pot, eating a crust, with the sun on her face.

She is thirteen now, or near enough; her mother has told her the exact day, and she has decided she likes it. Her hair is short and black and cut properly, except at the front, where it sticks out, and always will. Her boots are mended. There is a faded red ribbon round her left wrist. There is a fox beside her on the warm slates, red and russet and gold, with her tail curled round her feet and her eyes half shut, watching the swallows. And there is a little brass lamp in the girl’s coat pocket, burning gold, as it always has; though you would hardly see it, now, in all that sun.

She is not glaring at the sun. She has stopped doing that. She is only sitting there, with her face turned up to it and her eyes shut, the way you sit in front of a fire when you have come in from a long way off.

And below her, in Soot Lane, where the house with the green door is, a woman is singing. A small, sharp-chinned, black-haired woman, hanging out washing — because there is sun to dry it now, and a great deal of washing to catch up on — and singing an old song while she does it, all the way to the end. And at a bench in the open doorway, a big freckled sandy-haired man is mending a lamp, very slowly and carefully, with his tongue between his teeth, and humming along. Every so often the woman looks up at the roof of Thornbury House, just to see. And the girl on the chimney-pot opens one eye, and waves.

He is there yet, I am told: the Lampwright.

He did not go back up the Mountain. He walked down it, and through the towns, and along the roads, and he is walking them still, with his basket on his arm, and an old man in blue beside him who says “Hm.” He mends things. He makes breakfast. He burns the first piece of toast. I have not seen him myself, not as Wren saw him; but I know people who have, and they say he has not changed at all, and that he still calls everyone by their name. You will find him if you look. I am quite sure of that. People generally do.

The story goes on, of course. Stories like this one always do. There is a great deal more of it than could ever be put in a book — more than Mira will ever get into the Chronicle, though she is trying, and has filled forty pages already and is asking for more. There are the Delvers and their windows. There is Tobin, who is going to build a lighthouse at Skerrow that works by clockwork, and has drawn it nine times. There is Nettle, who has decided to be a sweep. There is Pim, and the Pellows, and the blue-doored house at Lantern Steps, which is not too quiet any more. And there is Wren, who is thirteen, and has a great deal of her life left to live, all of it in the sun.

But this is the end of the part that I can tell you.

So I will leave them there: on the walls, and on the roofs, and in the open doorways, in the light. And I will tell you only one thing more, which is the thing the song says, and which Wren knew, without knowing she knew it, every night of her life, on every chimney-pot in Emberwick, in the long grey dark.

It is not the night that has the last word.

Morning comes.
